#5507. Ohio Becomes the Epicenter of Data Center Backlash After Tax Credits Cost State’s Schools $374 Million

Angela Huffman, a sixth-generation farmer, spent 15 years in agriculture policy in Columbus, OH, and Washington, DC. But her focus lately has been 10 miles from her Wharton, OH, sheep farm.

On June 4, Huffman picked up her local newspaper, the Daily Chief-Union. The above-the-fold headline revealed a developer was eyeing a $900 million data center in nearby Upper Sandusky.

The headline "stopped me cold," Huffman says. The proposal would have planted a 146-acre Smartland Energy data center campus, with a natural gas power plant, on the north edge of town.

"We were already worried about a big development coming in and extracting the town's resources," Huffman tells Realtor.com®. Townsfolk were already concerned after another recent proposal for a soybean processing plant.

"What does that do to the community?" she says.

Huffman, CEO of Farm Action, says her family has owned its nearby farm for six generations. Organizing concerned neighbors, they began filling planning commission meetings and peppering officials with questions about the impact of the development. They also questioned if it should be approved on industrial zoning, as neighbors had hoped. A petition opposing the project drew 1,100 signatures.

Many residents worried about how such a major project could change their rural way of life. And Upper Sandusky wasn't alone.

Ohio was the heart of data center resistance in the midterms. Voters in 18 of its 88 counties backed 21 bans or restrictions on development of those projects. One of those was in Upper Sandusky, where voters approved a charter amendment blocking large data centers within the limits of the 6,600-person town.

"They wanted to use about a third of the water the whole town uses today," Huffman says. "I'm not against AI or development, but can a town of this size absorb a development like that?"

But the state already hosts dozens of large centers. And they already exact a cost.

A new study shows that the state's data center tax break derived its schools of almost $374 million in revenue in 2025 alone.

Republican Gov. Mike DeWine paused the tax breaks in May after the state realized developers were exempted from $2.1 billion in taxes in 2024 and 2025, far more than initally projected. Gov.-elect Amy Acton has promised further scrutiny.

Good Jobs First and Policy Matters Ohio studied where those missing tax dollars would have gone. The state's Fair School Funding Plan allocates some sales tax to schools. So by exempting data center developers from the 5.75% sales tax, those schools missed out on revenue.

“Ohio lawmakers made a choice to give data center companies a blank check, and now Ohio’s schools are paying the price,” said Hannah Halbert, Policy Matters Ohio’s executive director. “In 2025 alone, the state gave up enough revenue from this single tax break to fully update the Fair School Funding plan and close the gap.”

This comes at a time when homeowners were being asked to make up the difference. Many Ohio schools aimed to raise money through levies this year, but many were unsuccessful. The Ohio Policy Education Institute found just 24 of 66 levies on the May 2026 ballot had passed.

Upper Sandusky's school district was one of the losers—missing out on $383,000 in revenue, according to the report. While voters have approved levies for its schools in 2015, 2018, and 2023, it's still been forced to cancel classes this year because it can't install air conditioning in century-old buildings that are too expensive to rebuild.

"Our schools were struggling," Huffman says. "It tells you a lot about when these big tech companies come along, and if they are paying their fair share."

Voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. NBC exit polls show 76% of voters opposed data center building in their communities, and a majority considered them "crucial" to their votes.

Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs, raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas.

That's despite a major spending spree by the industry. Ohio was barraged with $1.8 million in data center ads in the fall, Pew Research Center found—more than Texas, Wisconsin, and other large states. AI and crypto political action committees spent an estimated $65 million backing Republican Sen. John Husted, who lost reelection to Democrat Sherrod Brown on Nov. 3.

Developers, after all, have big plans in the state, having pitched $168.7 billion in new projects.

Regulation of data center developments and AI could be a major factor for new Democratic leaders in Columbus and Washington, DC. Sober to that reality, tech stocks tanked after the election.

Acton says she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers. She wants to see them cover their utility costs, build with union labor, and abide by environmental standards. She also says she wants to see incentives "reined in" for the large developments.

Artificial intelligence companies have spent the days since the election promising they'll work with cities and residents on data centers. OpenAI published a "blueprint for responsible development" promising to slow the technology.

Meta spokesperson Andy Stone cited a commitment "to pay our own energy and water costs so they're not passed onto consumers, fund new and upgraded grid infrastructure, and support local communities."

Ohio isn't alone, either. Virginia, another data center hot spot, spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. It and other hot spots like California and Texas have also moved to restrict data center developments this year.

A recent study by the Wharton School indicates that data centers have indeed increased industrial electricity prices in the nation. But it also said that residential customers absorbed relatively little of that price gain.

Ohio, in the meantime, has seen its housing situation worsen in the past few years. National Housing Conference data put the state first in the union for how quickly middle-income earners have been priced out. The number of jobs that can afford a typical home at a 10% down payment fell about 41% from 2020 to 2025. Teachers, firefighters, and retail supervisors are among those priced out of median-priced homes.

But data center advocates say the large developments are still necessary in the modern economy.

Dan Diorio, vice president for public policy at the Data Center Coalition, told the Ohio Tax Credit Authority that the developments benefit all people and businesses, not just AI companies.

"This is a far more efficient way of doing all the computing, processing, and storage that we need to facilitate our daily lives in the 21st century economy," Diorio said at the May hearing in Columbus. "The need for connectivity, for the internet, is driving the digital infrastructure that supports that."

#5506. Pending Sales Down Over 16% as 2026 Market Craters

Pending home sales have slowed significantly according to the latest data from the National Association of Realtors® (NAR), sparking questions about the long-term health of the housing market as activity falls to levels seen three decades ago.

NAR’s Pending Home Sales report for October reveals that sales dropped by 4.7% month-over-month, and fell 16.7% on an annual basis. The monthly decrease is not as severe as September’s drop of 7.3%, but pendings are now far below the same point in the housing cycle last year as economists expect an even slower fall and winter market.

“October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said.

Prior to the report’s release, Realtor.com® Senior Economist Hannah Jones expected pending sales to fall, attributing high mortgage rates as the cause.

“Mortgage rates climbed nearly 75 basis points from late August to mid-October, adding roughly $200 a month to the typical mortgage payment on a median-priced home, assuming a 10% down payment. That is more than many already-strained buyers can easily absorb,” she stated.

The latest data from Freddie Mac showed the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 7.11%, down from mid-October’s high around 7.40%. Despite rates reducing, Jones noted that she expects affordability problems to persist.

“Markets now expect that a Fed rate hike is coming in December,” she added. “Until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a downward path, affordability problems are likely to persist, keeping contract signings and home sales subdued.”

Although Jones predicts one final rate hike before the end of the year, Federal Reserve Open Market Committee Chairman Kevin Warsh did not allude to housing or rate hikes in his Nov. 16 remarks. Rather, he honed in on the impact of “superintelligence”—an alternative term for AI preferred by President Donald Trump—on the economy at large.

In line with September’s data, October saw all four regions decline in pending home sales, both monthly and annually.

Western states experienced the greatest drop month-over-month, with a 6.9% decrease. Following the West was the South, Midwest and Northeast at declines of 6.3%, 2.7% and 0.8%, respectively.

Annually, the rankings are the same. The West’s pending home sales fell by 20.3%, South by 18.7%, Midwest by 14% and the Northeast at 11.1%.

On a local level, the report notes that pending home sales fell annually even in the strongest markets. Using data from Realtor.com, NAR highlighted the top 10 strongest markets for pending home sales, and found that they still experienced declines.

The slowing in pending home sales coupled with lackluster homebuilder confidence—which was last reported at a new 14-year low—leaves many questioning whether 2027 will see a turn-around for the housing market, as 2026 will likely end on a low note.

“It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million,” Yun concluded. “Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.”

#5505. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5502. Consumer Groups Request California Officials Investigate Zillow

Several consumer groups have penned a letter to California state officials, requesting an investigation into Zillow’s partnership with Redfin, as well as its referral and mortgage practices.

“We write because the California housing market is broken in ways that leave families suffering dire economic harm—and one of the most aggressive actors in distorting the market, to its own profit and to the detriment of the public, has been Zillow,” the letter reads.

Signed by five consumer-focused advocacy organizations—namely, the Consumer Federation of America, Demand Progress Education Fund, Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, Children’s Advocacy Alliance and Revolving Door Project—the the letter requested officials to investigate Zillow’s agreement with Redfin, and business practices the organization described as “steering.”

This is not the first letter of its kind made calling out the portal, as several consumer groups—also including the Consumer Federation of America—sent a letter to the National Association of Attorneys General back in September requesting investigations into Zillow for similar reasons.

In a statement on the letter, Zillow said its position is “unchanged” from previous challenges, denying any wrongdoing alleged.

The FTC had previously sued both Zillow and Redfin over the two portal’s rental-focused partnership, alleging Zillow effectively paid $100 million (and other benefits) to Redfin to end its advertising customers’ contracts, stop competing in the multifamily advertising market for up to nine years and serve as an “exclusive syndicator” of Zillow listings. That suit, however, has since been settled after the portals agreed to “unwind” some aspects of their partnership, with Redfin set to once again offer its own separate service.

The consumer groups’ Nov. 17 letter described said settlement as “far less than California consumers deserve,” as Zillow said it would maintain some level of partnership with Redfin “through at least 2030.”

“It (Zillow) retains the customer relationships the illegal arrangement produced and continues to benefit from the market consolidation it achieved during its term,” the letter reads. “And Redfin is left to rebuild its competitive position from scratch, in a market where Zillow remains the 800-pound gorilla.”

Zillow said in its statement that its partnership with Redfin “is pro-consumer and procompetitive.”

In terms of the allegations of steering, the letter referred to Zillow’s practice of having its “Contact Agent” buttons direct consumers to Zillow-affiliated agents rather than the listing agent as “deliberate consumer deception.”

“The Zillow Preferred Agent is essentially an interloper paying Zillow to execute a man-in-the-middle attack,” the letter read. “This has triggered class-action litigation that includes RICO claims, alleging that Zillow and the participating brokerages meet the definition of a criminal enterprise.”

This has also been the point of a lawsuit against Zillow, which was later combined with another suit against the portal over its alleged steering to Zillow Home loans through its preferred agents. The combined suit was dismissed back in July, with a judge saying that a “reasonable consumer” would not be deceived by Zillow’s “lead diversion” practices, but the plaintiffs have refiled with hopes to once again reopen the case.

On this suit, Zillow said in a statement that “The court dismissed all of plaintiffs’ claims in July, and the amended complaint simply repackages the same already-rejected theory related to free Zillow Home Loans pre-approval letters.”

The portal also noted that for its premarketed Zillow Preview listings, the “Contact Agent” button leads “directly to the listing agent, free,” and that “any listing agent revenue share is paid by Zillow at no additional cost to consumers or agents.”

“Zillow’s tools are free and optional, and our business relationships are clearly disclosed,” the statement continued.

Also in terms of alleged mortgage business steering, the letter referred to a previous suit from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) against Rocket Homes for similar allegations as are laid against Zillow.

However, this suit was later dropped by the CFPB in 2025 after what the letter described as the Trump administration’s “illegal effort to dismantle the CFPB in 2025.”

The letter also cited several academic studies as evidence for its allegations against Zillow, including a study from Georgetown University Law Center Professor Steven Salop that claimed to show Zillow Home Loan borrowers pay higher rates (that study, notably, was funded by CoStar, one of Zillow’s main competitors).

Zillow previously disputed these findings and alleged Salop relied on “selectively chosen data and inadequate controls to produce a distorted view of Zillow Home Loans.”

The letter requested that the California Department of Real Estate enact its “disciplinary and rulemaking authority” to investigate the alleged instances of steering.

Additionally, the letter requests the officials to bring “enforcement actions for the deceptive ‘Contact Agent’ and ‘Request a Tour’ interfaces, undisclosed Flex commissions, and the failure to disclose that agent recommendations reflect Zillow’s financial interests, not the consumer’s,” and potentially file an antitrust lawsuit.

Lastly, the groups asked that the officials “coordinate with the multistate coalition that brought the Redfin action so that Zillow cannot exploit jurisdictional gaps between state enforcers.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5501. Single-Family Construction Rebounds in November, but Permits Nosedive

Construction of new single-family homes rose a bit in October, but permits fell sharply, the U.S. Census Bureau reported Wednesday.

Single-family housing starts rose 4% last month from September, to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 864,000. On an annual basis, single-family starts were down 3.2% from a year earlier.

The monthly increase comes from upticks in the West and South, while the Northeast saw a larger increase in starts and the Midwest a slight decline. Single-family starts rose 15.7% on the month in Northeast, 4.2% in the South, and 3.4% in the West, but fell 0.8% in the Midwest.

Total privately owned housing starts, including more volatile multifamily units, rose 9.9% from September and 2.8% from October 2025. The month extends the uneven year for housing starts, which after a brief August rebound, then fell sharply in September.

Meanwhile, new building permits in October fell 7.4% month over month and 8.7% year over year to an annualized 1,295,000 units.

At the same time, housing completions increased 6.5% from September but fell 10.4% compared to last year.

Even so, the slowdown of building permits reflects greater pessimism in the housing market for builders. Many of the nation's major homebuilders have reported large year-over-year declines in revenue.

"The challenges facing builders have not subsided, and while there are some glimmers of hope in the housing starts figures, it must be noted that the current pace of single family home starts is still below last year’s actual total," Realtor.com® economist Joel Berner says. "This month’s data is an improvement, but from a very low baseline readout in both September and last October."

This week, the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) plunged to a 14-year low, reflecting the industry's growing pessimism amid high mortgage rates and strained affordability.

Berner says the permits number is the lowest since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic in May 2020. The pullback is clearest in single-family homes, with their 12.9% year-over-year decline. Multifamily homes, which tend to be more volatile, also fell 5.2% month-over-month.

"Builders are dealing with a litany of obstacles to selling homes, whether it’s rising costs of land, labor, and materials, high financing costs, or weak buyer demand," Berner says. "This month’s data shows them slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on."

With mortgage rates above 7%, housing affordability is a major constraint on buyers, says Selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality. Hepp pins that on high rates that keep payments elevated, high construction costs, rising insurance premiums, and elevated property taxes—not to mention everyday bills.

"For housing, the key question is not simply whether mortgage rates decline, but whether they fall enough to meaningfully improve purchasing power and bring more buyers and sellers back to the market," Hepp says. "Until then, I expect activity to remain relatively subdued, making the spring homebuying season an increasingly important test of whether the market can finally turn a corner."

The nation's housing supply shortage is complicated by red tape. American Enterprise Institute tracked 10 state bills passed this year and estimates they could potentially lead to 103,000 new homes a year. But people have to afford those homes.

So, Berner says, the slowdown in construction represents a "step in the wrong direction."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5500. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

#5499. Mortgage Demand Falls 2.3% as Rates Resume Climbing After 4 Weeks of Declines

Mortgage applications fell last week, as interest rates rose to their highest levels in three weeks amid inflation concerns, unease over war in the Middle East, and federal rate hike expectations.

For the week ending Nov. 13 the Mortgage Bankers Association's Market Composite Index—a measure of total mortgage loan application volume—decreased 2.3% on a seasonally adjusted basis from one week earlier.

The Purchase Index, which measures the volume of mortgage applications to purchase a single-family home, decreased 3% from one week earlier after seasonal adjustment. Purchase applications were down 18% from a year ago.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed mortgages with conforming loan balances jumped to 7.31% this week, an increase from last week's rate of 7.21%, according to MBA calculations.

A separate survey from Freddie Mac showed mortgage rates dropped to 7.11% last week from 7.18% the week before, although new data on Thursday is expected to show an uptick.

“Treasury yields rose last week amid data showing inflation accelerated in October and Fed officials acknowledging that additional rate hikes may be needed in the coming months," said MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist, Joel Kan, CMB.

“Purchase applications were down 18% from a year ago, as renewed affordability challenges from elevated mortgage rates have pushed prospective homebuyers to the sidelines," Kan continued.

In recent weeks, high interest rates had pushed more buyers toward riskier adjustable rate mortgages. However, this past week, ARM applications decreased to 10.8% of the total applications, down from 10.9% the previous week as the average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs increased to 6.38% from 6.28%.

The share of FHA loan applications increased to 16.1% from 15.5% the prior week. The VA share of total applications increased to 12.8% from 12.4% the prior week. And the USDA share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5%.

The refinance share of mortgage activity increased to 41.1% from 39.8% the previous week, but was 54% lower than the same week one year ago, as homeowners remain locked into their lower interest rates.

"Overall refinance activity was down over the week, but FHA refinances increased almost 7%," said Kan. "The FHA rate was around 30 basis points below the conforming rate, which supported refinance opportunities for some homeowners.”

Data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics last week revealed that overall prices rose 0.4% in October, surpassing the forecasted 0.2% increase economists expected.

Fed watchers believe that a rate hike is all but certain when Fed Chair Kevin Warsh meets with the Federal Reserve board next month. The odds of a 25-basis-point adjustment have climbed to 95%, according to CME FedWatch.The latest mortgage application data comes in advance of today's National Association of Realtors release on monthly pending home sales.

It also comes as the U.S. Census Bureau released the latest data on residential housing starts. In October 2026, there were 1,309,000 housing starts, up 9.9% from September. The bulk of that increase—24%— was thanks to multifamily construction, signaling that single family housing is still feeling a strain.

Not surprisingly builder confidence in new single-family home sales is at a 14-year low, according to a National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) survey.

Mortgage rates are calculated based on various factors in the economy, and the length of your loan and credit score will also factor into the mortgage rate you qualify for.

#5498. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5497. Pending Home Sales Tumble to New Record Low as High Mortgage Rates Freeze Buyers

Pending home sales descended to a new all-time low in October as mortgage rates surged to a three-year peak, keeping would-be buyers firmly on the sidelines.

Contract signings fell 4.7% compared to September, and plummeted 16.7% year over year, according to the National Association of Realtors® Pending Home Sales report released on Wednesday.

"October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out," says NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun.

The October readout comes on the heels of the previous record low set in September, when pending sales fell 7.3% month over month and 11.3% year over year.

"Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s," says Yun.

Same as in September, pending sales were down both month over month and year over year in all four U.S. regions. The West saw the largest monthly pullback with a 6.9% drop, followed by the South (-6.3%), Midwest (-2.7%), and Northeast (-0.8%).

Annually, the West was again at the forefront with a 20.3% drop, followed by the South (-18.7%), Midwest (-14%), and Northeast (-11.1%).

"Even though all four regions saw dramatic cooling, the relative strength of the Midwest and Northeast are clear, due largely to still-scarce inventory conditions," says Realtor.com® senior economist Hannah Jones.

At the metro level, pending sales fell year over year even in the hitherto most resilient markets. Across the 50 largest metros, the smallest decreases were recorded in Cincinnati, OH (-4.7% year over year), Austin, TX (-9.7%), and Hartford, CT (-10%).

"It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million," notes Yun. "Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans."

On Oct. 8, the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans reached 7.40%, the highest since Nov. 2023, eroding buyers' purchasing power. Rates have since retreated, but October’s hot inflation data released last week is expected to push them higher again.

"Until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a downward path, affordability problems are likely to persist, keeping contract signings and home sales subdued," says Jones.

Jones suggests that while uncertainty preceding the November midterm elections may have played a role in stalling homebuying activity, she strongly believes that surging mortgage rates were the more likely culprit.

Mortgage rates climbed nearly 75 basis points from late August to mid-October, adding roughly $200 a month to the typical mortgage payment on a median-priced home, assuming a 10% down payment.

"That is more than many already-strained buyers can easily absorb," argues Jones.

According to the economist, affordability remains the limiting factor in today’s housing market. The typical mortgage-holder would see a $1,100 increase in their monthly payment if they bought a median-priced home today.

While sellers have shown some flexibility, with lower asking prices and more price cuts, buyers have not responded with much enthusiasm at these rates.

"Sellers are only willing to come down so far and buyers are only willing to stretch so far, and a gap still separates the two," adds Jones.

As a result, transaction volume in October hit its lowest level in 16 years. However, there are upsides for buyers who can afford to act: less competition, more homes to choose from, and sellers who are willing to negotiate.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5495. Low Rates or Lots of Leverage? Buyers Rarely Get Both.

If you’ve been watching mortgage rates lately, you might feel a little stuck. Rates climbed above 7% this year, and a lot of buyers have decided to sit tight and wait for them to come back down.

But rates are only half the story. When you buy a home, you usually get one of two things: low rates or negotiating power. It’s rare to get both at the same time. And right now, you have a lot more of that second one than you might think.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. Rates were near 3%, and buyers rushed into the housing market. Those low rates sounded great, but they came with a catch. There were a lot of buyers just like you that you had to compete with – and there weren’t enough homes for sale to meet that demand.

That’s why homes got multiple offers, buyers paid over asking or waived inspections, and sellers held all the cards. Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com, shows just how one-sided things got:

“Seller’s markets peaked at 98 of 100 metros in spring 2022 after two years of mortgage rates near 3%.”

Then, in the second half of 2022, rates went up. As a result, the number of people buying homes went down, inventory grew, and the balance slowly started tipping from sellers back to buyers. Fast forward to today, and that flip is officially here.

In a recent report, Realtor.com found about two-thirds (66) of the top 100 metros now lean in favor of buyers (see graph below):

And while you may want lower rates, this shift in power has its own perks.

There are more homes for sale than there have been in years. And in a more buyer-friendly market like that, it means sellers have to work harder to get their homes sold. As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power.”

That shows up in the deals buyers are getting. According to Redfin, nearly half of buyers now get some kind of concession from the seller – like help with closing costs, money for repairs, or even the seller paying to buy down your mortgage rate (see graph below):

So when you find a home you love, even if the rate isn’t what you necessarily wanted, there are other levers to pull. Ask about a price cut or a seller-paid rate buydown, too. It could take some of the sting out of today’s rates.

And just in case you’re still thinking you’ll just hold off until rates drop, here’s what you should know. Experts at Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo don’t expect rates to fall much through 2027 (see graph below):

And here’s the whole point. Even if rates did drop in a big way, a lot of buyers would rush back in. More competition means fewer deals, fewer concessions, and sellers getting the upper hand again.

So waiting comes with a trade-off. You might land a better rate down the road, but you’d probably give up the bargaining power you have today.

That doesn’t mean you have to move right now. You should only buy when the numbers work for you. But if you’ve got a real reason to move, today’s leverage could help make your numbers work – even at today’s rates.

#5494. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

Described as "an extraordinary St. Charles estate," the property underwent extensive renovations during Wahlberg and McCarthy's time there, with the couple transforming it into a personalized retreat designed for both entertaining and relaxing.

Inside, the home boasts an expansive living room and family room, a formal dining room, den, game room, recreation space, exercise room, and finished lower level.

The kitchen comes with an island, breakfast bar, walk-in pantry, and butler's pantry, while hardwood and stone flooring can be found throughout much of the main level.

Adding to the home's cozy appeal are six fireplaces, which are spread throughout spaces, including the living room, family room, primary bedroom, and basement.

The primary suite serves as its own private retreat and features an en suite bathroom with a soaking tub, double sinks, and a full-body spray shower.

Outside, the couple created a resort-style setup with a swimming pool, waterslide, waterfall, spa, putting green, expansive patios, and lush landscaping.

Wahlberg and McCarthy also put their own stamp on the property through a number of highly personalized additions made during their renovations, including door handles shaped like their initials and a custom poker table bearing their names.

The property also holds plenty of sentimental value for the pair. In 2019, they revealed that it was the very first home they toured together while searching for a place where they could embrace the small-town lifestyle they envisioned.

Their decision to sell came after Wahlberg revealed in late 2025 that he and McCarthy had discussed the possibility of relocating to California to be closer to his adult sons, Xavier and Elijah, whom he shares with ex-wife Kim Fey.

At the time, Wahlberg explained that his sons were among the few things that could tempt him back to the West Coast, noting that one of them had repeatedly encouraged him to move closer.

“I have a 24-year-old son and I can’t tell you how many times he’s asked me in the last year to move back to California to be close to him. Probably the only thing that could ever get me back to California is my two sons. And if they keep asking, Jenny and I are going to start going on Realtor.com® and figuring things out," he told People in 2025.

It is not yet clear where Wahlberg and McCarthy plan to settle after selling their Illinois residence.

The couple have called the St. Charles property home for more than a decade, having purchased it one year after tying the knot in 2014.

The $2.8 million listing was held by Cory Jones of eXp Realty.

#5492. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? Talk to a local real estate agent.

#5491. Builder Sentiment Falls to 14-Year Low in November

Builder confidence fell sharply in November as higher mortgage rates, persistent affordability challenges, and rising construction costs continued to weigh on the new-home market, according to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB).

The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell four points to 25 in November, its lowest reading since April 2012. The index stood at 29 in October. Any reading below 50 indicates more builders view market conditions as poor than good.

“Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy,” says Bill Owens, chairman of the NAHB. “Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction.”

All three components of the HMI declined during the month. The index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, while the component measuring sales expectations over the next six months declined two points to 30. Prospective buyer traffic dropped two points to 16, its lowest level in 15 years excluding the onset of the pandemic in 2020.

In response to weaker demand, builders continued to rely heavily on incentives and price reductions to attract buyers. The share of builders cutting home prices increased to 46% in November, the highest level of the post-Covid period. The average price reduction remained at 6% for the eighth consecutive month.

Meanwhile, 68% of builders offered sales incentives, also a post-Covid high. November marked the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders reported using incentives. That represents a further deterioration from October, when 43% of builders reported cutting prices and 65% used incentives.

“The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability,” says Robert Dietz, NAHB chief economist. “Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence, and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back.”

On a three-month moving-average basis, builder confidence declined in every region. The Northeast fell four points to 34, the Midwest declined five points to 35, the South dropped three points to 27, and the West fell three points to 23.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5490. Glenn Close Details the Greenwich Upbringing That Served as a Beacon During Her Time in a ‘Restrictive Cult’ and Inspired Her ‘Family Sanctuary’ in Montana

Glenn Close has told many incredible stories on-screen, but during a recent acceptance speech, “The Hunger Games” star shared some insight on her own eventful past.

The actress, 79, was awarded an honorary Oscar at the Governors Awards on Nov. 16. After receiving a standing ovation from the audience, she revealed, “It’s been very difficult for me to process this incredible honor because the truth is, I carry the epigenome of an outsider.”

The Greenwich, CT, native added that “from the ages of seven to 22,” she was “under the thumb of a restrictive cult.”

She also rattled off a few of the rules she was forced to follow: “Don’t look at yourself in the mirror. No flirting. Dress this way. Talk this way. Say it’s OK when your parents are routinely sent away from you for months on end.”

In a 2025 interview with the Guardian, Close explained that her father, a surgeon named William Taliaferro Close, decided to move to Switzerland and join Moral Re-Armament, a group the publication described as a “rightwing religious cult.”

The “All’s Fair” actress has shared little of her experience in the cult, but she has noted the importance of the earliest years of her upbringing—when her family lived in New England and the “landscape” of her childhood and she was a “little feral child” enjoying the “pastoral” land of her grandfather’s farm in Greenwich.

“I was always on the outside looking in,” she remarked in the speech. “But due to my earlier childhood, running free in the woods and fields of Connecticut, I was able to retreat into my imagination.”

Close went on to describe how the “great Disney animated features” such as “Fantasia” and “Snow White” became a “secret world” that “sustained” her and “fed” her “insatiable imagination.”

“In 1970, I found the strength to leave the cult, and enrolled as a 22-year-old freshman at the college of William and Mary,” she continued, noting that her first move was to head “straight to the theater department,” where she auditioned and was cast as Olivia in Shakespeare’s "Twelfth Night.”

While Close would become a successful star, she said she never shook the feeling of being different.

“As an outsider, I have never worried about whether I was going to win or not,” she said. “Though some years, I thought that I might have a chance. I have always felt that the great honor is to be in the room.”

She explained that she now feels like she is no longer “looking in the window,” but is a meaningful part of the “extraordinary community” she’s worked with in her 43-year career.

Although Close holds New England in high regard, she has since settled down in a home in an equally-beautiful destination on the other side of the country: Bozeman, MT.

According to property records, Close purchased her three-bedroom, three-bathroom abode through a trust in 2016 for an undisclosed amount. In a 2021 Mountain Outlaw interview, she revealed she had relocated to be closer to her sisters and brother, who have homes in the area.

Close shared more details about the home in a 2025 chat with the Wall Street Journal, where she detailed the homes she’s lived in throughout her life.

“Today my home is in Bozeman,” she explained. “All of my siblings live here. My modest, 1982 house has a porch where I can see the mountains and say hi.”

At the time, she revealed she was “building a larger house about a half-hour outside of town,” that will serve as a “Zen farmhouse” and a “family sanctuary.” Close said a stone cottage, designed to remind her of the “best years” of her childhood, were also part of the plans.

Close maintains a very close relationship to her siblings, and even thanked her “beloved sisters, Tina and Jesse” in her award acceptance speech. She often shares glimpses of their family life in Montana with her Instagram followers, capturing the idyllic views seen from the property.

In an Aug. 25 post, Close posted a video to mark how grateful she felt to be home, showcasing the stunning Montana mountains.

“I’m home, calming down, wearing my mama’s shirt, letting the wind blow through my white hair, watching the sun go down,” she boasted. “I feel blessed.”

#5489. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. But you can start making a plan.The earlier you figure out what needs to be done, the more time you'll have to do it right. And that means less rushing, fewer last-minute surprises, and a better chance to make a great first impression when you're ready to sell.Thinking about selling in 2027? #5486. A Fixer-Upper Could Be Your Path To Homeownership

When the homes you love keep landing outside your budget, it may be time to look at the ones other buyers skip.

A fixer-upper won’t be the right call for everyone. Plenty of buyers want a home that’s ready on move-in day. But homes that need some updating could get you in the door for a lot less.

More buyers are starting to realize it too. And Danielle Hale, Chief Economist at Realtor.com, explains why:

“Fixer-uppers give buyers a way to break into the housing market at a time when affordability is still stretched thin. For those with the vision. . . fixer-uppers provide both a starting point in the market and the chance to create a home that’s truly their own.”

If that sounds like you, here’s why a fixer-upper could be worth a closer look.

Because these homes need work, they tend to have a lower asking price up front. According to AmeriSave, fixer-uppers usually sell for 20% to 30% less than what they’re worth on the market.

Here’s what that could look like. KCM applied a 25% discount – the middle of that range – to the median home price from the National Association of Realtors (NAR). This is an example, not the average price of a fixer-upper. But it shows the savings could top $100,000 (see graph below):

That’s a big difference up front and it could be what gets you into a home today. And odds are you don’t have to tackle all the repairs at once – you can space them out over time as it works for you.

Just remember repair costs can add up quickly and eat into those savings if you don’t plan ahead. So, before you make an offer, get estimates from a contractor and set a repair budget you’re comfortable with. There are even some loan types designed to help pay for the work.

With a renovation loan, you can roll the cost of the work into your mortgage, so you don’t have to cover it all out of pocket once you move in. Here are a few options from FHA, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the VA (see visual below):

Each program has its own rules, and not every lender offers all of them. So, talk to a trusted lender to see which options are available to you and which make sense for how you plan to tackle updates and repairs over time.

Some cities even offer tax breaks to buyers who renovate a fixer-upper and raise its value. These programs vary by location, so check with your city or a tax professional to see what’s available where you want to live.

If you want to check for more information yourself, go to your local county or city official dot-gov website. Then, use the search bar and look for: [City or County Name] AND “home rehabilitation” OR “property tax incentive” OR “housing repair”

A local agent can also help you find fixer-uppers in the neighborhoods you have your heart set on.

If move-in-ready homes keep coming in over budget, a home that needs some TLC could be your way in. #5485. Real Estate of GTA VI: What It Would Cost To Live in the Real Locations That Inspired Vice City

On Thursday, video game fans around the world will rejoice when Grand Theft Auto: VI is released.

GTA VI is the long-awaited follow up to 2013's GTA V, which took place in Los Santos, a fictionalized version of Los Angeles. This new release follows "Bonnie and Clyde"-esque couple Lucia and Jason as they make their way across Leonida—a thinly veiled version of Florida.

The game features notable locations in Vice City (based on Miami), but also includes locations throughout the fictional state.

The game in the main GTA series to be set in Vice City was released in 2002. Since then, home prices in the real Miami have increased a staggering 301%. The median listing price in Miami is now $496,000.

GTA V, released in 2013, netted Rockstar Games an astounding $1 billion in just three days, and so far, GTA VI has been preordered by 15 million fans.

Acolytes of the game are already planning to come down with Grand Theft Auto Flu, when the game comes out on Nov. 19, taking time off work to immerse themselves in Vice City.

To mark the game's release, Realtor.com® takes a look at some of the key locations in GTA VI and what it would cost to buy a home in their real-world counterparts.

The Grassrivers region is described by Rockstar Games as "the untamable jewel of Leonida's crown" and is believed to be a stand in for the Everglades region.

The Everglades spans around 7,800 square miles in the Southwestern-most part of the state, and is one of the largest wetlands in the world, home to alligators, manatees, and dozens of bird species.

Given its swampy nature, fans are theorizing that gamers will need to use airboats and seaplanes to get around.

Around 1.5 million acres of the region is protected land, but there are still small cities and towns dotting the area. Homestead, FL, with a population of around 60,000, is the largest city in the Everglades region. The median listing price in Homestead is $440,000, but the median price across the region is just $165,000.

Ambrosia is where "the battle for the health and wealth of Leonida begins."

"The Allied Crystal sugar refinery provides the jobs, while the local biker gang provides almost everything else,'" according to Rockstar Games.

That's led fans to speculate that the fictional area is a stand in for Lake Okeechobee and Clewiston, FL, though Rockstar has yet to confirm this. The area's climate and unique soil conditions make it an optimal environment for the staple crop.

The Okeelanta Sugar Mill and Refinery, located in South Bay, FL, about 30 miles from Lake Okeechobee, is a major sugar processing plant, while the U.S. Sugar company has a processing plant and its corporate headquarters in Clewiston.

With a population of just over 7,000, Clewiston is the largest city in Hendry County. The median listing price in the county is $330,000.

Of Leonida Keys, Rockstar Games wrote: "The dress code is casual, the bars are loaded. Life in this tropical archipelago isn’t flashy but it’s easy. Get your buzz on and pull up a deck chair but look out: you are right on the doorstep of some of the most beautiful and dangerous waters in all of America."

It's easy to see how Leonida Keys might sub in for the Florida Keys, though again, Rockstar has yet to confirm it.

The Florida Keys have drawn everyone from Ernest Hemingway (and his polydactyl cats) to Truman Capote to Tom Hanks through the years. The Keys, located at the southernmost tip of Florida, are hard to get to, and perhaps even harder to buy property. The median listing price for a home on the Keys is $1.195 million.

Rockstar describes Port Gellhorn as Leonida's "forgotten coast." Its "cheap motels, shut-down attractions, and empty strip malls won’t bring the tourists back, but there’s a new economy in this once-popular vacation spot. It’s fueled by malt liquor, painkillers, and truck stop energy drinks. Jump on a dirt bike and hold onto your wallet."

While that description is less than enticing, fans of the game have posited that it's a surrogate for Panama City, FL, and the Florida panhandle. Fans reported seeing several specific real-world locations in stills for the game, including Panama City's Tidal Wave Auto Spa, as well as local churches and pawn shops.

Panama City is a bay-front community of around 35,000, that's adjacent to the tourist-heavy Panama City Beach. The median listing price in Panama City is $396,000.

"A national landmark up against the state’s northern border, Mount Kalaga offers prime hunting, fishing, and off-road trails," Rockstar describes. "In the lush surrounding backwoods, hillbilly mystics and paranoid radicals live far from the prying eyes of the government."

Fans have speculated that Mount Kalaga National Park is modeled after Providence Canyon State Park, a park located on the southern border of Georgia, which is called Gloriana in the game.

One of the closest real-world towns to Providence Canyon is Eufala, which sits on the border between Alabama and Georgia. The historic town of Eufala has around 12,000 residents and sits on the banks of the Chattahoochee River. It's home to the Eufala National Wildlife Refuge. The median listing price in Eufala is $298,000.

#5483. 3 Housing Questions That Might Come Up at Your Next Family Dinner

This time of year usually means more time spent with family and friends. And in recent years, when everyone gets together, the conversation has a way of drifting to housing.

Your uncle is sure home prices are about to crash. Your cousin heard foreclosures are surging. And someone across the table brings up the word “recession.”

If you’ve wondered about any of this yourself, that makes sense. There’s a lot of noise out there. So let’s look at what the data actually shows, so you’ll have real answers the next time it comes up.

Let’s start with your uncle’s crash prediction. The short answer is no. Experts project home prices will keep climbing nationally in 2027.

On average, forecasters expect prices to rise about 1.4% next year (see graph below). That’s slower than the big jumps of a few years ago, but it’s still growth, not a crash.

Prices are dipping in some markets, though. It just depends on where you live. Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), explains why:

“Price declines are occurring mainly in southern states, where there has been robust new home construction in recent years. Given the region’s faster job growth, these price drops should be viewed as temporary and as a second-chance opportunity for those previously priced out of the market.”

So, the dips that are fueling all the social media chatter are limited to select areas, and experts think they’ll be short-lived. It doesn’t mean a crash is looming.

If you’re thinking about moving, look at the numbers for your area.

Then your cousin chimes in about foreclosures. They’ve ticked up lately, but here’s some important context. That’s compared to very low levels. They’re still below where they were before the pandemic, according to ATTOM.

So, why doesn’t today look like 2008? Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . we have had many recessions post-WWII but only one foreclosure crisis. That foreclosure crisis started with a massive credit boom from 2002-2005, and then a credit bust. . . none of that is happening now . . .“

Today’s homeowners also have something a lot of people didn’t have back then – equity. In every state, the average homeowner with a mortgage has more than $100,000 of it, according to Cotality (see map below):

If a homeowner hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house instead of facing foreclosure.

While someone in your family may be convinced a recession is coming, experts don’t agree. The average forecast from The Wall Street Journal’s survey of economists puts the odds at about 24%, so most experts aren’t expecting one. And that’s a good thing.

But even if one hits, history shows a recession doesn’t mean home prices will automatically fall. In 5 of the last 6 recessions, prices actually went up, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) (see graph below):

The one exception was 2008, the only one of these recessions that started in the housing market itself.

So, the next time your uncle predicts a crash or your cousin brings up 2008, you’ll know prices aren’t crashing, foreclosures are still low, and a recession doesn’t automatically spell trouble for housing. If a move in 2027 is on your mind, connect with a local real estate agent to look at what prices are doing in your neighborhood so you can plan with real local numbers, not scary headlines.
