#5481. Housing Starts Jump, But Drop in Permits Paints Dim Picture for Homebuilding

Construction has seen a significant slowdown from continued market challenges in supply chain and affordability issues. Despite a surprising uptick in housing starts in this month’s New Residential Construction report, economists say the overall picture remains troubled.

The latest data from the Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Census Bureau saw housing starts jump 9.9% month-over-month to a rate of 1,309,000, also seeing a 2.8% year-over-year rise.

The rise was directly due to a leap in multifamily starts, up 25.5% month-over-month and 22% year-over-year to a rate of 433,000. Multifamily construction did see an uptick in building permits in September by 5.9% month-over-month and 1% year-over-year, which appears to have translated into the uptick in starts.

Single-family starts also saw a month-over-month rise of 4% to a rate of 864,000, but were still down year-over-year by 3.2%.

Notably, September’s original starts rate of 1,221,000 was negatively revised to 1,191,000, reflecting the continuation of the slower trend in construction. Single-family starts were also negatively revised from a rate of 859,000 to 831,000.

National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) Chairman Bill Owens said that the gain in starts this month is “encouraging,” but “does not necessarily signal a sustained recovery.”

“Builder confidence weakened in November as higher mortgage rates and affordability challenges weighed on buyers,” he continued. “Stronger demand is needed to sustain construction, while meeting the significant long-term need for more housing requires easing regulatory barriers to home building.”

Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington—NAHB’s assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis—agreed with Owens’ sentiment, adding that the gain is “welcome,” but the “market remains constrained by elevated borrowing costs, rising construction costs and weakening builder confidence.”

“The monthly gain should be viewed cautiously as affordability challenges and economic uncertainty persist,” she continued.

Looking regionally, the Midwest and the South were up month-over-month and year-over-year, while the Northeast and the West were down on both counts.

The Midwest was up 48.4% month-over-month and 17.2% year-over-year. The South was up 10.5% month-over-month and 12.2% year-over-year. The Northeast was down 20.8% month-over-month and 34.5% year-over-year. The West was down 2.6% month-over-month and 11.6% year-over-year.

Realtor.com® Senior Economist Joel Berner described the signals presented in this month’s report as “mixed,” and noted that single-family construction is still down year-over-year.

“This month’s data is an improvement, but from a very low baseline readout in both September and last October,” he continued.

Despite the rise in starts in October, building permits did not paint a picture of a continued upward trend.

Permits were down 7.4% month-over-month and 8.7% year-over-year to a rate of 1,295,000. Both multifamily and single-family permits were down month-over-month and year-over-year. Multifamily permits were down 5.2% month-over-month and 0.4% year-over-year to a rate of 475,000. Single-family permits were down 8.7% month-over-month and 12.9% year-over-year to a rate of 772,000.

Berner noted that this was permitting’s “lowest level since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic in May 2020.” He also called this month’s permit data a “disappointment,” as it demonstrated that builders are “slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on.”

Permits were also down both month-over-month and year-over-year in the Northeast, South and West, while the Midwest was up on both counts.

Housing completions had a more mixed result in October. Completions were up 6.5% month-over-month to a rate of 1,272,000, but were down 10.4% year-over-year. Both single-family and multifamily completions were also up month-over-month (6.3% and 9%, respectively), and were also down year-over-year (-10.7% and -9%, respectively).

“If you focus on home starts, this month’s new construction data is a welcome improvement from last month’s, but zooming out for more context shows a residential construction industry that is still struggling to find its footing,” concluded Berner. ”(S)oftening permits will put downward pressure on starts and completions in the months to come. In a country facing a supply gap of over four million homes, this represents a step in the wrong direction.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

While speaking to People, the actor, 56, opened up about their at-home rules he ensures his wife, Luciana Damon, and their daughters Alexia, Isabella, Gia, and Stella follow.

“I tell my kids, it’s the same rules as when we go to the theater: no phones, no talking. I try to create the movie experience as much as I can in my house. That’s not easy to do. ... "This generation is really coming back to theaters, which is wonderful," he said. "So I just try to instill in them that it can be like that at home, too. If you give it that same kind of reverence, it can be just as fun.

"Because being on this side of it and knowing what it takes to make every shot and how much love and care and work is put into every single shot that you’re seeing, you want to give the director and the team your complete attention as much as you can."

#5478. The Thanksgiving Hosting Stress Test: Is Your Place Ready for the Big Day?

Hosting Thanksgiving in your first home is exciting, but it can also feel overwhelming.

“You likely want everything to look and feel ‘put together’ as soon as possible despite the fact that a fresh move-in is typically anything but,” says Kate Pechinka, founder and principal designer of Kate Kelly Interiors in Chester Springs, PA.

The pressures of living up to the warm environment you’ve either experienced growing up or seen in movies or advertisements combined with the added demands on your home’s systems don’t make things any easier.

“Suddenly, multiple people are using the bathrooms, the dishwasher and garbage disposal are running frequently, the oven is working for hours, and guests are moving through spaces that may not have been arranged for entertaining,” explains Kevin Vander Hyde, vice president of Vander Hyde Services in Grand Rapids, MI.

Here’s the good news: With a little preparation and planning, you can ensure your home is Thanksgiving-ready and alleviate a great deal of stress long before your guests arrive.

These expert tips can help you address safety concerns, secure your belongings, and prevent common hosting mishaps this Turkey Day—all while keeping your sanity and budget in check as a new homeowner.

Ensure keepsakes, special family heirlooms, and other high-value items are either put away, well protected, or displayed in a place that invites appreciation, but not direct interaction like a high mantel or glass-front china cabinet.

“Anticipate that curious guests of all ages might not be able to fight the urge to touch,” Pechinka explains.

Chances are guests will set drinks or food items down on your tables, couches, and other furniture. That’s why it’s important to shield them from accidental spills, stains, and scratches.

For pieces with inviting tabletop surfaces you don’t intend to move, Pechinka recommends  having a piece of glass cut at your local glass shop to place on the surface.

“This option can create a polished look and provide a high level of protection. It’s also cost-effective when you consider the cost to refinish or replace a piece of furniture,” says Pechinka.

No matter where you live, your home is likely filled with trip hazards like step-downs into family rooms, or area rugs that change the height of flooring surfaces. These potential hazards can create unique challenges for guests of all ages.

“To reduce their risk, improve lighting in these areas. You can also use rug tape to keep rug corners down,” Pechinka explains.

Children or nosy adults may walk into bedrooms and other rooms you might not want them to venture into.

Make sure you know how many dishes, coffee cups, and utensils you need.

“This simple check keeps you from washing dishes midparty and lets you remain fully engaged with your guests,” Pechinka adds.

Make sure the oven heats properly, the stovetop burners work, and the dishwasher completes a cycle without leaking.

“If you're preparing several dishes, plan out cooking times and oven space in advance. Avoid plugging multiple high-wattage countertop appliances into the same overloaded circuit,” says Vander Hyde.

Run the kitchen and bathroom faucets, flush the toilets, and check that sinks and tubs drain properly.

“Slow drains, low water pressure, dripping faucets, or unusual odors can be signs of a plumbing issue you should address before guests arrive,” Vander Hyde explains.

Remember that catching and resolving a small problem early on is always easier and less expensive than dealing with an unexpected and much larger repair once the holiday is over.

Resist the temptation to treat the garbage disposal like a trash can.

Avoid putting grease, cooking oil, large amounts of food, or fibrous scraps down the drain. Run cold water while operating the disposal, and feed food scraps gradually rather than trying to grind everything at once.

“Grease and food buildup are common contributors to holiday drain clogs,” says Vandrer Hyde.

With multiple guests showering, washing dishes, and using hot water, demand can increase significantly. That’s why it’s vital to ensure the water heater is operating normally.

“Watch for signs of trouble, such as inconsistent hot water, leaks, or unusual noises. If you notice any of them, it’s time to call a plumber,” Vander Hyde explains.

Before guests arrive, test the thermostat, replace a dirty air filter, and make sure vents aren't blocked by furniture or rugs.

“If the furnace is making unusual noises or struggling to maintain the temperature, arrange an inspection before the holiday,” adds Vander Hyde.

#5475. Lot Supply Rises for Ninth Consecutive Quarter

The supply of vacant developed lots continued to loosen in the third quarter as slower construction activity brought the national lot market further into balance, according to Zonda.

Zonda’s New Home Lot Supply Index rose to 88.5 in the third quarter, up 20.8% from a year earlier and 3.9% from the second quarter. It marked the ninth consecutive quarterly increase in the index.

The index measures the supply of single-family vacant developed lots relative to the rate at which builders absorb those lots through housing starts. Zonda rated the national market “appropriately supplied” in the third quarter.

In the second quarter, the index sat at the boundary between “slightly undersupplied” and “appropriately supplied.” The third-quarter increase placed the national market in the latter category.

“The national lot market is moving more firmly into balance,” says Sean Fergus, vice president of economic research for Zonda. “But that balance needs to be viewed in the context of today’s housing market.”

Fergus noted that affordability pressures and widespread incentives continue to challenge builders’ ability to convert demand into sales. An appropriately supplied lot market indicates that lot availability is better aligned with the current pace of construction, he said, but does not mean the industry’s longer-term land constraints and cost pressures have disappeared.

Lot supply increased year over year in every major metropolitan area tracked by Zonda except Boise, Idaho. Among the markets where supply increased, the average annual gain was 32%.

Baltimore, Portland, and Seattle posted the largest year-over-year increases in lot supply. Boise was the only market where supply tightened, with its index falling from 65.7 in the third quarter of 2025 to 51.9.

Despite the broader improvement in availability, 12 of the 30 markets tracked by Zonda remained “significantly undersupplied.” Eight markets changed supply ratings during the quarter, Zonda points out.

Zonda also reported a modest increase in the future lot pipeline. Total upcoming lots increased 1% year over year and 1.6% from the second quarter.

Upcoming lots include properties in the later stages of development that are typically expected to become vacant developed lots within 12 to 18 months.

The increase suggests additional lots are moving toward delivery, although the pipeline is expanding much more slowly than the current supply index. The divergence reflects the role of softer starts in loosening lot conditions: available lots are lasting longer as builders respond to weaker demand and elevated mortgage rates.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5472. Fed Officials Expect Further Interest Rate Hikes After Pausing Last Month

Leaders at the Federal Reserve held firm on interest rates in October, but also thought a future rate hike "would likely be appropriate" as some mulled a larger hike in December, according to meeting minutes released on Wednesday.

At the Oct. 27–28 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), policymakers voted 10-2 to keep the overnight rate at its previous 3.75%-4.00% range. The decision came days before the 2026 midterms, even as FOMC members agreed inflation was a persistent concern.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh joined the majority, while Fed Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both voted in favor of a quarter-point increase. One month before, the FOMC voted to raise rates for the first time in three years in an effort to clamp down on inflation.

The minutes—which don't name FOMC members specifically while discussing their deliberations—show that some of the FOMC members considered that, while the impact of tariffs on the economy was waning, high energy costs continue to pressure Americans.

Indeed, some participants even noted that, if the inflation numbers got too unfavorable, they would consider a rate hike of more than a quarter-percent in December. Bond markets still view that as unlikely, with the probability of a larger half-point hike next month at just 5%, according to CME FedWatch.

Still, Federal Reserve Gov. Christopher Waller told CNBC on Wednesday it may be necessary to "shock people" with a larger rate hike. He said in a speech this month that a half-percent point hike might be necessary next month.

"Inflation's been above our target for over five years, so if you really want to get it down, you have to start taking more aggressive actions," Waller told CNBC.

FOMC members also said the rapid artificial intelligence buildout was contributing to inflation. But more scrutiny of the industry could slow spending and reduce inflation pressures.

Those members later determined holding rates steady at the October meeting would allow for time to "assess the durability of AI-related investment demand, the evolution of financing conditions, the transmission of the September rate increase to the economy, or geopolitical developments.

"A couple of participants noted that, at the current juncture, a gradual approach to policy firming wouldgive businesses and households time to adjust to higher interest rates," the minutes state.

Inflation remained hot in October. Overall prices rose 0.4% from September, according to the consumer price index (CPI) data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics last week.

Some numbers look better. After a disappointing September, U.S. payrolls came roaring back in October as employers added 165,000 new jobs, pushing the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.

CME FedWatch currently prices a roughly 95% chance of the FOMC raising the federal funds to a 4.00%-4.25% range in December, followed by a 69% probability of 4.25%-4.50% in January.

The meeting minutes show that Fed leaders are aware that public sentiment broadly expects the December rate hike.

"Some participants," the minutes state, judge those estimates to be "broadly consistent with their assessments of the appropriate policy rate path."

Several of the meeting members also said it was a "close call." In the meantime, Cook and Hammack said that inflation remained too high and they didn't see enough signs that it was letting up. They worried that delaying the rate hike any further could risk higher inflation becoming entrenched. That, in turn, could mean more drastic rate hikes in the future.

Waller isn't the only Fed leader saying that the market needs more than one quarter-point rate hike.

"The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said this week at a conference in Argentina.

Realtor.com® Chief Economist Danielle Hale said the market ultimately anticipates two or three hikes over the next six to eight months. The market has reacted. Pending home sales in September dropped to their lowest level on record.

"While the market and the Fed both seem to agree that some monetary policy restriction is warranted, most investors currently expect more restriction than the Fed has projected," Hale said last month.

But there is still an opportunity for homebuyers in this environment. Hale recommended homebuyers set themselves up for a better mortgage rate by boosting their credit score, making a higher down payment, and shopping around for a mortgage.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. #5471. Nick Cannon Pulls Back the Curtain on the Drama of Raising 12 Kids Across Multiple Homes in Netflix’s ‘Raising the Cannons’

Nick Cannon is lifting the lid on what it takes to raise a family across multiple homes—and his kids have a few things to say about it, too.

In “Raising the Cannons,” premiering on Dec. 18 on Netflix, the father of 12 gives viewers a glimpse of home life with his blended family.

Among those offering their own take are Moroccan and Monroe, the 15-year-old twins he shares with ex-wife Mariah Carey, who have some candid thoughts about their dad’s choices.

For a family spread across several households, the Cannons live surprisingly close together. According to Netflix’s Tudum, the six mothers of his children—Carey, “Selling Sunset” star Bre Tiesi, Abby De La Rosa, Alyssa Scott, Brittany Bell, and LaNisha Cole—all live within a 5-mile radius of one another.

That proximity comes in handy for school pickups. For Cannon, it also makes something more personal possible. He wants the time his children spend with him to give them a chance to grow up together, even when they go home to different houses.

“I want my children to have relationships with one another,” he says in the trailer.

Cannon credits the mothers with helping him bring the kids together. De La Rosa, who shares twins Zion and Zillion and daughter Beautiful Zeppelin with him, wants that for her children, too.

The radio personality and DJ is also open to getting to know the other mothers better.

She and Cannon first met through morning radio, where they bonded over music and entertainment. As parents, Cannon says, they’ve found they also share many of the same values about how they want to raise their three children.

Cole offers a different perspective in the trailer. The photographer, who shares daughter Onyx with Cannon, says she feels little need to present the entire group as one big, happy family.

Cannon tells Tudum it took him time to find his footing with Cole after their romantic relationship ended in 2022. When she moved on with a new partner, he says, he had to put his ego aside, respect her boundaries, and focus on what worked best for Onyx.

For “Selling Sunset” fans, one of the bigger surprises may be what Tiesi gets up to in her own home.

Viewers know the luxury real estate agent for showing palatial properties. Cannon, who shares son Legendary Love with her, knows her as someone who’s just as happy taking on a project around the house.

He tells Tudum that “at home she’s always decorating and baking—DIY projects all around the house, building chicken coops.”

The series also follows Cannon as he balances fatherhood and work while managing lupus nephritis, a condition that affects the kidneys. The trailer shows him in a hospital bed as a voice expresses concern about the toll stress is taking on him.

Elsewhere in the preview, Moroccan questions whether his father can sustain the way he’s living.

Moroccan and his sister were just 5 when Cannon and Carey divorced in 2016. The twins are now in high school, and Cannon says he and Carey still speak regularly about parenting and what comes next for their children. Of all his co-parenting relationships, he points to theirs as the model he hopes to follow with his younger kids.

These days, the twins have advice of their own for their father, particularly when it comes to his love life.

“They’re the parents, I’m the kid,” Cannon jokes to Tudum.

Monroe gives viewers a sense of just how frank those conversations can be. In one exchange in the trailer, she tells her father that if he hadn’t gone on to have more children, she thinks he and her mother would have found their way back to each other.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. #5470. Weichert, Realtors Joins HouseCanary’s Google Listings Program

Housing-focused data and analytics company HouseCanary announced today that Weichert, Realtors® has joined the Google Listings Program as the tech giant continues to expand its latest foray into residential listing.

The active listings for Weichert’s company-owned offices in its five-state footprint of New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Maryland are now live and available for display in Google mobile search results in live markets, according to a release from HouseCanary.

Weichert is only the latest to join the program, following three others that included REMAX Advantage, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Florida Properties Group and ENRG Realty.

According to HouseCanary, these listings are now among those that appear in a carousel at the top of Google mobile search results. Each listing shows basic property details and listing brokerage attribution, and consumers can tap through to a detail page with more information about the home, the listing agent’s name and a click-to-contact button.

“Weichert is one of the most recognized names in residential real estate, and its decision to join reflects how the US’s largest brokerages are recognizing the value of getting as much exposure for their listings as possible,” said Chris Rediger, CEO of HouseCanary. “We are thrilled to have Weichert, Realtors in the Google Listings Program.”

HouseCanary also connects directly with brokerage companies, such as Weichert, Realtors®, to bring their listings into the program, via a participating MLS.

“Joining the Google Listings Program is an exciting step forward toward maximizing visibility for Weichert listings and delivering high-intent leads to our agents,” said Joseph McDonald, president of residential sales and real estate services for Weichert, Realtors®. “The initiative creates a streamlined home search experience for consumers and a direct path for buyers to connect with Weichert agents. It also reinforces our commitment to keeping our agents ahead of the curve in digital real estate marketing.”

All the maneuverings come as HouseCanary tries to wind down following court approval of its Chapter 11 bankruptcy reorganization. In an email to RISMedia, a HouseCanary spokesperson wrote that “(t)he company continues to operate normally. Its proposed plan, subject to court approval, targets emergence (from Chapter 11) before year-end, with full recovery for all approved creditors.”

Launched in early 2026 and expanding to all eligible U.S. markets this fall, the Google Listings Program is powered by HouseCanary, which establishes agreements with MLSs to feed their brokerage members’ listings to Google.

The listings of Weichert’s company-owned offices come via My State MLS. Other MLSs participating in the Google Listings Program include ARMLS, Bright MLS, California Regional MLS, IRES MLS, Permian Basin Board of Realtors®, REcolorado and San Diego MLS.

#5469. The ‘Twilight’ Home in Forks, WA, Is Hiring a Social Media Manager—and the Job Comes With Complimentary Stays

First, Robert Pattinson was announced as the next James Bond. And now, the original Swan House in Forks, WA, is offering a rare opportunity to work and stay in the storied property.

“We’re looking for someone who genuinely loves Twilight, understands the fandom, and is excited about sharing the story of this very special house and the town of Forks,” the home’s owner, Christine Haning, tells Realtor.com®.

The vacancy was first announced in a Nov. 17 job listing, which calls for a “creative, ‘Twilight’-loving social media manager to help grow Bella Swan House.” The post says the team is looking to hear from anyone who loves “creating Instagram Reels, keeping up with "Twilight" fandom news, dreaming up fun content ideas, and connecting with fellow fans.”

While they’re not necessarily looking for someone with an established platform of their own—or many years of experience—Haning hopes to find someone who shares the same passion for the now-iconic vampire stories. And the paid, part-time, remote opportunity comes along with a major perk: complimentary stays at the house for content creation.

“We’re actually almost completely booked for the next 12 months, and that’s only because we don’t open our calendar any further in advance!” Haning notes. “So, the complimentary stays are a pretty unique perk. Not just because they’re free, but because getting a reservation at the house can be difficult.”

The home is available to book directly on the Swan House website, or through Airbnb. Pricing begins at $400 a night.

Haning explains that certain dates are “intentionally” blocked off throughout the year for “maintenance, photography, and content creation.” These are the times the social media manager will be able to stay at the home and experience its magic firsthand.

“I think being able to actually spend time in the house and explore Forks is such a valuable part of creating authentic content that fans will connect with,” she says.

The historic farmhouse was built in 1905, and while it’s not the St. Helens, OR, home fans may recognize from the films, the Swan House’s connection to the franchise goes back much further.

“One thing I’ve realized since taking ownership of the house and running its social media account is how few people know the history behind the books versus the movies,” Haning adds. “Most fans are familiar with the house in Oregon where the first movie was filmed, but before the movies, there were the books!”

Haning confirmed the abode is the original home that inspired Bella and Charlie Swan’s dwelling in the books—a linkage that’s been recognized by the town of Forks since 2006.

“That literary connection is what makes it so special to me,” says Haning.

Haning says the house has “so much history and character.” She purchased it in June 2025, and has worked to create a “really special blend of the books and films” in the time since.

There’s a yellow kitchen, just like Bella mentions her mom, Renee Dwyer, painted in the books. Haning also decorated one of the three bedrooms with purple bedding and wall art to closely resemble Bella’s room in the films. There's even a cardboard cutout of Edward Cullen to watch you sleep.

Charlie’s dining table makes an appearance, too.

The home sleeps eight, and has a fully-equipped kitchen, as well as a gourmet coffee and tea bar with a waffle breakfast station.

It’s also stocked with all of the “Twilight” DVDs, as well as a record player with the saga’s complete soundtrack collection.

A recent addition includes a display featuring “all the different editions of the ‘Twilight’ books,” which Haning notes includes some “rare, hard-to-find editions and memorabilia.” She says she’s having lots of fun acquiring “little treasures” to add to the home.

“What I love is that it doesn’t feel like a movie set or a themed hotel,” she says. “It’s a real, historic home in the actual town of Forks, filled with little details that fans recognize and appreciate. It brings together the literary history, the visual nostalgia of the films,and the experience of actually being in the place where the story takes place. It’s really the best of both worlds.”

Given Forks’ major role in the series, the home’s central location in the town is a major plus. The Swan House is surrounded by the Olympic Peninsula’s stunning landscape.

“It’s honestly one of the most beautiful places I’ve ever been,” says Haning, adding that the entire town has embraced the world author Stephanie Meyer created.

There are stores with “Twilight” merchandise, the real Forks High School is nearby, and the hospital even has a reserved parking spot for Dr. Carlisle Cullen. And of course, the coastal community and Native American reservation of La Push is “just down the road.”

“It’s such an immersive experience. Sometimes when I’m there, I find myself getting a little bit lost in it all, and the story starts to feel surprisingly real,” Haning gushes. “I’d love to find someone who shares that excitement and can help us bring it to life through creative content.”

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5467. Dell bets liquid-cooled, software-defined storage can keep AI factories fed

AI factories are growing so dense that storage, not just compute, now decides how quickly they turn data into tokens. For Dell Technologies Inc., the answer starts with turning its PowerEdge servers into flexible, software-defined storage nodes that can change roles as workloads shift.

The move from training toward inference and agents has put new pressure on time to value. Dell has spent the year extending its AI Data Platform with a semantic layer for agentic workloads. Its AI factory pitch now reaches well beyond compute and graphics processing units, according to George Papadopoulos (pictured), senior vice president of product and engineering at Dell.

“We look at our AI factory not just as a set of CPUs and GPUs, but networking becoming more and more important, particularly around speed, reliability of storage and the ability to take your raw data and generate context and knowledge from it,” he said.

Papadopoulos spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Dell is adapting its storage and cooling to keep AI factories running at scale. (* Disclosure below.)

Customers want storage they can buy for today’s needs and repurpose later. For instance, a customer might start with file and move to object or parallel file as workloads evolve. Agentic workloads lean on small input/output operations rather than streaming, so the right storage type can shift quickly, Papadopoulos explained. Dell’s answer is Dell Exascale Storage, which runs as licensed software on Dell servers.

“It’s our really purpose-built software-defined solution for allowing us to take a PowerEdge-based node and … with flexible licensing, allow you to deploy a file persona, a block persona, an object persona or a parallel file persona, and allow that flexibility to change over time as your needs change,” he said.

Density is also forcing a rethink of cooling. The power envelope of today’s AI systems is so large that customers are planning for 100% liquid-cooled data centers, according to Papadopoulos. That requirement now extends to storage.

“The conversations have really gotten down to how can we most effectively provide a direct liquid-cooled solution — and the storage, that means even liquid cooling the drives, which is something that hasn’t been done as of yet,” he said.

At SC26, Dell unveiled a 2U, 32-drive node with 100% liquid cooling, which it bills as the first direct liquid-cooled storage for rack-scale AI. The node deploys as an Exascale system with any persona. Separating the software from an appliance also lets Dell bring new PowerEdge generations to market faster. That flexibility matters for neocloud operators, who need an off-ramp for every purchase, Papadopoulos noted.

“That allows them to make an upfront purchase and know that they won’t be locked into one particular storage type,” he said, “or have a set of data silos that they can’t leverage as they go forward.”

#5466. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5465. Oklahoma City, OK, Struggles With Low Starter Home Availability Compared to Other Cities

A recent metro-by-metro analysis by Realtor.com® reveals where buyers can still find a starter home. For many would-be homeowners, these options have felt increasingly scarce as rising prices and climbing mortgage rates compound affordability challenges.

Furthermore, research from economists supports this trend. Nationally, the share of starter homes in active inventory fell from 38.1% in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026. During that same period, starter home prices rose 30.8%, from roughly $260,000 to $340,000.

As a result, some markets like Oklahoma City have experienced a downturn in available starter homes in recent years.

A starter home is typically defined as a property priced at roughly 80% of a metro's median list price. This captures the relative affordability of homes at the lower end of a local market. These homes are generally smaller and less expensive, making them accessible to a first-time buyer or a household with an Income at or below the area median.

In Oklahoma City, OK, the share of starter homes has seen a steady decline. The portion of these homes was 34.8% in 2019, which then decreased to 33.1% in 2022. As of 2026, the share has fallen further to 31.4%.

Therefore, this represents a total decrease of 3.4 percentage points between 2019 and 2026. This trend indicates a shrinking market for entry-level homes in the area, presenting a challenge for new buyers.

For those weighing the decision of renting or buying, current data suggests that renting is the more financially prudent choice for now. A July Rent Report from Realtor.com found that the cost of buying a starter home in the 50 largest metros was $858 higher per month than renting one. This 50.6% premium on homeownership makes renting the more affordable option across all 50 of the largest metros.

In Oklahoma City, OK, this trend holds, offering a clear financial advantage to renters. The median rent for an apartment was $915 as of July 2026.

Moreover, the local rental market has seen prices decrease by 1.50% year-over-year, making it an even more attractive alternative to purchasing a home with a significant down payment. (A rent vs. buy calculator can help individuals assess their personal financial situation.)

#5464. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

#5463. OpenAI rolls out GPT-6.2 Astra for professional work and GPT-6.2 Sol for everyday work

OpenAI Group PBC today announced the launch of GPT-6.2 Astra, a new frontier artificial intelligence model for complex professional work that is claimed to outperform its predecessor at less than a third of the cost, along with an updated version of its everyday model, GPT-6.2 Sol.

The new models are aimed at businesses and developers looking for frontier performance at a cost that works at scale, with both said to deliver better results on demanding tasks while using fewer output tokens.

According to OpenAI, GPT-6.2 Astra sets a new high on Agents’ Last Exam, a benchmark that tests multistep professional work, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra while costing under a third as much. It is claimed to have finished 5.5 points ahead of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.

OpenAI is positioning GPT-6.2 Astra as the best model in the world for scientists, with the model scoring 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a benchmark for scientific work carried out in a terminal. On Harvey LAB-AA, a test of legal assignments, the model more than doubled the pass rate of Fable 5.2 at about one-sixth of the cost.

Along with improved benchmark scores, GPT-6.2 Astra was trained to create slides, spreadsheets and documents that more closely follow the conventions used by professionals in fields such as law, sales, finance and accounting. The model can match a slide template from an original file or a screenshot, including layout, colors and typography down to the exact font size.

Early testers of the model include accounting AI startup Basis, which said that its average time for long-horizon accounting work fell by 50%, with the time for its most complex work falling by up to 73%.

Described by OpenAI as its go-to model for everyday work, GPT-6.2 Sol is claimed to let users complete more tasks on the same paid plan than GPT-6.1 Sol did. According to OpenAI, the model came within 0.5 points of GPT-6.2 Astra on Cognition AI Inc.’s FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark at about one-fifth of the cost.

GPT-6.2 Astra comes less than two months after OpenAI called off the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra, after internal testing found the model fell short on staying within scope and authorization. The decision was announced the day before the company’s DevDay event in September, where GPT-6.1 Sol launched on its own.

Like GPT-6 Astra, both GPT-6.2 models meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, and their increased capabilities have led the company to launch them with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance that are also said to restrict some legitimate vulnerability research. The company said it will work to bring the GPT-6.2 models to Daybreak, its program for vetted cyber defenders.

GPT-6.2 Astra is also the first externally released OpenAI model to meet the High threshold for AI self-improvement, a measure of a model’s ability to accelerate AI research. OpenAI tracks the capability because models that help build future AI systems could outpace safeguards and human oversight, and earlier this month it disclosed Control Room, a system already deployed across its research infrastructure that can halt model output when intervention is needed.

The company noted that in two of its alignment tests, the new models were more likely than GPT-6 Astra to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work, such as a missing file. OpenAI said it has added instructions in Codex that substantially reduce the omissions and is continuing to investigate the behavior.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available starting today to Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, with Enterprise and Edu access requiring a workspace admin to enable it. Developers can also access both models through the OpenAI API. API pricing for GPT-6.2 Astra is $8 per million input tokens, 40 cents for cached input and $40 per million output tokens, a 20% discount on input and output tokens compared with GPT-6 Astra. GPT-6.2 Sol carries forward GPT-6.1 Sol’s rates of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

#5462. ‘Momentum is the cure of all fear’: Mauricio and Alexia Umansky talk ‘Special Forces’

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

It’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

To leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

Season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

At the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Mauricio voluntarily withdrew after a rib injury sustained during a hand-to-hand fighting challenge with former NBA player Matt Barnes. Mauricio said the injury took two or three months to heal.

The following challenge involved gas, and Mauricio didn’t think his ribs could take it. He said he feared having a bad lung injury in the Malaysian jungle. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

What follows is the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

I think for me, 100 percent, the heat. I think I anticipated intense heat and intense humidity, but you don’t know what it’s like until you really feel it … It was so unbearably hot, and in our barracks that we slept in, there was no windows, and when you were inside, you actually couldn’t tell like what was even happening out there. But it was almost like … “Good, let me be locked in this metal box because the outside is crazy.”

Mauricio: I think for me, it was just the intensity of what a jungle really is. The first day we got there … when we were all showering and waiting to shower, there was a scorpion crawling on my leg, about to go in my boot, which I felt it and took it off just in the nick of time. Because if it went in my boot, it would have stung me, no question, right?

Alexia: It’s so hard to choose because literally every single thing was hard. Part of me wanted to say the car rides leading up to each challenge, because we didn’t know what was coming, and it was always so intense in the car. My heart would start pounding … the bottom line is the hardest part is just making sure that your mindset is correct [in] doing all these things and waking up each day and moving forward because that’s really what gets going is just moving forward and choosing to keep on going.

Mauricio: Yeah, I think Alexia nailed it. I mean, for me, it was really all about the little victories. The only way to survive is by looking at small victories, small steps … we used to say just make it to the next meal, just make it to the next day, just make it to tonight.

For me, the hardest part was leaving, was having to voluntarily withdraw. I did not want to have a medical withdrawal, so I didn’t want to go see the doctor and have them withdraw me.

Mauricio: Not one thing for me. What about you, Alexia?

Alexia: No. There’s nothing about this that’s easy.

Alexia: We loved everybody so much. I mean, we still talk all the time, and we still love each other so much. The words of affirmation we all told each other to this day are so special … But I think my first answer would have to be Candace [Cameron] Bure … she’s so strong, and we got looped together for a bunch of things because of our height similarities.

Mauricio: Well, I have to say that the person who surprised me the most was Alexia … the strength of her mind, her strength and what she did was extraordinary.

Alexia: Oh my god, yeah. Are you kidding me? All the time.

Alexia: Definitely thought it was pretty cool. It was an honor to be punched in the chest by DJ Tanner … I actually appreciated very much that she didn’t hold back because I just felt like I was treated like an equal, an individual.

Alexia: I’ve never punched anyone or anything … the second she threw the first punch, I knew she was so much stronger than me. But my goal was to just not fall down. I really didn’t want to fall down, so I was just trying to stay up the entire time. It felt like a fight went on for so long.

Alexia: I had zero plans on talking about that while we were there. Before we go into the course, they make you talk to some psychologists … they do ask you before the show, “What’s the worst thing that you’ve ever been through?”

And I remember thinking, like, “Are we gonna go there? … That would be so inappropriate. Everything’s in my power, and I’m not gonna go there” … Once I was finally in there, I understood why they asked … you’re stripped down to the very core of you, and you’re tired, and you’re pushing yourself, and you’re emotional, you’re exhausted … And Bre Tiesi, she got emotional, and [she said to me] ”I haven’t cried in years. I hate crying.”

It was really about discovering and repurposing the strength that I always felt that I had, but there was a time that I had felt that I had lost that.

And each night, as I was going to sleep, I just remember thinking to myself, “This is so rewarding, and this is so empowering, and this is so incredible for someone that has gone through what I have” … some people [feel like they] get their voice back. I always felt like I had my voice, but I feel like I got to discover a strength I always knew I had that someone had pushed me to question, and feeling that was just incredibly healing.

Alexia: No, not my parents. I had told two of my sisters before, and then, obviously, I told my dad on the course, and then, before the show aired, I ended up calling my mom and [sister] Portia to tell them because I obviously did not want that to be the first time they read it. And even though I spoke about it on the course, I’m still very, very afraid to tell them afterward, too.

Mauricio: It was extremely difficult … I was just proud of Alexia every single day, every single moment … hearing that story was just another revelation of her conquering and finally talking about something that I wish she never held back … I just wanted to reach out and just hug her. But by the same token, I also wanted to give her space and let her be her in that moment that she was sharing with everybody. So there was like a lot of stuff going through my mind.

There was anger toward this kid that did this … But [watching her let go of it] was beautiful to watch … from my perspective, it was like, “Do I reach over and become a dad and just give her a big hug, or do I let her go through this moment, psychologically speaking, of letting it all come out?”

And I was just proud of her all the way around.

In hindsight, I love that she was able to share that, get it off her chest with us, with everybody, with the world. I think it’s super powerful.

Yes, I live by a lot of different small philosophies. Certainty versus doubt. Momentum is the cure of all fears. All of these are the different things where you just have to move forward, right? In order to accomplish something, you kind of just have to move forward, right? … the moment that I went from being an agent to opening up a brokerage, you jump off the cliff; you hope the parachute catches.

To today … here we are in a really difficult real estate market. I mean, it is not fun out there right now whatsoever. Yet [The Agency is] still growing. We’re still putting money out there. We’re still doing things right. So yeah, to me that’s just a philosophy that I always live by.

Mauricio: I don’t know. We’ll just keep going. I really like that show Traitors. I would love to be on that show. That could be a fun one for me, so I’m putting that out into the universe.

Alexia: My dream would be to do a reality TV show with my family … We did Buying Beverly Hills, and we’ve done Real Housewives for like [16] years now. But we’ve never done something all of us together, just us, and I think that’ll be really cool.

Mauricio: I’m going to leave that one on the table. If anything, it’s for 2030. There’s still plenty of time to do that and make that decision. But I love LA, and I think I can help LA a lot. I think we live in an amazing city, and if the moment comes, and I’m set up in the right position in the business and I feel like I can actually win, I might do it. But I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t feel like I could actually win.

Mauricio: It’s an absolute mess, what’s going on in our in our in our industry right now, particularly with the listings. My take is, it’s quite simple. I think that there’s a lot of change that’s happening. I believe that it’s somewhere in the middle. Like I do everything.

I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a big, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.

#5461. Token sticker shock pushes enterprises from frontier labs toward open-weight AI factories

Enterprises have spent the AI boom racing to secure graphics processing units, or GPUs, but the harder decisions now sit above the hardware. Token bills, data sovereignty and model choice increasingly decide which AI pilots reach production, a shift on display at the SC26 supercomputing conference.

Dell Technologies Inc. has spent the past year pushing its AI Factory beyond servers and storage. Customers now want a full-stack outcome that covers software, open-source tools, models and operations, according to Brad Maltz (pictured), senior director of AI solutions at Dell.

“The hardware’s key because that drives the tokens,” he said. “You really, truly need a full-stack AI factory view above and beyond just the hardware stack.”

Maltz spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how token bills and data sovereignty are steering enterprises toward open-weight models and a full-stack AI Factory. The interview came as Dell rolled out AI Factory updates at the conference. (* Disclosure below.)

Many enterprises are still stuck in pilot mode, and coding assistants are often the easiest place to start. Employees have already tried tools from Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, so teams want to apply that experience to business use cases. Once those pilots grow, the bill arrives, Maltz explained.

“The token spend right now in the frontier labs and the hyperscalers — that’s a little more than we expected,” he said. “We didn’t expect to spend $10,000, $20,000 per person per month.”

Cost is only one trigger. Data sovereignty, intellectual property leakage, security and governance all have to be addressed before a pilot goes live. Those requirements are steering many enterprises toward open-weight models they can fine-tune and run on-premises, including U.S. options such as Nvidia Corp.’s Nemotron, according to Maltz.

“There will always be frontier labs. There will always be open-weight models,” he said. “The question is going to be: do we have enough diversity with the open weights to meet the enterprise use cases?”

To keep pace, Dell launched its AI Ecosystem Program to validate software partners on its AI Factory. About 60 more partners have applied or are under evaluation, and each addition lets Dell solve 10 to 30 more customer problems, Maltz noted. For sovereign deployments, that often means disconnected, on-premises systems that keep models next to the GPUs and data enterprises already control.

“People understand data is the lifeblood of AI,” he said. “It’s the thing that trains the models. It’s the thing the models operate against. It comes from your enterprise business applications.”

#5460. Dorit Kemsley Reveals She’s Found a New Home After Eviction From the L.A. Family Estate She Shared With Estranged Husband PK

"Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" star Dorit Kemsley has revealed she has moved into a new property after she and her estranged husband, PK Kemsley, were "ordered" to list their longtime Los Angeles mansion following a prolonged legal dispute during which the businessman admitted they were experiencing a "financial crisis."

While attending the Maison D’Or cocktail launch at The Sun Rose West Hollywood, Dorit told Page Six that she and her children, Jagger, 12, and Phoenix, 10, have found a new place to call home.

“As everyone knows, we were going to court to be evicted by a certain date, which is pretty crummy, but I did find another house. The kids and I are moving into a new home imminently. Fresh beginnings, fresh start. We are all welcoming it," she told the outlet.

Dorit, 50, and PK, 58, are embroiled in a contentious divorce that has been exacerbated by significant monetary woes, including the looming threat of foreclosure on their $7 million Encino, CA, home.

In July, PK requested a judge allow him to sell the property while accusing the reality TV star of leaving their children with her parents in Florida—while providing no information about when she plans to return to the U.S., while he has been left to fight for their home alone.

PK alleged that Dorit was gone for a "minimum of three weeks," per court documents seen by the New York Post, stating that her "extended trip" demonstrates her "prioritization of personal travel over addressing the urgent financial crisis facing [their] family home."

In August, TMZ reported that PK's wish was granted after a judge ordered the sale of the six-bedroom, 10-bathroom Los Angeles abode, while noting that the TV personality had to move out by November.

According to the outlet, a hearing was held on Aug. 26, when PK alleged that Dorit had not been paying the mortgage on the home.

Meanwhile, Dorit, who is being represented by lawyer Samantha Spector, claimed that PK should be paying the bills, adding that he has enough money to cover the debt as well.

The back and forth between the acrimonious exes continued when PK accused Dorit of delaying the home's listing, while she alleged that he had refused to sign an agreement with celebrity real estate agent Zach Goldsmith of The Agency, whom Dorit said she hired to help market the property.

Goldsmith has loose ties to the "Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" world. Not only does he work for Kyle Richards' estranged husband, Mauricio Umansky, he is also expecting a baby with the reality TV star's daughter Farrah Aldjufrie.

Neither PK nor Dorit will be able to delay the sale any longer after a judge determined that the property must be listed, with Goldsmith as the agent, while also ruling that PK should become a manager of the LLC through which they bought the dwelling to ensure a swift sale.

The judge also ruled that Dorit will have to cover the cost of utilities, as well as the past-due amounts.

Meanwhile, PK was ordered to pay the mortgage until Dorit moves out. However, he will be reimbursed for all the payments made using any profits from the sale.

The businessman will also get back the funds he put into the home following their split. The judge denied his request for sanctions.

It marked the latest in what has been a very ugly separation battle between the two reality TV stars.

Just last month, Dorit came under fire from PK when she jetted off on a lavish European vacation, during which she celebrated her 50th birthday in true style, enjoying a lavish lunch alongside Hermès executive Michael Coste.

Dorit's European getaway infuriated her estranged spouse, who filed legal documents on July 13 in which he slammed his former partner for taking the trip while they are still going through a "financial crisis."

The home has come close to hitting the foreclosure auction block in recent months. However, each planned sale was postponed, according to reports—although PK's legal team noted in its filing that the risk of their losing the dwelling has "escalated" significantly.

He further claimed in the filing that he stopped the property from falling into foreclosure after splashing out $300,000.

PK alleged that Dorit has not made any mortgage payments, despite raking in a substantial income from "The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" and spending what he estimates to be $1 million on luxury getaways and designer clothing.

PK argued that she has put her travel plans ahead of the family's financial troubles, requesting that the court allow him to move forward with selling the property.

Dorit filed for divorce from PK in 2025 after 10 years of marriage, citing "irreconcilable differences."

At the time, she asked the judge to award her sole custody of their kids, in addition to spousal support.

The filing came just one day after PK was photographed sharing a kiss with Shana Wall.

One month after Dorit filed for divorce, PK requested joint custody of their children, while also waiving his right to spousal support and asking the court to do the same for Dorit's plea.

They announced their separation in May 2024 in a joint statement: "We have had our struggles over the last few years and continue to work through them as two people who love each other and share two amazing children together. We have made the mutual and difficult decision to take some time apart and reevaluate our relationship while we prioritize our children.”

Dorit and PK purchased their sprawling Encino abode for $6.48 million in 2019, according to records, and have since made several attempts to sell it, beginning in September 2020, when they listed the property for $9.5 million.

They reduced their asking price to $7.99 million a few weeks later, before whipping the home off the market altogether.

It was relisted for the same price in April 2021, but once again vanished from the market within a matter of weeks.

The couple have made substantial upgrades to the home since buying it—and have also proudly showcased the property in numerous episodes of their hit Bravo show.

#5459. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends.
