#5458. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

#5457. Business as usual for Nvidia as it beats expectations in first earnings call after Huang’s resignation

Nvidia Corp. delivered earnings and revenue that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations and offered strong guidance for the current quarter in its first earnings call since the shocking resignation of its iconic co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang.

The results were so impressive that they slammed the brakes on a weeklong slide, as Nvidia’s stock rose more than 4% in late trading today.

The chipmaker reported third-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.68 per share, surpassing Wall Street’s target of $2.48 per share by a comfortable margin. Revenue for the period came to $115.84 billion, more than double a year earlier and above the $109.1 billion consensus estimate.

The vast majority of those sales stemmed from Nvidia’s core data center business, which delivered revenue of $107.6 billion, higher than the Street’s $101.87 billion forecast. For the current quarter, Nvidia said it’s expecting its revenue to grow by about 90%, to $130 billion. Though that suggests a slowdown sequentially from the prior quarter, it’s still nicely above Wall Street’s target of $125.1 billion.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress (pictured, with Huang in the background) has become a familiar face to analysts on Nvidia’s conference calls, but today she found herself in a very different position. For the first time, she was fielding questions as the company’s interim CEO, which means her responsibilities now go well beyond the numbers. She was joined on the call by Nvidia’s Chairman of the Board Harvey Jones, who insisted that the board has no intention of bringing Huang back as CEO.

Nvidia has been under a cloud all week following the abrupt resignation of Huang, which came days after he admitted to having an affair with a businesswoman who’s alleged to be a Chinese spy. In the days that followed that scandal, which included rumors of a second affair with an Nvidia executive and also a potential third fling with yet another company employee, the chipmaker’s stock had been in a downward spiral. But that trend was finally reversed following the company’s strong guidance today.

One of the central questions investors had going into the call was if Nvidia would scrap its previous forecast for 70% revenue growth in the fiscal year ending January 2028. However, Kress did the opposite and raised the company’s full-year guidance to 75% growth.

In raising the company’s outlook, Kress told analysts on the call that “it’s business as usual at Nvidia,” despite all that has happened. And indeed, throughout much of her commentary, she focused strictly to the numbers that revealed a business still in good health. With regard to the guidance, Kress stressed that this forecast “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of customer demand and our customers’ access to capital.”

“Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week to support both what we are doing here at earnings, but also supporting all of our different employees around the world,” Kress said. “Remember, we have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class, multiyear roadmap. And I think that’s important from a business perspective.”

Kress said Nvidia expects frontier labs such as OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic Group PBC and others to account for about 15% of its data center revenue this year, in a sign that they’re increasingly standing up their own data center infrastructure rather than renting from cloud providers.

“As frontier models become more capable, adoption and revenue are scaling rapidly, with Anthropic annualized revenue reaching $181 billion at the end of October,” Kress said.

Another big chunk of Nvidia’s revenue comes from so-called neocloud infrastructure providers. Much of the money those customers spend on its chips stems from a complex web of financing, with much of it being traceable back to Nvidia itself. Kress told analysts that the company is continuing to help neoclouds and frontier labs to secure the land, power and data center capacity they need to grow, and that it may be willing to share revenue from neoclouds together with the upfront sales of its products, if they meet certain conditions.

Kress said Nvidia currently has more than $32 billion in total commitments to neoclouds through 2032, but insisted that these take effect only if those customers are able to “secure the funding they need to purchase the data center infrastructure products they require, and if the related compute capacity is deployed and made operational.”

Another closely watched number is Nvidia’s gross margin, which has narrowed in recent quarters as its supply commitments have slowly piled up. Investors will have been pleased to see that Nvidia beat Wall Street’s expectations on that metric, with its nonstandard gross margin ending the quarter at 74.9%, above the forecast of 74%. Its margins still declined compared to the previous quarter, though, blamed on the ramping up of production of its latest generation Rubin graphics processing units.

The results prove that AI demand remains as strong as ever. But the bigger question for the market now is not how long Nvidia can sustain its growth, rather whether or not it can sustain its current level of profitability, Forrester analyst Naveen Chhabra told SiliconANGLE.

“The next battle is not against competitors. Nvidia must navigate export controls, sovereign AI initiatives, supply chain expansion and rising capital intensity, all while trying to protect its industry-leading margins,” Chhabra said. “Nvidia continues to defy gravity with triple-digit growth, software-like margins and a strong outlook despite trade restrictions. The next test is whether it can preserve its economic dominance as geopolitics and AI infrastructure costs rise.”

Despite the after-hours gain, Nvidia’s stock is still down 24% this month, and last Friday it completed its sixth successive weekly decline. That’s the company’s longest losing streak since 2012, and its shares are now trading at their lowest level since July 2025.

The decline began several weeks before news of Huang’s extramarital escapades became public knowledge. The company has also faced rising concerns about a possible slowdown in the artificial intelligence industry and a political shift in Washington D.C. as a result of the Republicans’ stunning losses during the midterm elections earlier this month.

Despite Jones’ insistence that Huang will not be returning to the CEO role, the prospect of his doing so cannot be ruled out. In his first public comments since his ousting, Huang said in a post on X that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

There are plenty of people who would like to see Huang return, including U.S. President Donald Trump and various luminaries from the technology world. Last Thursday, someone created an online petition calling for the reinstatement of Huang, and it has been signed by names including Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games Inc. CEO Tim Sweeney.

It could be possible that Huang ends up returning to the company in a different capacity than CEO. Susquehanna analyst Chris Rolland told CNBC that the chipmaker could end up taking him back under a new role, such as a consultant or a strategic adviser.

“I think that helps bridge the gap here, he can give technical and strategic advisory services that I think would be incredibly important to the company,” the analyst said.

#5456. Christie’s International Real Estate Names Art Tobani National VP of Affiliate Development

Christie’s International Real Estate announced it has named Art Tobani as its national vice president of affiliate development, bringing the longtime industry business-development executive on to accelerate the network’s expansion across the U.S.

Tobani brings more than 20 years of real estate business development experience, Christie’s noted, including 12 years in brokerage affiliate sales and advisory services. Throughout his career, he has driven business growth through new affiliate signings, mergers and acquisitions, and high-impact recruiting.

“Art has a real talent for looking at brokerage businesses from different angles, identifying opportunities, and bringing the right people together to unlock value,” said Gavin Swartzman, president of Christie’s International Real Estate. “I’ve seen his abilities firsthand, and I’m excited to have him on our team as we enter our next phase of growth. His experience and relationships will be a tremendous asset as we expand our U.S. presence.”

At Christie’s International Real Estate, the brokerage added that Tobani will leverage a similar multifaceted approach, strengthening the brand’s presence in key U.S. markets while helping existing affiliates identify opportunities to expand their businesses.

“While Christie’s International Real Estate is an established iconic brand, I see a lot of potential growth, and that’s what excites me about this role,” said Tobani. “We’re in an interesting time. There’s a lot of industry disruption and market challenges, and brokers and agents are looking for new ways to compete and build their businesses. We’re in a great position to help them do that with Christie’s International Real Estate’s reputation, global referral platform, technology, and relationship with Christie’s auction house.”

In addition to identifying prospective new affiliates for Christie’s International Real Estate, the brokerage stated that Tobani will serve as a resource to existing broker-owners across the network, helping them evaluate opportunities to expand into new markets, attract top-producing teams, and pursue acquisitions that complement their existing businesses. Tobani will also help identify and develop new markets for @properties.

“Our affiliates have had a lot of success with the @properties brand, and it’s ripe for expansion. They’ve embraced our approach to technology, marketing, agent development, and building a strong brokerage culture, and the results have been outstanding. I’m excited to see what Art does with both brands,” said @properties Co-Founder and Co-CEO Thad Wong.

For more information, visit https://www.christiesrealestate.com/.

#5455. In Portland, OR, Entry-Level Buyers Suddenly Have More Options

A new metro-by-metro analysis from Realtor.com® reveals where buyers can still find a starter home. These options have felt increasingly scarce as rising prices and climbing mortgage rates create challenges for many would-be buyers.

According to research, the national share of starter homes in active inventory fell from 38.1% in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026. During that same period, starter home prices rose 30.8%, from about $260,000 to $340,000.

However, some cities are bucking this trend, and Portland, OR, has seen an encouraging uptick in starter homes in recent years.

A starter home is defined as a property priced at roughly 80% of a metro's median list price, capturing the relative affordability of an area's lower-end market. These homes are typically smaller and less expensive, making them accessible to a first-time buyer or a household with an Income at or below the local median.

In the Portland-Vancouver, OR-WA, metro area, the share of starter homes has shown positive growth. The share was 28.0% in 2019 and dipped slightly to 27.8% in 2022 before rising to 32.0% in 2026.

This represents a total increase of +4.0 percentage points since 2019, signaling growing opportunity for buyers in the market.

For those deciding between renting or buying, current data suggests renting is the more affordable path for now. A July Rent Report found that the cost of buying a starter home in the 50 largest metros was $858 higher per month than renting one. This financial advantage to renting holds true across all 50 of the largest metros.

In the Portland-Vancouver, OR-WA, market, the median rent cost was $1,606 as of July 2026.

This figure represents a 1.60% decrease year-over-year, making an apartment an even more financially sound choice while saving for a down payment. Prospective buyers can use a rent vs. buy calculator to weigh their options.

#5454. Alphabet’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5B to accelerate drug discovery with AI

Isomorphic Labs Ltd. today announced that it has closed a $5 billion investment led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital.

The venture capital firms were joined by more than a half-dozen other backers. The group included Isomorphic parent Alphabet Inc., which made a “significant investment.” The search giant provided the capital through its GV and CapitalG startup funds.

Isomorphic offers a software platform called the Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine, or IsoDDE for short. It uses artificial intelligence to speed up several of the tasks involved in developing new medicines. The Alphabet unit says that multiple pharmaceutical companies are already using IsoDDE to power drug discovery programs.

Pathogens such as viruses comprise numerous proteins that each power a different biological process. Drugs work by neutralizing a single, particularly important protein without which the pathogen can’t function. Developing a new drug requires researchers to find a vulnerable protein within a pathogen and then develop a compound that can effectively target it.

The first step of the workflow is mapping out the shape of a target protein. Researchers look for so-called binding pockets, recesses on the protein’s surface to which a drug can be attached. The task is highly complicated because proteins don’t have fixed shapes. Their configuration changes when they interact with other molecules or encounter new environmental conditions, which happens often.

Isomorphic says that IsoDDE speeds up the task of finding binding pockets. When there are no such pockets, it helps researchers develop compounds that cause a target protein to form them.

Once scientists identify a binding pocket, they have to find a way of attaching a drug molecule to it. The pharmaceutical industry searches for such binding mechanisms using a method called FEP. FEP algorithms can be highly hardware-intensive, which makes them costly. Moreover, they often require a detailed, three-dimensional model of a target protein.

The process of creating 3D protein models for FEP algorithms is itself a highly complex task. It requires scientists to freeze a target protein in a crystal and scan it using specialized X-ray equipment.

IsoDDE skips that step of the research workflow. Furthermore, Isomorphic says that the software can generate higher-quality output than FEP algorithms.

“Our drug design engine is generating molecules with unprecedented precision and speed,” said Isomorphic Chief Executive Demis Hassabis. “This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials.”

Isomorphic added that it plans to build new bioengineering infrastructure and grow its partner ecosystem.

#5453. Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the company said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment issues, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

#5451. Kris Jenner Turns Her $20 Million California Mansion Into a Holiday Spectacle With a ‘Magical’ Christmas Light Display

Kris Jenner is welcoming the holiday season with a glowing display at her California mansion, where warm white lights outline the gates, hedges, roofline, and doorways.

The reality TV star, 71, shared a look at the decorations in a video posted to Instagram on Nov. 13, giving followers a view of the home’s exterior as the entrance gates opened.

The clip is set to “Somewhere in My Memory,” the instrumental piece associated with the film "Home Alone."

As the gates move apart, the lights come into view across the landscaping and around the house, creating a bright welcome along the property’s entrance.

“It’s my favorite time of the year!” Jenner wrote in the caption. She described the setup as “the chicest Christmas lights in all the land” and “just magical! I could stare at them all night.”

The display extends beyond the immediate entrance. Trees, bushes, and other landscaping are also illuminated, making the lights visible throughout the grounds.

The video focuses on the home’s exterior, where the warm white lighting brings attention to the landscaping and the architectural outlines of the mansion.

Jenner’s post arrives as her family begins sharing its holiday decorating for the year.

Her daughter Khloé Kardashian showed off the lights at her own Los Angeles home earlier in November.

Thousands of white lights were arranged around the trees, windows, and doors, giving the exterior a gingerbread house-inspired look. Kardashian credited lighting installation company The Christmas Brothers with the work.

The holiday displays have become a recurring part of the Kardashian-Jenner family’s seasonal social media posts.

Last year, Jenner’s daughters Kim and Kourtney Kardashian gave followers a peek at another festive detail at their mother’s home: a bunk room prepared for the grandchildren.

The sleeping area featured several sets of bunk beds dressed with red checked bedspreads, Christmas wreaths, and twinkling lights.

Kourtney described the setup as “magical” in an Instagram Stories post, while Kim shared her own reaction to the room, asking how cute her mother’s bunk bed room was for the children.

Jenner also shared glimpses of the family’s interior holiday decorations in photos from their Christmas Eve celebration in 2025.

The images showed a fireplace dressed with garland and lights, with stockings hanging from the mantel.

A collection of Christmas trees stood beneath the staircase, each dripping in ornaments. The dining table was arranged with red linens, plaid dishes, greenery, and reindeer-inspired candleholders.

This year’s video turns the attention back outside, offering a quick look at the lights welcoming guests to Jenner’s home.

With the gates opening onto illuminated landscaping and the house outlined in white lights, the display gives the family’s holiday season a festive start.

#5450. General-purpose robot maker Genesis AI reels in $500M at $3.5B valuation

Genesis AI SAS today announced that it has raised $500 million in funding from a group of prominent investors.

Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse led the Series A round. They were joined by the venture capital arms of Nvidia Corp., Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Zoom Communications Inc., Samsung Electronics Co. and Ericsson. Former Google Chief Executive Eric Schmidt contributed as well along with other tech executives.

Paris-based Genesis develops a general-purpose robot called Eno (pictured). Unlike humanoid robots, it moves using a wheeled base rather than legs. The wheeled base can adjust Eno’s height using a mechanism that consists of two large panels connected by a hinge. The module enables the robot to adapt its configuration to each task.

Eno is powered by a custom artificial intelligence model called GENE. Genesis says that the algorithm is easier to train than traditional robotics-optimized neural networks, which can translate to higher output quality.

The dataset on which an AI model is trained must be tailored to the robot it’s intended to control. If a company is building an AI model for a four-legged robot, the training dataset must include footage of four-legged robots. The more specialized the robot, the more difficult it is to collect the necessary training data.

Genesis has come up with a workaround to that challenge. Eno’s palms and fingers are based on a custom design closely modeled after the human hand. As a result, the robot can be trained on demonstrations in which humans perform tasks with their hands. That kind of training data is much easier to produce than footage of robots performing work.

Eno’s robotic hands have 20 degrees of freedom, which means they can perform that many motions. The human hand has 27 degrees of freedom. Additionally, Genesis covered the hands with a soft material designed to mimic skin.

The GENE foundation model that powers Emo can perform tasks comprising dozens of steps. Genesis has released demo videos that show the system playing the piano, cooking and solving a Rubik’s Cube. According the company, that versatility enables Eno to operate in not only industrial environments but also homes.

“We’re working to build the world’s best general-purpose robot,” said Genesis co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian. “By building it all ourselves, we can obsess over every detail and improve the entire robot faster in one closed loop. This funding will accelerate our efforts to deploy our robots in the real world at scale.”

The company will use the capital to hire more AI researchers and roboticists. Additionally, Genesis will step up its training data collection efforts in a bid to expand its AI model’s capabilities.

#5449. Mortgage Applications Dip as Rates Hit Three-Week High

House keys with a house shaped keychain resting on a mortgage application form

Mortgage applications dipped slightly this week, in keeping with the average 30-year mortgage rate rising to a three-week high.

The latest Market Composite Index from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)—its measure of mortgage loan activity volume and includes purchases and refinances—shows mortgage application activity decreasing 2.3% on a seasonally adjusted basis after last week’s 6.2% increase. On an unadjusted basis, the Index decreased 5% compared with the previous week.

This week’s decline follows weeks of fluctuations as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate still solidly remains over 7%–last week decreasing to 7.11% according to Freddie Mac but currently sitting at 7.46%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Freddie Mac’s next rate report will be released Thursday.

“Mortgage applications dipped as mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed mortgage rate up to its highest level in three weeks at 7.35 percent,” said Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “Purchase applications were down 18 percent from a year ago, as renewed affordability challenges from elevated mortgage rates have pushed prospective homebuyers to the sidelines.”

MBA’s Refinance Index decreased 2% from the previous week and was 54% lower than the same week one year ago. MBA’s seasonally adjusted Purchase Index–its weekly measurement of nationwide home loan applications based on a sample of about 75% of U.S. mortgage activity–decreased 3% from one week earlier. The unadjusted Purchase Index decreased 7% compared with the previous week and was 18% lower than the same week one year ago, according to the report.

The refinance share of mortgage activity saw an increase this week–to 41.1% from 39.8% the previous week, with Kan pointing to a rise in FHA refinances as most notable.

“Overall refinance activity was down over the week, but FHA refinances increased almost 7 percent,” Kan stated. “The FHA rate was around 30 basis points below the conforming rate, which supported refinance opportunities for some homeowners.”

The FHA share of total applications increased to 16.1% from 15.5% the week prior, with MBA listing the VA share of total applications increasing to 12.8% from 12.4% the week prior. The USDA share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5 percent from the week prior.

Kan also pointed to additional macroeconomic indicators as potentially weighing on home-purchase application activity into the new year.

“Treasury yields rose last week amid data showing inflation accelerated in October and Fed officials acknowledging that additional rate hikes may be needed in the coming months,” he said.

#5448. Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

“Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he said. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”

Hale said jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Yun said rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”

However, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

#5447. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

#5446. Brain implant technology startup Science Corp. raises $400M to bring its medical devices to market

Brain-computer interface company Science Corp. today revealed it has raised $400 million in a late-stage round of funding that brings its valuation to $3.5 billion.

The Series D round, announced in a blog post today, was led by high-profile venture capital firm Khosla Ventures. It was joined by the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator and PLC Neurotech. The Ackman Oxman Institute’s participation is notable, as it appears to be one of brain research center’s first ventures after being established by the hedge fund billionaire Bill Ackman and his wife Neri Oxman earlier this year.

The money from today’s round will give Science the capital it needs to bring its flagship product PRIMA to the U.S. healthcare market, having already established traction in Europe. PRIMA is a specialized chip that’s implanted into the eyes of patients suffering from age-related macular degeneration or AMD, which is one of the most common causes of vision loss among older adults. It’s paired with a special pair of glasses that help restore partial vision to AMD sufferers, and it has already been approved by some European countries.

For instance, PRIMA has already been implanted in the eyes of several patients in Germany, and the company has dozens of additional surgical procedures scheduled to help more patients restore their vision. In addition, the device is expected to be made available in Italy, France and the U.K. in the coming months. Science wants to offer PRIMA to patients who are willing to pay for it out of pocket at a special unit at Moorfields Private Eye Hospital in London, but it has not disclosed how much people would have to pay.

As for the U.S., PRIMA is currently being vetted for its suitability by the Food and Drug Administration. Science founder and Chief Executive Max Hodak, who previously served as the CEO of Elon Musk’s Neuralink Inc., told Bloomberg in an interview today that he’s hoping it will be made available to U.S. patients early next year.

That’s because PRIMA is being pushed through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption pathway, which allows for the rapid approval of experimental medical technologies that can treat rare conditions. Though AMD is not uncommon, the company has argued that it’s rare to see the condition affect people in both eyes.

In the future, the company also plans to make PRIMA available as a treatment for Stargardt’s disease and retinitis pigmentosa, which also cause blindness.

The PRIMA device consists of 378 pixels that are each equipped with a tiny electrode. When infrared light hits a pixel, it activates the attached electrode, which in turn simulates cells in the patient’s retina. The electrodes thereby substitute for retinal tissue lost to disease.

The infrared light that activates the implant’s pixels comes from a pair of glasses worn by the patient. According to Science, the glasses generate infrared signals based on footage from a forward-facing camera. The camera, which records the user’s surroundings, includes a lens that filters interference such as strong sunlight.

While Science is focused on PRIMA for now, its long-term vision is not limited to restoring people’s sight. It’s also developing the Biohybrid implant, which connects directly to the brain.

It’s built from cultured neurons that are combined with silicon chips and integrated with the brain’s circuits. The company says it has already identified the first disease it intends to treat with Biohybrid but has not disclosed what that condition is.

For now, it’s focused on testing Biohybrid. So far, it has conducted tests only on animals, but it hopes to launch its first human clinical trials within the next 16 months. To do this, it has recruited the respected Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who has previously said that the device holds promise for treating Parkinson’s disease and other brain illnesses and injuries.

#5445. Florida Homes Are Flooding in the Dry Season—and Too Many Owners Are Unprepared

The Sunshine State is facing an unusual bout of heavy rain and flooding in the middle of its dry season, which usually begins in November.

The unexpected weather has put pressure on drainage systems and left standing water in many communities, particularly those in South Florida’s Broward County and along Central Florida’s Atlantic Coast in places like Daytona Beach and Cape Canaveral.

On Nov. 18, the western part of Broward County faced what meteorologists refer to as a “rain bomb.” In just 24 hours, West Hollywood received over 15 inches of rain, while surrounding neighborhoods saw about 10 inches.

Due to the severity of the situation, which has led to issues such as stranded cars and out-of-service traffic signals, Broward County and Hollywood declared states of emergency, with Hollywood officials encouraging residents to shelter in place and avoid unnecessary travel.

Forecasters expect additional rainfall through the end of this week as well as 2 to 4 inches across Eastern Florida, with about 4 to 8 inches from Miami to Jacksonville between Tuesday and Friday. Some areas may even get hit with up to 12 inches.

While the wet and windy conditions are expected to improve, the Southeast may see a cooler, rainier Thanksgiving this year. The rain could linger from the upper coast of Texas toward the southern Atlantic Coast throughout the holiday weekend.

“The dry season doesn’t mean your house is in the clear. Florida is currently showing us that heavy rain can flood homes miles from the beach,” says John Espenschied, owner at InsuranceBrokers.com in O'Fallon, MO.

If you’re a Florida homeowner, these unexpected weather conditions are a reminder that flooding may occur year-round—even outside of the traditional summer, hurricane season.

They can also give you a nudge to review your home insurance policy as it relates to flooding and take precautionary steps to protect your property and loved ones.

Florida’s current flooding is drawing attention to the fact that many homeowners do not have enough insurance coverage to recover from the damage.

The Realtor.com® 2026 Housing and Climate Risk Report highlights the financial consequences. It found that over 6% of U.S. homes face severe flood risk, representing almost $3.4 trillion in property value.

At the same time, the number of active flood insurance policies from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) fell by 4.5% between May 2025 and May 2026, decreasing from 3.62 million to 3.45 million.

And the issue goes beyond coastal communities.

Moody's U.S. flood risk analysis, which accounts for flooding from heavy rain and overflowing rivers rather than just coastal storms, found that potential uninsured residential flood losses could exceed $375 billion in a modeled 1-in-100-year flood scenario. This may result in a national insurance protection gap of 65%.

According to Chris Bacon, chief operating officer of Openly in Boston, there are four primary factors that explain why many homeowners are lacking adequate flood protection.

First, most homeowners do not live in the highest-risk flood zones, so they don’t consider it a significant peril. Second, the cost of flood insurance can be high, especially for homeowners in higher-risk flood zones.

“The additional cost can be a constraint of homeowners’ budgets, and thus they choose to not purchase the coverage,” explains Bacon.

Third, mortgage companies do not require flood coverage unless the home is located in a high flood risk zone, so homeowners simply skip it to save money. Finally, the coverage from the NFIP, which goes up to only $250,000, is often lower than what a consumer needs should there be a major loss.

While there are private flood providers that can cover higher limits, premiums can be significantly higher because pricing reflects each property’s individual flood risk.

“That’s why working with an independent insurance agent is so critical. They can provide the right coverage advice and show multiple options so you can make an informed decision for your unique situation,” Bacon adds.

If you own a home in Florida (or any other state where flooding may occur), take a close look at your home insurance coverage. Determine whether it covers water that rises from the street or yard. Unfortunately, most policies don’t.

In the event you don’t have flooding insurance, get quotes from both the NFIP and private insurers.

“The federal program caps building coverage at $250,000. You can buy up to $100,000 in separate coverage for your belongings. If your home would cost $400,000 to rebuild, ask what it would cost to insure the extra $150,000,” adds Espenschied

Don’t forget to compare deductibles and start dates, and remember that federal coverage usually takes 30 days to kick in.

John Dickson, president and CEO at Aon Edge, a private flood insurance provider based in Kalispell, MT, points out that deciding whether to purchase flood insurance is a question of values.

“When you get a picture of how much you can lose, choosing to purchase flood insurance becomes an easy decision,” Dickson explains.

Fortunately, there are a number of precautions you can take to reduce the risk of serious flood damage on your property.

“Keep gutters clear of debris, and remove or clear debris blocking nearby storm drains and install a sewer backflow check valve,” says Bacon.

If you have a basement, elevate HVAC equipment, electrical panels, and water heaters above expected flood levels where possible.

Outside of your home, grade soil away from the foundation and extend downspouts to improve drainage. Finally, keep sandbags or flood barriers on hand, and know your evacuation routes.

If you have a swimming pool, proper pool preparation is key. Avoid draining the pool completely, as hydrostatic pressure from waterlogged soil can cause the pool shell to pop out of the ground.

“Instead, lower the water level slightly (no more than 1 to 2 feet) to allow room for heavy rainfall, turn off power to the pool equipment at the breaker, and secure or store loose pool furniture and equipment inside to prevent severe damage,” Bacon explains.

To protect personal property, particularly high-value, irreplaceable, and sentimental items, move them off ground-level floors and store them on upper levels or high shelves. Keep important documents, family heirlooms, and electronics in sealed, waterproof containers, and create digital backups of critical financial and personal records.

For furniture or heavier items that must remain on the ground level, use blocks or risers to elevate them above potential floodwater lines before severe weather arrives.

“None of these steps eliminates risk, but together they reduce damage and help lead to faster recovery,” adds Bacon.

#5444. He sold Bibles door to door. Now he runs a 35,000-home luxury exchange club in 103 countries

What do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

On this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

He explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking big risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy says many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

For agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

#5443. At Ignite 2026, Microsoft reinvents Copilot as the autonomous engine of enterprise work

Business knowledge workers spend their days running a gauntlet of emails, spreadsheets, messaging platforms, meetings and productivity applications, wasting hours of their time switching from one to another to get mundane tasks done.

Microsoft Corp. is now proposing an alternative: It wants Copilot to evolve from a somewhat useful generative artificial intelligence assistant into the autonomous foundation for all business work. At Microsoft Ignite 2026 today in San Francisco, it unveiled a slate of powerful new capabilities and features for its favorite autonomous tool as part of its ongoing effort to transform Copilot into the new workplace operating system.

The company’s new vision was outlined in a blog post by Microsoft Chief Marketing Officer Jared Spataro, who pointed to its comprehensive intelligence layer for work, called WorkIQ, as the critical engine behind this shift.

Spataro explained that enterprise work is notoriously messy. Microsoft 365 stores roughly 19.5 exabytes of customer’s business data, and it’s adding billions of new files, documents, emails and messages each day. For businesses, it’s not enough to just give an autonomous AI agent access to this data and expect it to start making sense of it. It needs WorkIQ, which acts as the centralized reasoning layer for all Copilot agents, retrieving data, understanding its intent, identifying what’s important for the task it has been assigned while ignoring everything else.

While WorkIQ sits under the hood, Spataro says, the average worker’s day will soon begin in “Home,” which is the new user interface for Copilot. Home merges traditional chat with a portal called Cowork, which is where people can start delegating different tasks to AI agents. Spataro said Home is like a grounding anchor, or a place where workers can log in each day to pick up where they left off.

Home’s key element is Auto, which is an intelligent composer that dynamically routes users’ requests and prompts to the most suitable AI model. It’s the place where most people will typically begin each new task.

“Tell Copilot what you want to accomplish and it intelligently routes the work to the right models and effort for the task,” Spataro explained. “For more complex work, Auto may recommend moving from Chat to Cowork. If you agree, Copilot transfers the tasks seamlessly, helping to deliver the outcome with the right level of investment.”

Another key part of Home is called Today. It’s a “proactive command center” that’s currently available in private preview that scans a user’s email, calendar and Teams threads in order to highlight the things they have to get done that day.

Best of all, it won’t leave users feeling overwhelmed, Spataro said, because it also helps them to complete that work. For instance, it can quickly draft replies to emails, propose alterations to someone’s schedule and queue other messages for the user to review.

Copilot’s ability to get work done has been advanced by its deeper integration with Microsoft’s Office suite. Spataro said the company is bringing the full capabilities of Office directly into the Copilot application.

As a result, users will be able to move effortlessly from ideation on a notepad or whiteboard to conjure up a completed Word document or Excel spreadsheet based on what they just outlined. Those files will live entirely within Copilot, which gains the ability to co-author alongside human colleagues. Because Office is now native to Copilot, every document and file will be secured by Microsoft 365’s strict security and compliance controls, Spataro said.

Human-to-agent collaboration is being boosted too with the arrival of Copilot Workspaces, which is a kind of canvas that both can access, Spataro said. Within Copilot Workspaces, an agent might draft a section of a document, then notify a human to come and review it when they get the chance. The human will be able to leave comments for other agents to address.

Autopilot is very different from standard AI agents that are programmed to wait for a user’s prompts. It’s continuously available, watching various Teams channels and the user’s email inbox for updates. It can automate recurring work processes, and it can manage entire project pipelines, such as a multistep supplier review, fully autonomously, Spataro said.

Autopilot is powerful, but safeguards are in place. Information technology teams have complete control over what it can and can’t access, and if something goes wrong they can step in and block it from doing anything else at a moment’s notice.

“Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail,” Spataro explained. “Powered by WorkIQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions. You decide what work Autopilot takes on and it will always check with you before key actions.”

Coding continues to be a major focus, and now Microsoft is giving everyday knowledge workers the ability to build software that can help them get their work done even faster. With Copilot Code, launching in a few week’s time, users will be able to generate interactive dashboards, persistent desktop widgets and lightweight business applications from simple, natural language prompts.

All of these Copilot-generated apps will be hosted within Copilot Managed Runtime, which is a new, highly-secure environment that IT teams can monitor to ensure none of them pose a risk to the company’s data.

To reassure organizations that their AI agents are not only secure, but also providing real value, Microsoft has updated the Agent 365 platform to give teams more control and visibility into their AI spending. Agent 365 now comes with a Business Analytics feature that brings a FinOps-style approach to AI budgeting.

Whereas most platforms just track token consumption, it goes further, measuring each agent’s return on investment by looking at the “work completed” and the number of hours it took. According to Spataro, this will give companies a much clearer picture of the benefits of their AI investments.

Finally, there’s a lot going on in terms of business data connectivity. For one thing, Microsoft said, it’s making sure that Dynamics 365, its combined customer relationship management and enterprise resource planning platform, doesn’t live in isolation. With Dynamics 365 in Copilot, its AI agents gain more than 100 prebuilt “skills” that allow them to perform tasks in sales, service and finance.

But Dynamics 365 isn’t for everyone, and Microsoft recognizes that many of its customers prefer to use alternative CRM tools. That’s why it announced a major new partnership with Salesforce Inc. that gives Copilot unprecedented access to the Salesforce platform too.

Their new offering is called Copilotforce, and it’s enabled by two-way “Zero Copy” integrations between Microsoft Fabric and Salesforce Data 360. The idea is that Copilotforce will bring trusted context from Salesforce directly into Copilot and also productivity and collaboration tools like Teams and Office. The new platform has 38 prebuilt skills to help Copilot start automating sales-related tasks, allowing them to retrieve customer data, generate meeting follow-ups and update CRM records based on tasks they’ve just completed.

There’s a lot to digest, but the deluge of updates sends a clear message that AI agents are on the march, expanding their role as they take on much more complex enterprise work.

#5442. This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.
