#5441. The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

Wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in New York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

That shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an important question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

The mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

At The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

As brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

Rainy Hake Austin is president of The Agency in Los Angeles. Get connected on Instagram.

#5440. CloudBackend grabs €6.6M to turn AI-generated prototypes into productive business applications

Just about anyone can knock up a working prototype application these days using artificial intelligence coding tools, but what happens when they want to turn that app into a viable business?

That’s the question that Swedish AI infrastructure startup CloudBackend AB thinks it can answer after raising €6.6 million ($7.25 million) in seed funding today. Leading the round was the family office of Carl-Henric Svanberg, formerly chairman of the Swedish government’s AI Commission, with participation from M2 Asset Management.

CloudBackend says it’s targeting the parts of application development that can’t be whipped up in seconds by generative AI tools. While vibe coding platforms such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex can deliver a working application, they can’t go the whole hog and turn it into a revenue-generating product.

The problem is that although vibe coding tools are great at generating application logic and user interfaces, they don’t know much about building the backend infrastructure. There’s a lot to do, because applications can’t just function – they also need robust security in place, the ability to scale up to thousands of users, they need to provide customer support, and they must work reliably in every situation. There’s also the question of how to monetize the app, getting insights from users, pricing considerations and marketing operations.

All of this is what CloudBackend’s Operations Platform is designed to handle, founder and Chief Executive Daniel Arthursson (pictured) told SiliconANGLE. It provides all of the backend infrastructure needed to turn any AI-generated prototype into a viable and profitable business within a single, accessible environment. “AI has made it much easier to build the first version of an application, but the challenge comes when customers sign in and expect the service to be secure, reliable and available every day,” he said.

Arthursson said the Operations Platform has five key components, including the extremely flexible Singularity Database that unifies relational data, object storage, caching and user files within a single platform. It offers robust identity and access controls integrated at the data layer, so users don’t have to stitch together multiple services to secure their application data.

Another key component of CloudBackend’s platform is “Build,” which allows skilled developers to create application frontends using declarative XML or native software development kits and then bind them to live data and deploy them in cloud environments without a continuous integration and deployment pipeline. Then there’s “Run,” which provides built-in tools for user subscriptions, customer relationship management and support, and revenue tracking within a single interface.

CloudBackend also offers collaboration tools that allow apps to keep their user’s data in perfect synchronization so multiple users can work together on projects. Finally, there’s a data sovereignty component that’s aimed at European organizations that must ensure all customer data is stored in Europe.

“We’re building the AI cloud infrastructure that helps creators make the leap from prototype to production without extensive technical knowledge,” Arthursson said. “It’s a new type of infrastructure designed for applications built with AI.”

CloudBackend’s infrastructure has been up and running with early access users so far, and with today’s funding round under its belt, it’s now planning to open it up to more users, with a free developer beta slated to open Nov. 24. The money from today’s round will also help CloudBackend to build deeper integrations with select vibe coding tools and large language models, Arthursson said.

The long-term vision, according to Arthursson, is to make the backend infrastructure and business operations as simple as the generative AI coding process has become.

Hans Lindroth, CEO of the Svanberg Family Office, said there will be lot of demand for what CloudBackend is offering, because it makes generative AI coding tools much more attractive when anyone can use them to start a business.

“AI makes it easier to build applications, but turning them into production-grade solutions for businesses is a different challenge,” he said. “We see a growing need for infrastructure that helps businesses to operate securely, serve customers reliably and expand their offerings. Daniel and his team have the experience and expertise to address that need and that’s why we chose to lead this round.”

#5439. Resident of Collapsed Brooklyn Building Sues for Negligence After Losing $100K Record Collection

The first of what is likely to be several lawsuits was filed in Kings County Superior Court on Monday, alleging widespread negligence by a host of landlords, construction companies and contractors in last week's deadly Brooklyn building collapse.

Dengane Omari Jack lived at 1321 Flatbush Ave., which collapsed last Wednesday, tragically killing eight and wounding 18 others. Jack was at work at the time of the collapse, but rushed home to see if his extensive reggae vinyl record collection, valued at $100,000, might be salvaged. It was a total loss.

"He was one of the lucky ones," a friend wrote on a GoFundMe campaign to support Jack. "But surviving came at an unimaginable cost: in a matter of seconds, he lost his home, everything he owned, and a lifetime's worth of memories and work."

Now, Jack is suing his landlord and management company, as well as half a dozen companies affiliated with 2625 Bedford Ave., the lot adjacent to his Flatbush building. None of those entities have filed a response to the complaint yet in court.

The suit alleges the building's owner, Isolag Realty Group, and the property manager, Olufemi Falade, failed to take action after he pointed out cracks in the facade of 1321 Flatbush Ave earlier this year.

According to the lawsuit: “During October 2026, Plaintiff observed cracks at or near the Building's entrance, photographed those cracks, and reported the condition to the landlord or management responsible for the Building.”

The suit goes on to allege that Falade “personally received or responded to the report of the cracks on behalf of the Building's ownership or management. Plaintiff was falsely told, in substance, that the condition was not the landlord's fault or could not be fixed.”

Falade has appeared on the city's "Worst Landlord" watch list, put out by the city's Public Advocate office, six times in the last decade.

Jack’s suit also names several entities tied to 2625 Bedford Ave., the adjacent lot where excavation work was taking place at the time of the building collapse.

Those defendants include general contractor Townhouse Builders, d/b/a Promont; New Jersey-based LMW Engineering Group and its president, Jieming Wang; W6 Facility X, an LLC affiliated with Robert Fischman; and LLCs affiliated with lot owners Faigy Fischman and Judy Swimer.

The suit points to a pre-construction survey commissioned by the builders which documented that the facade of 1321 Flatbush Ave. was in "poor" condition prior to the excavation.

"The Defendants, who were responsible for excavation, design, supervision, inspections and monitoring received, or in the exercise of reasonable care, should have obtained and considered, the Pre-Construction Survey to evaluate all relevant Pre-Construction Site Conditions and, in particular, the Building's condition and its need for support and protection before proceeding with work at the Construction Site," the suit alleges.

Further, the suit says the defendants "had actual notice through the surveys, reports, observations or complaints applicable to their respective work, or constructive notice because the conditions were discoverable through the inspections and monitoring they were required to perform."

Further, the suit claims that "the excavation, inadequate structural protection, negligent engineering orinspection services, and failure to address the Building's developing dangerous conditionproximately and/or substantially caused the Building to collapse, causing Plaintiff's losses."

The 2625 Bedford construction project had a history of safety violations noted by the Department of Buildings. The demolition of a building that had previously been on the site was halted in March of this year after demolition contractor N Tech Design of America had failed to take proper safety precautions, including installing netting and putting up sidewalk shields, records show.

A month later, inspectors returned to the site and found that the demolition had gone ahead anyway, in defiance of the stop-work order, according to city records. A $10,000 fine was issued.

In May, a city inspector issued additional citations and another stop-work order against the contractors for allegedly failing to ensure adequate protections of neighboring buildings and for deviating from approved construction plans. Within a week, the city lifted that stop-work order.

Jack is suing for compensatory damages, rent relief, and punitive and exemplary damages.

In an interview with Gothamist, he valued his lost record collection at more than $100,000.

“ Nobody has contacted me from the city for, like, ‘We found some stuff that is still usable.’ I didn't hear anything like that,” Jack told the outlet. “And I don't know who to reach out to either.”

Thankfully, he'd been transferring many of his vinyl treasures into digital files prior to the collapse and had his hard drive with him at work when the building fell.

“ Every single day I was just backing up stuff. I don't know if it's intuition was telling me to do this. But I was doing it every day for the past week,” he added.

The GoFundMe to support Jack, who DJs under the name Roots Outernational, has raised more than $12,000 so far.

Last Wednesday, hours after the collapse, Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez opened a criminal inquiry into the collapse. No charges have been filed yet.

Realtor.com has reached out to Townhouse Builders, LMW Engineering, Jack, and Jack's lawfirm, Antin, Ehrlich, & Epstein, LLP, for comment.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5438. Scripts can’t run AI factories: Dell moves cluster management from the server to the rack

As artificial intelligence clusters grow to supercomputing scale, the hard part of the AI factory is no longer buying hardware. It is keeping racks, switches, GPUs and cooling running once they are switched on.

That operational burden is reshaping what infrastructure providers sell. Dell Technologies Inc. has spent the past year pushing its AI Factory beyond servers and storage, and customers are now asking for best practices and better tools to stand up and run what they buy, according to Andrew Vaz (pictured, left), vice president of product management for the Telecom Systems Business at Dell.

“What we are seeing is a fundamental shift from procuring supply to actually standing up and running these very complicated AI clusters and data centers,” Vaz said. “One of the interesting things that we’ve seen is it’s actually now impossible to manage these things with just a few scripts, manually, in an old world manner. The toolsets are becoming more important.”

Vaz and Saurabh Kapoor (right), director of product management and strategy for AI compute and networking solutions at Dell, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed supercomputing, rack-scale management, AI observability and why networking sits on the critical path for AI clusters. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell used the conference to introduce Dell OpenManage Rack Scale and Dell Fabric Manager, two tools for running AI infrastructure from deployment through daily operations. OpenManage Rack Scale manages 100,000 devices in its first release, up from 8,000 servers for its predecessor, OpenManage Enterprise, Kapoor explained. Systems such as Nvidia Corp.’s NVL72 racks bundle compute, power shelves, switches and coolant distribution units into one unit.

“OpenManage Enterprise, the previous product we had, was perfect for servers. Server was the unit of compute,” Kapoor said. “But you have seen in the last 18 months, the world has moved very quickly to larger ecosystems and infrastructures. Rack is the new unit of play.”

Visibility is the other half of that equation. Dell’s iDRAC controller pulls more than 320 metrics from every server, and an AI-assist chatbot can query that telemetry through local large language models, according to Kapoor. A single cooling leak can damage millions of dollars of gear, so every layer has to report in, Vaz noted.

“It could be something as simple as, ‘Hey, this transceiver’s about to die that you can’t diagnose with metrics you have today,'” Vaz said. “You need to use AI to go look at it. You need telemetry off the system to go collect all of that, correlate it, run your algorithms on them, train it and understand what’s happening.”

The network is where those pressures concentrate. Dell Fabric Manager turns validated designs built with Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. into deployable blueprints across different network operating systems and silicon. Agentic AI is also reshaping traffic, and enterprise bandwidth is outrunning a projected 3.5-fold increase, Vaz noted.

“We’re getting blown away by it. It’s more like nine to 10x,” Vaz said. “It’s going everywhere: east, west, north, south.”

#5437. Exclusive: Wherobots AI agents automate complex spatial data engineering

Cloud-native spatial analytics and artificial intelligence startup Wherobots Inc. today introduced an artificial intelligence agent that enables users to build and deploy spatial data pipelines using natural-language instructions, reducing the need for specialized programming expertise.

Called Waldo, the agent can discover data sources, generate queries, perform analysis, visualize results and schedule recurring operations. It’s designed for applications involving location-based information such as satellite imagery, road networks, GPS tracking data and geographic features.

Spatial data presents unusual processing challenges because it combines multiple data types, including geographic coordinates, imagery and geometric shapes. Analyzing this information at scale often requires specialized tools and scarce technical expertise.

A recent survey by Global Marketing Insights Inc. concluded that the global geospatial workforce is 10 to 15 years behind in building the skill levels employers need.

Wherobots, which was founded in 2022 by the creators of the open-source Apache Sedona spatial analytics engine, said Waldo can compress development projects that traditionally take weeks into days.

“Waldo is our new agentic interface,” said Damian Wylie, Wherobots’ head of product. Unlike general-purpose AI coding assistants, he said, Waldo can invoke specialized computational engines that can process enormous geographic datasets.

“We’re not deploying some net-new [large language model] under the hood,” Wylie said. “We’re connecting existing LLMs to our product and also giving it the context it needs to speed up that spatial data workflow.”

The agent orchestrates several components of Wherobots’ platform. Its Havasu spatial data and knowledge catalog discovers and prepares public geographic datasets alongside customers’ private information. RasterFlow, Wherobots’ serverless Earth intelligence and inference engine,  processes satellite and aerial imagery using computer vision models to identify features such as buildings, roads and land-use changes.

WherobotsDB executes the resulting analysis using more than 300 spatial functions, while Wherobots Maps visualizes the results. Completed pipelines can be scheduled to refresh automatically as new data arrives.

The distributed processing platform uses existing cloud storage and enterprise data catalogs, including Amazon Web Services Inc.’s Glue and Databricks Unity Catalog, eliminating the need for customers to migrate their data, Wylie said.

In a demonstration, he showed how Waldo could identify the drainage area surrounding Montana’s West Boulder River using geographic and elevation data. The agent located relevant datasets, constructed a geographic representation of the watershed and displayed the results on a map.

The resulting geometry could support subsequent analysis of snowfall, water runoff or changing environmental conditions, Wylie said. Waldo can also process satellite imagery using specialized machine learning models, including Meta Platforms Inc.’s Segment Anything Model 3.

Potential commercial applications include identifying delivery vehicles that deviate from planned routes, assessing weather-related transportation disruptions and analyzing advertising impressions based on billboard locations and mobility patterns.

Wherobots said customer Action Engine Inc. is using the technology to build recurring fleet analytics pipelines and reports that it can deliver new spatial analyses two to three times faster that was possible with manual processes. Another customer used the platform’s distributed computing architecture to reduce a large-scale data-joining operation from approximately a week to less than an hour, said Benjamin Pruden, Wherobots’ go-to-market executive.

Waldo isn’t intended to eliminate human oversight, executives said. Users can inspect generated queries, review geographic visualizations and create Jupyter notebooks to examine individual processing steps. Wylie acknowledged that the technology can’t guarantee accurate results from every prompt.

“That’s an area we’ll invest,” Wylie said. “We’re not at the stage where we’re going to say every prompt is the best quality you’ll ever get.”

Waldo is available in public preview, with agent tokens currently included at no additional charge in Wherobots Professional Edition. Customers pay primarily for the computational resources they consume, with controls to select processing capacity and monitor costs.

#5436. West Virginia Official Accused of Stealing 9 Properties for Friend With Ties to His Used Car Dealership

A West Virginia state auditor has been indicted for his role in an alleged scheme to steal nine properties from their owners and sell them to benefit a longtime friend and business associate—who also owns the land where the official operated a used car dealership.

Mark Hunt, 66, is accused of using his position as a state official to improperly transfer several tax-delinquent properties to a real estate company owned by the wife of his friend, Charleston attorney Robert Johns, despite the warnings of other state employees that such transactions violated state law.

Federal prosecutors announced on Monday that a federal grand jury had indicted Hunt, Johns, and three employees of the State Auditor’s Office in connection with the alleged scheme, alleging the group bypassed legal requirements to transfer ownership of properties located in Kanawha and Boone counties.

The charges against Hunt come on the heels of a West Virginia Watch investigation that revealed his used car dealership, After Hours Used Auto, operated on land owned by Johns' company, NAJ LLC.

At the center of the alleged scheme were nine properties in Kanawha and Boone counties whose owners were behind on their property taxes.

Under state law, tax-delinquent properties can eventually be transferred to investors who meet certain legal requirements. But prosecutors allege those requirements were ignored in this case.

A real estate company called MAPA Inc., owned by Johns' wife, Patricia Johns, attempted to purchase the properties, according to West Virginia Watch. But federal prosecutors allege the purchaser, who is not named in the Department of Justice release, failed to make required payments and submit paperwork within the deadlines established by state law.

Federal prosecutors say career employees in the Auditor's Office found that the properties were not eligible for deed transfer and told Hunt that the transactions could not be completed.

Hunt, however, allegedly ignored these warnings and signed deeds for eight of the properties on March 28, 2025, and the ninth one on June 6, 2025, according to prosecutors, who alleged that the transactions were effectively stealing the properties from the rightful owners.

“Public officials are entrusted to serve the people, not use their offices for personal benefit,” U.S. Attorney Moore Capito said in the news release on Monday. “When there is evidence that trust has been violated, our office will follow the facts and enforce the law, regardless of title or position.”

The indictment follows revelations that Hunt and Johns had financial ties that go beyond the disputed property transfers.

West Virginia Watch reported that Johns’ company, NAJ LLC, owns the land that Hunt’s After Hours Used Auto dealership is located on, less than a mile from the state Capitol in Charleston.

Hunt opened the small used-car dealership in July 2024, months before being elected to the State Auditor’s Office.

He acknowledged that he and Johns have been friends for years but denied any suggestion that their landlord-tenant relationship was connected to the disputed deeds. Johns also briefly worked as special counsel in the Auditor's Office in 2025.

“There’s not a ghost behind every door. It's just coincidental,” Hunt told West Virginia Watch. “He happens to have all of these vacant lots, and most of this property is scrub property. It's hillsides, it's vacant lots, it's right-of-ways, and he just happened to own this.”

The relationship, however, raised questions among state lawmakers about whether Hunt received favorable rental terms in exchange for signing the deeds.

“This new information raises significant additional questions about Hunt's relationship with Johns,” Republican Delegate Tristan Leavitt told the news outlet. “Is Hunt's car dealership paying market price for rent on the lot owned by Johns' company, or did Hunt illegally sign his landlord's deeds as payback for a sweetheart lease? Regardless, this business relationship further underscores Hunt's cronyism and why he should resign as auditor immediately for signing those deeds.”

West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey said the state Division of Motor Vehicles launched a separate investigation into Hunt’s used car dealership that stemmed from a consumer complaint. The monthlong investigation uncovered “significant and unexplained anomalies” in the dealership’s paperwork that could indicate violations of state and federal DMV and tax laws, he said.

DMV Commissioner Everett Frazier suspended the dealership’s license on Nov. 6. Morrisey said the findings were referred to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for possible criminal and civil prosecution and, along with the federal indictment, warrant the state House of Delegates considering articles of impeachment.

Prosecutors have not accused Hunt of receiving favorable rent in exchange for the property transfers. Hunt said the dealership had since closed after losing approximately $40,000.

Hunt and Johns each face nine counts of theft of property. Two senior Auditor's Office employees, Deputy Chief of Staff David Cole and General Counsel Frederic Caudill, face the same charges for allegedly helping to issue the deeds. Cole and Caudill are also accused of lying to federal investigators.

Patricia Johns’ company allegedly benefited from the transfers, but she has not been charged in the federal case.

In a separate alleged scheme, Hunt, Cole, and state employee Marie Ann Hoffmann face bank fraud charges related to accusations that Hoffmann collected government wages while performing work for Hunt's private law firm, according to federal prosecutors.

The indictment has prompted calls for Hunt's resignation from lawmakers of both political parties, including West Virginia House Speaker Roger Hanshaw.

“Auditor Hunt should immediately resign from his office," Hanshaw said at the press conference on Monday. “If he resolves to do otherwise, the House of Delegates will take swift action in January to restore integrity to the Office of the West Virginia State Auditor.”

Hunt has denied wrongdoing and said he intends to remain in office.

“I am innocent of these charges,” Hunt said in a statement on Facebook. “This indictment is an insult to the principles on which this country was founded. I am presumed innocent and will vigorously defend myself against these charges.”

#5435. Strategy Bitcoin vs. BitMine Ethereum: Which Crypto Treasury Is Better Positioned for a Market Recovery?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Strategy is buying more Bitcoin while Tom Lee’s BitMine keeps loading up on Ethereum. Both companies are doubling down as crypto prices slide. But their latest purchases reveal two very different bets on the next bull market. Strategy added another 485 BTC, taking its treasury to 850,849 Bitcoin. Meanwhile, BitMine’s Ethereum holdings have climbed to more than 6.07 million ETH, worth $11 billion at current prices.

Neither company is backing away. In fact, both are positioning themselves for a recovery that could dramatically revalue their massive crypto treasuries. The question is which strategy has the better chance of delivering the biggest payoff.

Michael Saylor’s Strategy acquired 485 BTC for $33.4 million between November 9 and November 15, according to its latest SEC filing. The company paid an average of $68,887 per coin, bringing its total holdings to 850,849 BTC.

Strategy has acquired 485 $BTC and repurchased $228M of $STRC. As of 11/15/26, we hold 850,849 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets. $MSTR https://t.co/cACnaFSMsr

Strategy has now spent $64.2 billion accumulating Bitcoin, with an average acquisition price of $75,452. At Bitcoin’s recent price near $64,200, the treasury is worth roughly $54.6 billion, leaving the company with an estimated $9.6 billion unrealized loss.

That is a substantial paper loss, but Saylor’s accumulation strategy has never depended on buying every Bitcoin at the bottom. Strategy continues using capital markets to expand its position, betting that Bitcoin’s long-term appreciation will eventually overwhelm short-term volatility.

Its latest filing also revealed $244.7 million in proceeds from common stock sales. Strategy allocated $33.4 million toward Bitcoin purchases, while spending $228.1 million repurchasing its STRC preferred shares.

That second transaction is worth watching. Strategy is managing its capital structure while maintaining its Bitcoin accumulation machine. It also reported $4.75 billion in its USD Reserve. The company already controls more than 850,000 BTC, giving shareholders enormous exposure to Bitcoin’s next major move.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Tom Lee is playing a different game. BitMine’s Ethereum holdings reached 6,070,092 ETH following its latest disclosed purchase of 9,587 ETH. The position represents 4.97% of Ethereum’s circulating supply, bringing the company within touching distance of its ambitious 5% accumulation target.

🧵1/BitMine provided its latest holdings update for November 16, 2026$11.8 billion in total crypto + "moonshots":– 6,077,745 ETH at $1,823 per ETH (per @coinbase)– 216 Bitcoin (BTC)– $180 million stake in Beast Industries @MrBeast– $67 million stake in Eightco Holdings…

At recent prices around $1,820, those holdings are worth $11 billion. But BitMine has another advantage that Strategy cannot replicate with its Bitcoin treasury: staking income.

The company has already staked 5.23 million ETH, or more than 86% of its holdings. Tom Lee projected that fully staking its Ethereum treasury could generate approximately $359 million in annualized rewards.

That creates a potentially powerful combination. BitMine is accumulating a substantial share of Ethereum’s supply while putting most of its holdings to work.

Lee’s thesis extends beyond ETH price appreciation. He sees Ethereum benefiting from institutional tokenization, financial infrastructure moving onchain, and growing demand for blockchain-based settlement.

If those trends accelerate, BitMine could benefit from both Ethereum appreciation and recurring staking rewards.

This is where the competition gets interesting. Strategy has the larger dollar-denominated crypto treasury, but BitMine has a compelling argument for capital efficiency. Bitcoin offers a straightforward scarcity thesis, while Ethereum adds staking and exposure to expanding blockchain activity.

Strategy’s biggest advantage is its enormous Bitcoin position. With 850,849 BTC, even a substantial recovery in Bitcoin could translate into billions of dollars in additional treasury value.

BitMine, however, has built an Ethereum position approaching 5% of circulating supply. Its staking operation gives the company another potential source of returns while waiting for the next market expansion.

There is also a difference in what investors are buying. Strategy offers a concentrated Bitcoin treasury vehicle, while BitMine offers a leveraged corporate bet on Ethereum’s future financial infrastructure.

Our verdict? BitMine has the more productive treasury model, but Strategy remains the heavyweight in corporate crypto accumulation.

If Bitcoin leads the next recovery, Saylor could quickly reclaim the spotlight. If Ethereum outperforms and institutional adoption accelerates, Lee’s strategy could look considerably smarter.

Both companies are effectively making the same bet: today’s market weakness will look insignificant when the next major crypto cycle arrives.

The winner may ultimately depend on which asset leads that recovery. But neither Saylor nor Lee appears interested in waiting for confirmation before accumulating.

#5434. Paychecks are growing, but buyers are still falling behind

Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

The October jobs report showed employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

The gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

At October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS said a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

Existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

The median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

Forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

The October data overall shows an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

Brokerage Engine helps real estate brokerages run on a stronger operational foundation, according to a release. Its all-in-one back-office platform streamlines commission processing, accounting, agent billing, compliance and reporting. Replacing manual workflows and duplicate entries, Brokerage Engine helps create efficiency and accuracy within brokerages, without adding overhead.

#5432. From store outlets to methane leaks: AI’s hunt for power

AI factories are outgrowing traditional data centers as models grow and distributed inference moves from concept to deployment. The infrastructure behind those models now has to span racks, sites and even scattered pockets of power.

Dell Technologies Inc. is betting that the answer lies in building complete systems rather than components, from rack-scale management to fully liquid-cooled designs. The size of modern AI clusters dwarfs anything high-performance computing has handled before, according to Ihab Tarazi (pictured), senior vice president and chief technology officer of AI, compute and networking at Dell.

“The difference with AI is the scale is massive: tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of GPUs that are all on a single fabric. It may be multiple clusters, but they end up being a single fabric at the end of the day,” he said.

Tarazi spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and host Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed Dell’s 100% liquid-cooled networking system, distributed inference and turning stranded energy into AI capacity. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell’s latest move takes liquid cooling beyond the graphics processing unit. The company is shipping what it calls the first 100% liquid-cooled networking system, with switches, optics and cabling pretested in its factory and delivered as a single rack, Tarazi explained.

“The fact that it’s pretested as a single-rack system means [that] instead of having to assemble hundreds of pieces on-site and take maybe two weeks or three weeks to find the bugs, it all comes in, you install it [and] we turn it up in hours,” he said.

The networking launch follows Dell’s debut of liquid-cooled storage for AI racks. Compute, networking and storage can now operate within a common cooling and power architecture.

“Instead of building two data centers — one for GPU, one [for] network — being able to do one is a massive reduction in time and cost for us,” he said.

Software is the next lever for distributed inference. Customers want a single control plane that can work across different GPUs and CPUs and link as many as 1,000 small sites, each with some spare power, Tarazi noted. That approach turns stranded energy into AI capacity for companies that can’t quickly build a massive data center.

“You’ll be surprised what power availability means,” he said. “It doesn’t mean just that you have power in your store. It could also mean methane coming out — every source of power possible. People are going backwards to say, ‘How do I leverage that power for compute and enable inferencing in a distributed manner?'”

#5431. Stalled data center buildouts send inference chips hunting for space in telco and colo sites

Demand for inference is outrunning the construction of new AI data centers, as power, capital and permitting delays push fresh capacity further out. That gap is sending chipmakers to hunt for room in existing facilities.

Many older telco and colocation sites have the space and power. But most can’t take today’s dense, liquid-cooled GPU racks without costly retrofits, which opens the door for air-cooled inference systems, according to Anton McGonnell (pictured), vice president of core product at SambaNova Systems Inc.

“We as an industry are just encumbered by the velocity of data center buildouts, and that’s been slowed down by just the physics of how long this takes, by the access to capital, and more and more by legislative hurdles — particularly in the U.S.,” McGonnell said.

McGonnell spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI data centers and the demand for air-cooled inference racks. (* Disclosure below.)

SambaNova’s fifth-generation chip, the SN50, targets the decode phase of inference, where output tokens are generated and data movement becomes the bottleneck. Its racks stay air-cooled and light enough to fit existing facilities, McGonnell explained. Newer GPU racks, by contrast, can demand reinforced flooring and 120 to 250 kilowatts of power per rack, he noted.

“On all of this stuff — the power and the cooling gear — there’s 18- to 24-month lead times to get this equipment into the data centers. Never mind all of the construction costs,” McGonnell said.

SambaNova, which investors valued at $11 billion in July, pairs its decode chips with partners that handle prefill, the compute-heavy first phase of inference. At SC26, it is demonstrating Intel’s D-Series GPUs for prefill alongside its SambaRack SN50 for decode in an air-cooled heterogeneous setup.

“They have developed a chip that has much, much better cost performance for the prefill phase of inference,” McGonnell said. “They’ve sacrificed HBM, which isn’t needed for prefill because it’s a compute-bound problem.”

#5430. 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely shows you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s update calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the company can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same company that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

In real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

If the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

How to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The company running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

How to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”

How to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your plan, not the floor under it.

The average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

#5429. Humyn Labs raises $47M to bridge the gap between AI training and real-world robotics

Humyn Labs, a company turning human experience into training for robots and artificial intelligence, today announced it has raised $47 million in early-stage funding to accelerate intelligent robotic deployment readiness in real-world environments across Brazil, South Korea and India.

Accel led the $26 million equity portion of the round, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence through Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton and Jump Trading LLC. Lighthouse Canton led the remaining $21 million in venture debt, with participation from Trifecta Capital.

Founded in early 2026, Humyn’s proposal is that AI models for humanoid robots don’t learn dexterity from staged demonstrations; they must learn by observing how humans move in real environments. This provides actual behaviors showing how hands work on objects, reach, touch, handle and recover without explicit instructions.

Unlike generative AI models that learn from vast amounts of text, images and video, physical AI models must learn how to interact with the world around them. That means understanding not only what objects look like and where they are, but also how to manipulate them, how much force to apply and how to respond when something goes wrong.

“The results can be very, very, very dramatic and catastrophic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Manish Agarwal (pictured) told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

Agarwal pointed out how mistakes that might be inconsequential for a chatbot can have serious consequences for a robot operating alongside people. That makes access to diverse, high-quality data about how humans physically interact with their environments critical for training robots to work safely and reliably in the real world.

To address this, the company built a video corpus captured from head-mounted cameras as participants performed everyday household tasks, comprising up to 200,000 hours of intentional human motion. The company also shipped a dataset of 120,000 faces across five regions for facial recognition, including adjustments in lighting, pose, expression, glasses, hairstyle, facial hair, accessories, age and locale.

That’s combined with more than 50,000 hours of representative speech data for underserved language markets, including Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Odia, Assamese, Korean, Tagalog, Arabic, Vietnamese and Portuguese. Voice AI models that understand natural language already have vast amounts of data for widely spoken languages such as English, Mandarin or Spanish, but real-world customer support within South and Southeast Asian markets lacks routine coverage.

Humyn’s engine uses sound, sight, motion and touch as data inputs, which it curates, normalizes and labels so that AI models can understand the kinematics of motion, force and environmental factors. Together, this provides training patterns for physical AI models, world models, general foundation models, and audio and voice AI.

Geographic diversity is also important because robots must understand the environments and cultural practices where they will operate. “Diversity gets you in the room. The quality ensures that you stay in the room,” Agarwal said.

To make this point, Agarwal emphasized the importance of geographic and cultural diversity in collecting training data. A household robot trained in the United States may struggle with tasks in an Indian home, where everything from cooking utensils and kitchen appliances to laundry practices and room layouts can differ. These regional differences mean that robots need experience with the specific environments and practices of the people they will eventually serve.

By collecting data across more than 20 countries, Humyn can train models on data that more closely resembles their intended deployments, potentially accelerating readiness for real-world work.

Agarwal added that the company is seeing interest from customers building household robots for domestic tasks and elder care, alongside industrial applications involving object manipulation and movement through factories, warehouses and commercial environments.

“The next phase in the deployment cycle is about how well these models perform in the wild,” Agarwal said.

In the end, data is only the beginning. Humyn wants to measure where robots fail in real-world conditions and use that to feed the AI flywheel and build better models. That means using virtual simulations, physical replicas and partnering with the enterprise and researchers to have field deployment labs to identify the differences between expected and actual performance.

The company said it intends to use the new funding to build deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India, develop its hardware and enrichment engine, and expand its on-the-ground presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul. Agarwal said this will also involve testing robots in real-world environments to identify gaps between their expected performance and actual behavior, feeding those results back into model development.

#5427. Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the company.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The new complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

On Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the issue in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS announced plans for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

#5425. Starburst adds context support to give AI agents consistent access to business data definitions

Starburst Data Inc. is expanding its data federation platform into business context management with the introduction of Context Studio, a new capability designed to help artificial intelligence agents produce more accurate and trustworthy answers from information distributed across enterprise systems.

Context Studio collects business definitions from existing data catalogs, business intelligence tools, metric stores and documents, making them available alongside data when AI agents respond to prompts. The system is intended to eliminate conflicting definitions that can cause AI agents to produce incorrect results.

The new capability addresses a problem the company encountered as customers began deploying its Aida natural-language data assistant in production environments, said Starburst co-founder and Chief Executive Justin Borgman.

“We’ve found that as you get into production, the biggest issue is context because you need to trust the answers the agent gives back,” he said.

The challenge is particularly acute in large organizations where different departments may use different definitions of common business metrics, such as revenue or active customers. Without a consistent understanding of those terms, AI models can produce plausible but inaccurate answers.

“When those definitions conflict, the [large language model] doesn’t know any better; it’s just going to guess,” Borgman said. “That’s what leads to bad answers and an erosion of trust.”

Context Studio builds on Starburst’s existing data products architecture, which allows organizations to create curated views spanning multiple data sources. Those products incorporate business definitions, metadata and access controls that can be applied consistently when agents retrieve information.

Unlike conventional semantic layers that require organizations to consolidate definitions within a single platform, Context Studio federates existing definitions without requiring customers to move or rebuild their underlying data.

Built-in approval workflows resolve conflicting definitions, and a feedback mechanism is provided through which agents can propose improvements. Human reviewers approve changes before regression testing checks their impact on other queries.

Borgman characterized the expansion as an evolution of Starburst’s longstanding strategy of querying distributed data without centralizing it.

“We think context is going to live everywhere, just like we think data will live in multiple places,” he said. “Our approach treats [context] as a first-class principle in our design.”

Starburst hasn’t yet disclosed quantitative evidence of Context Studio’s impact on AI accuracy or productivity. The company said it is collecting benchmark data from private preview customers.

The company is also emphasizing traceability to increase confidence in AI-generated answers. Context Studio records which data sources agents access, the SQL queries they generate and the information used to produce responses. Access controls remain attached to underlying data products.

“Context is going to increase the probability of a good answer, but there’s also a need to trace how it got to that answer,” Borgman said.

An agent can interview domain experts to capture business knowledge and convert it into draft data products. Starburst is also extending its Aida data assistant to answer questions across multiple data products and introducing an agent that automatically generates dashboards.

Other platform enhancements include Mission Control for monitoring usage and costs, automated Apache Iceberg maintenance, a bring-your-own-cloud deployment option and graphics processing unit-accelerated querying. Starburst claims its recently introduced Torin query engine delivers up to sevenfold performance improvements in company benchmarks.

Context Studio is available in private preview for Starburst Galaxy and Starburst Enterprise. A public preview is planned for January, with general availability expected in the first quarter of 2027. Pricing hasn’t been finalized.

#5424. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5422. How Will Amendment 3 Affect Florida Real Estate Sales? Experts Weigh in

Mortgage rates business concept of investment housing real estate interest rates 3d home appraisal. planning savings money of coins to buy a home concept for property ladder, mortgage, real estate.

(TNS)—Sweeping property tax cuts are on the horizon for some Florida homeowners following the passage of Amendment 3.

The measure will raise the statewide homestead exemption to $250,000 over the next two years. It will also place stricter limits on tax increases for all other properties.

But will it give Florida’s real estate market a leg up during tough economic times? Industry leaders are divided, with most taking a wait-and-see approach.

The total number of homes sold in the Tampa Bay metro area is down about 5.2% compared to this time last year. That’s according to the latest statistics from the Suncoast Tampa Association of Realtors.

Related: Before the election, data showed there was not a strong case for either the measure passing or failing.

Some real estate agents are urging out-of-state buyers to move before the end of the year to lock in tax savings. Anyone who moves after 2026 will have to wait five years to receive the full homestead exemption.

Corina Lessa Silva, president of the Suncoast Tampa Association of Realtors, said she’s not expecting a dramatic bump in sales over the next couple of months. You don’t have to buy a home to establish residency, she said; renting works, too.

Still, “If a big piece of that monthly payment—which is property tax—is going to be lowered…it could help more people get into homes in the long term,” Lessa Silva said.

Savings will vary widely. The nonpartisan nonprofit Florida Tax Watch estimates that by 2028, homestead property owners could save an average of $1,133 in Hillsborough County, $956 in Pinellas and $1,150 in Pasco.

For renters trying to break into the housing market, those savings probably aren’t enough to make up for the other costs of homeownership, said Lei Wedge, an assistant professor of finance at the University of South Florida’s Muma College of Business.

Freddie Mac pegs the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at a steep 7.18%. The median price for a home in Tampa Bay is about $400,000, according to the Suncoast Tampa Association of Realtors.

“Just because your future property tax will be cheaper, it does not help you with your down payment right now,” said Wedge.

Though most of the focus has been on single-family homeowners, commercial property owners are bracing for major changes, too.

Bowen Arnold, principal of Tampa-based DDA Development, said in the past 3 or 4 years, he’s seen the taxes on commercial properties he owns shoot up more than 10% in some cases.

Under the new rules, local property appraisers cannot increase the assessed value of non-homestead properties by more than 5% per year.

But don’t expect to see a spike in commercial sales as a result, said Andrew Frey, a managing director at the commercial real estate firm JLL.

“This will be of zero benefit for the buyers, it’s just a windfall for the current owners,” he said.

The biggest question hanging in the air is how local governments will fill major funding gaps caused by these tax cuts.

One solution might be by increasing the millage rate used to calculate our tax bills. That would end up canceling out some of the savings promised to homesteaded property owners, while raising everyone else’s taxes in the process, Wedge said.

Developers could also end up shouldering greater costs if cities decide to charge higher impact fees or raise the cost of construction permits, said Arnold.

All this uncertainty could put a damper on commercial markets, said Frey. “Investors like predictability. It could cause investors to push pause for a while until these things are sorted out.”
