#5377. Fix-and-flip margins tighten in Q3 as prices dip and costs rise

The Burns + Kiavi Fix and Flip Market Index dropped to 53 in Q3 2026, the lowest reading in nearly 4 years. Investors cited mortgage rates above 7%, softer prices and labor constraints that pressured margins.  AI Summary

The U.S. fix-and-flip market weakened in the third quarter as mortgage rates above 7% slowed buyer demand, while falling home prices and higher labor costs squeezed investors’ margins, according to a survey from Kiavi and John Burns Research and Consulting.

The Burns + Kiavi Fix and Flip Market Index fell to a reading of 53 in the third quarter, down from 59 in the second quarter and 56 a year earlier. The index, which measures market conditions on a scale of 0 to 100, reached its lowest level in nearly four years.

Readings below 50 indicate market contraction, while readings above 50 indicate expansion. The November 2026 report is based on a proprietary quarterly survey of approximately 280 fix-and-flip investors.

Only 23% of flippers expect good sales over the next six months, the lowest share in four years. Meanwhile, 19% anticipate poor sales, the highest share since Q4 2022.

The slowdown is affecting investors of different sizes. Large flippers, defined as those who bought or sold at least eight homes over the previous 18 months, reported worse market conditions than smaller operators for the first time since Q3 2022.

Higher mortgage rates have also reduced pricing power for investors. Forty percent of flippers said home sale prices in their markets were lower than a year earlier, compared with 16% who reported higher prices. Another 36% said prices were largely unchanged.

The Southwest reported the greatest share of flippers experiencing lower prices, at 67%, followed by Southern California at 50%. In Texas and the Southeast, 47% reported lower prices, while 44% of Florida respondents said the same.

About one in five flippers said they were selling homes mostly below their initial after-repair value estimates, approaching the highest level recorded by the survey since 2021.

The survey also found that immigration enforcement is affecting renovation labor availability and costs. Forty-one percent of flippers said increased immigration enforcement had negatively affected their labor force, up from 33% when the question was asked in Q2 2025.

Respondents reported difficulties finding workers, higher labor costs and longer project timelines. The impact was particularly pronounced in Florida and the Southeast, although flippers in other regions also reported challenges.

More available inventory is creating additional acquisition opportunities for investors. Twenty-four percent of flippers said competition for deals was lower than usual, the highest share in the survey’s history.

Despite the increased availability, investors remain cautious about how much they’re willing to pay. The average flipper targeted a maximum purchase price of 67% of a property’s after-repair value, down slightly from the previous quarter.

Renovation costs also varied significantly by region. The national average cost per flipped home was $72,000 in the third quarter, with costs reaching $133,000 in Southern California and $86,000 in the Northeast. Costs were lower in the Southeast and Texas, at $47,000 and $46,000, respectively.

The survey’s findings point to continued pressure on investors as higher financing costs, weaker buyer demand and labor constraints complicate project economics. As a result, John Burns recommended that flippers remain disciplined when acquiring properties and build in sufficient margins to account for potential price declines and higher labor expenses.

The firm also advised lenders to underwrite properties based on expected sale prices at the time of disposition rather than relying solely on recently closed comparable sales, which can lag in a declining market.

#5376. Recent spate of outages attributed to technical issues amid accelerated AI bug discovery

U.S. authorities don’t believe that the recent outages at federal agencies and top tech firms were caused by cyberattacks.

The Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines, Apple Inc. and Microsoft Corp. were among the affected organizations. All four said that their systems were disrupted by technical issues rather than hackers. Experts noted that artificial intelligence models’ ability to find software bugs has made patching more complicated, which may increase the risk of outages.

The first major service disruption hit Exchange Online on Thursday. The Microsoft-operated email service went offline for nearly a day, which left 450 million users without access to their inboxes. The company attributed the downtime to two separate bugs in the software that powers its network. The first one went undetected for three months, while the other cropped up a day before the outage.

The FAA experienced a network disruption of its own on Friday. An issue with a router at the agency’s El Dorado, Arkansas campus disrupted aircraft communications and radar data feeds. The outage led to more than 12,000 flight cancellations.

United Airlines reported a fairly extensive, but brief infrastructure disruption a few days later. The issue took several of the carrier’s pilot-facing applications offline for 30 minutes. Fewer than 150 flights were affected.

Yet another high-profile network outage occurred on Tuesday, this time at the U.S. National Security Agency. A technical problem cropped up in NSANet, an internal network that agency staff use to exchange classified information. The cause of the outage and its duration were not specified. However, officials did tell NBC the disruption wasn’t caused by a cyberattack.

U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton reiterated that point in a Tuesday interview. He added that officials have “looked very closely” into the other outages that occurred over the past week and ruled out cyberattacks as the cause. According to Clayton, authorities believe that the disruptions occurred because companies are patching vulnerabilities “on much larger scale” than before.

Frontier AI models have found thousands of software vulnerabilities over the past few months. That accelerated pace of discovery is creating more work for administrators, who have to roll out patches more frequently than before. The less time there is to prepare a patch, the greater the risk of human error.

“As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and development cycles, pressure is mounting on companies to deploy fixes quickly, often without fully understanding how those changes will affect interconnected systems, “ said Prince Kohli, the chief executive officer of software testing provider Sauce Labs Inc. “The only way to prevent these issues is continuous testing and release validation in their development processes, even more so for critical software updates.”

Apple and Workday Inc. are also among the companies that have experienced outages in recent days. Separately, several financial services temporarily became unavailable because of an issue with one of JPMorgan Chase’s on-premises systems. All the incidents have been resolved.

#5375. Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 16, 2026 at 10:09 am

Gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.

If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

Mel Clark, president and CEO of the CleanTech Alliance, an industry trade group, welcomed the news as the state struggles to get clean power plugged into the grid.

“Washington needs more energy generation, more clean energy, and more manufacturing,” Clark told GeekWire via email. “We’re excited to see the Governor take action to change our last-place ranking in building new clean energy projects.”

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business, ultimately withdrew its plans.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.

Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall, but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

Editor’s note: Comment from CleanTech Alliance President and CEO Mel Clark added 11/16.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5373. Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on AI startup Applied Compute as earnings top forecasts

Cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc. today announced that it has agreed to acquire artificial intelligence model training and inference startup Applied Compute Inc. in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion.

The news came alongside fiscal first-quarter earnings and revenue that were well ahead of Wall Street expectations. Shares of Palo Alto Networks rose more than 8% in late trading, adding to a gain of nearly 10% during the regular session.

The acquisition, subject to regulatory clearance, is expected to close in Palo Alto Networks’ fiscal third quarter. Once the deal closes, Applied Compute co-founder and Chief Executive Yash Patil will become co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks, with the startup’s research team also joining the company.

Founded in 2025 by former OpenAI Group PBC researchers Patil, Rhythm Garg and Linden Li, Applied Compute offers a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight models. The platform is designed to make it easier for companies to train, serve and improve their own models, with an autoscaling inference engine and a model router called Shift-1 also included.

Applied Compute raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation earlier this month in a round led by Elad Gil, with Nvidia Corp., Shopify Ventures and HubSpot Ventures also participating. At the time, the company said that its annualized recurring revenue had topped $100 million. Notable customers include Microsoft Corp. and DoorDash Inc. Coming into its acquisition, Applied Compute had raised more than $500 million in total.

Palo Alto Networks is pitching the deal as a bet that enterprise AI will be hybrid, as a large share of companies run open-weight models tuned to their own data. According to the company, no large provider is currently delivering those models securely. With Applied Compute, enterprises will be able to train and deploy open-weight models with security built in, either in the public cloud or in sovereign environments.

“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” Chairman and Chief Executive Nikesh Arora said. “Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we’ve seen, and its research team is exceptional.”

The deal came on the same day Palo Alto Networks reported what Arora called a record first quarter. For the quarter that ended on Oct. 31, the company reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.05, up from 93 cents in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $3.44 billion, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 97 cents per share on revenue of $3.31 billion.

Next-generation security annual recurring revenue grew 66% from a year earlier, to $9.73 billion. Remaining performance obligations rose 35%, to $21 billion. Helped by a tax benefit of $457 million, net income on an unadjusted basis came to $482 million, up from $334 million in the same quarter a year ago.

Chief Financial Officer Dipak Golechha said that given the current threat environment and the demand ahead, the company is “materially raising” its full-year guidance.

For its fiscal second quarter, Palo Alto Networks expects adjusted earnings per share of $1.01 to $1.03 on revenue of $3.53 billion to $3.55 billion. Full-year revenue is now forecast at $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion, up from the $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion guided in September, with adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 per share ahead of the $4.18 expected by analysts polled by FactSet.

#5370. ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am

Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.)

Microsoft said Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”

The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5369. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO priced at $83 per share, higher than expected

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic PBC today priced one of the most eagerly anticipated initial public offerings in history at a price of $83 per share, setting the stage for the biggest stock market listing ever.

The pricing, which has been reported by multiple news outlets including Bloomberg, Reuters and the Financial Times, is even higher than the company’s expected range of $70 to $78 per share.

If that price is correct, and if Anthropic sells all of its shares, it would raise in excess of $68 billion from the sale. Including the $26 billion in private placements, that puts Anthropic’s offering at more than $94 billion, surpassing even Space Exploration Technologies Corp. blockbuster $86 billion listing back in June.

In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last week, Anthropic had said its expected price range would give it a valuation of $1.4 trillion, but its market capitalization could well be even higher than that. The company’s shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange on Thursday under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Its debut might help the AI industry to push back against growing concerns that it’s entering into unsustainable bubble territory after years of breathtaking technological advances that has seen investors pour billions of dollars into almost any AI bet they can.

The listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has recently been beset by numerous setbacks, including the U.S. population’s backlash against data center building that was evident during the midterm elections, and then the ousting of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang last week. Those events raised concerns even higher in a market that was already jittery about the prospect of rising interest rates that could put debt financing out of the reach of many smaller AI infrastructure companies.

Some of the technology industry’s biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as customers, partners and shareholders. For instance, both Amazon.com Inc. and Google LLC have sizable stakes in the company, and others including Microsoft Corp., Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. have invested billions into its IPO. Meanwhile, the company is one of the biggest buyers of AI chips from those firms.

“If we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia,” said Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei (pictured) in a roadshow video last week. “We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time.”

Anthropic has been surrounded by immense hype and equally sizable controversy, generating billions of dollars in revenue while raising even more, and sparking serious concerns over the safety of the technology it has pioneered. Amodei has emerged as one of the biggest sources of the numerous doomsday stories surrounding AI, writing essays and repeatedly warning anyone who will listen of the dangers of humans losing control. In addition, he has attracted the ire of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after refusing to let the Pentagon do as it pleases with the company’s tools.

“If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian,” Amodei wrote in a viral essay in September.

Industry analyst Dan Ives told the New York Post that most investors view Amodei’s comments as “background noise” relative to the growth opportunity Anthropic has as one of the perceived leaders in frontier model development. “It’s a white-knuckle period and it’s a vote of confidence that Anthropic could have a successful IPO with the black cloud around Nvidia, Jensen and the AI trade,” he said.

Going forward, Amodei and his team will try to defy a stock market that has looked increasingly volatile this year. But even if they fail, they will walk away from this as incredibly rich men, with some reports suggesting that he and his six co-founders could each earn around $18 billion from today’s sale.

“Anthropic’s IPO will test just how much value frontier AI companies can capture as the industry moves from building increasingly capable models to putting them to work,” DatologyAI Inc. CEO Ari Morcos told SiliconANGLE.

Wall Street anticipates massive growth for the company in the coming years. Anthropic has been engaged in a titanic struggle with OpenAI Group PBC and Google LLC to develop the best AI models and recruit enterprise customers, and it appears to be winning. It has enjoyed a meteoric rise this year driven by the success of its popular AI coding tool Claude Code.

According to its IPO prospectus, it generated revenue of $33.24 billion in the nine month period ending Sept. 30, up around 1,200% from the same period one year earlier. During that period, it recorded a staggering $104 billion net loss, though most of that was due to a change in the value of convertible notes issues to investors and its derivative liabilities, the Financial Times said. Over the same stretch in 2025, Anthropic’s total losses came to $25.1 billion.

In a recent amendment to its IPO filing, the company said it had achieved a revenue run-rate of $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the prior month.

Regarding projections, some analysts have forecast Anthropic’s revenue to hit $53 billion by the end of its fiscal year, rising to between $135 billion and $137 billion in fiscal 2027 and between $270 billion and $280 billion by 2028.

Anthropic’s rival OpenAI had originally hoped to beat it to the public markets, but its founder and CEO Sam Altman later delayed its listing. While it has confidentially filed paperwork for an IPO, it’s not expected to make its market debut until sometime next year.

#5367. Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 14, 2026 at 2:10 pmNovember 14, 2026 at 2:10 pm

Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.

The organizers of one, called “Stand with Jensen,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU, paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.

Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”

One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi, SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia.

He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi, Ian Buck, the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian.

A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017.

The AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers, and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.

Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis, who now leads a new organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.

In 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton. In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.

He knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

The other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.

The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:

The insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker, a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s new, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

One more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.

Jassy said it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.

In a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang said he hoped his successor was already inside the company. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.

Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5365. Google upgrades Gemini’s agentic Task mode with new model, e-commerce features

Google LLC is releasing a new version of its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant that is better at performing multi-step tasks.

Josh Woodward, the vice president responsible for the Gemini app, detailed the update in a Thursday blog post.

The AI assistant has two modes that are accessible through separate interface tabs. The first, Chat, generates quick, relatively simple responses to prompts. The second mode, which is called Task, enables Gemini to perform complex tasks such as booking appointments and comparing online product listings. Task is the focus of this week’s update.

Google is switching the feature to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, its newest large language model. It’s somewhat less capable than Gemini 4 Carbon, the search giant’s most advanced LLM, and significantly more cost-efficient. Hydrogen is also fast: Google says that it can process some tasks 2.8 times faster than its previous entry-level model.

One way Hydrogen reduces wait times is by parallelizing project steps that are usually performed one after another. According to Woodward, users of Gemini’s Task mode can give the model feedback after each step to guide its work. The model proactively asks users for instructions before performing a sensitive task such as making an online purchase.

Today, Gemini’s Task mode uses Google Wallet to process transactions. Woodward said that the search giant is working with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa to add support for a technology called payment tokenization. It replaces the user’s card number with a placeholder value called a token. That token is shared with merchants instead of the card number to reduce the risk of data leaks.

Google also plans to add support for a second technology called the Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP. It makes it easier for AI agents such as Gemini to interact with online stores and thereby lowers the risk of errors.

Gemini’s Task mode can use data in other Google services such as Gmail to inform its decisions. For example, the agent might take the user’s past purchases into account when generating shopping suggestions. One of Gemini’s main selling points is that it can use such data without moving it off Google infrastructure, which is often not the case with competing agents.

“When you assign Gemini a task, it uses Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users,” Woodward wrote. “Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams.”

Google has made Gemini’s Task mode free in the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India as part of the update. That’s notable because Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC charge for the comparable features they offer as part of their chatbot services. Google’s move may prompt them to revise their pricing.

PAYETTE, Idaho, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Valley Family Health Care, Inc. ("VFHC") is providing notice of a data security incident that may have involved personal and/or protected health information belonging to certain individuals.

On or about March 13, 2026, VFHC experienced a network disruption and immediately initiated an investigation of the matter. In doing so, VFHC engaged cybersecurity experts to assist with the investigatory process. As a result of the investigation, VFHC determined that an unauthorized actor accessed and acquired certain files. Upon making this determination, VFHC undertook a comprehensive review of the files and learned that personal information and/or protected health information was involved. VFHC then worked with a third-party vendor to obtain the necessary information to effectuate formal notification. This process was completed on October 9, 2026.

The accessible information varied by individual and may have included individuals' names in combination with a Social Security number, driver's license or state identification number, date of birth, financial account information, medical information, and health insurance information. Not all data elements were affected for all individuals. Please note that there is no evidence of any misuse, or attempted misuse, of the potentially impacted information.

#5362. 13 Friday the 13th facts, from Jason's burlap sack to the calendar math

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Friday the 13th trivia covering Jason's hockey mask, his mother's killing spree, Tom Savini's effects, Kane Hodder and why the date itself is considered unlucky

The most recognizable part of Jason Voorhees is something he did not have at the start. The white hockey mask now tied to the whole Friday the 13th series first appears in the third film. By then, the franchise had already gone through two movies, a different killer and a different disguise.

That gap between the image and its origin runs through much of the series. The first Friday the 13th opened on May 9, 1980, and Jason was not the one doing the killing. When an adult Jason finally arrived in the sequel, he hid his face behind something other than a hockey mask. The look most people picture took shape gradually, one film at a time.

The franchise grew to 12 films between 1980 and 2009. Across those releases, Jason drowned as a boy, returned as a grown man, was killed and came back again. He eventually shared the screen with another horror villain. More than one actor played him. One sequel opened in 3D, and more than one release landed on a Friday the 13th.

The title also stretched beyond the films. Friday the 13th: The Series ran on television from 1987 to 1990. Despite the shared name, it does not feature Jason. The show used the brand without the character.

This collection of Friday the 13th trivia covers 13 points. It runs from the burlap sack Jason wore before the mask to the sound cue built from a few repeated syllables. It also covers the effects artist behind the original film's deaths, the actor who played Jason in four films and a sequel twist that put a copycat behind the killings.

The final slide steps away from the movies and looks at the date itself. Fear of Friday the 13th has a formal name. The calendar math behind how often the date comes around is more exact than the folklore about why it is unlucky. Each slide stands on its own. Readers can start with the mask or skip ahead to the superstition.

Jason Voorhees first wears his hockey mask in Friday the 13th Part III, the 1982 sequel directed by Steve Miner. Before that film, Jason did not wear a hockey mask.

After Part III, the mask stayed. It became Jason's permanent look, and the character kept it in the sequels that followed Miner's film.

How the mask came to be used is less settled. Accounts of the production disagree on who chose it. They also disagree on how it reached the set. With no agreed version, no single person can be credited with the choice.

Jason Voorhees first appears as an adult in Friday the 13th Part 2, released in 1981. In that film, he wears a burlap sack over his head rather than a hockey mask.

Part 2 is the starting point for the grown-up version of the character. The original 1980 Friday the 13th never shows an adult Jason.

The burlap sack is the first face covering an adult Jason wears on screen in the series. Its 1981 release came one year after the original film.

The original Friday the 13th was filmed at Camp No-Be-Bo-Sco, a real camp in Hardwick Township, New Jersey. On screen, those grounds stand in for Camp Crystal Lake, the fictional summer camp at the center of the 1980 film.

The movie uses two names for one place. Camp Crystal Lake is the name viewers hear in the story. Camp No-Be-Bo-Sco is where the production shot its scenes.

Camp Crystal Lake is an invented name. A search for it on a map will not turn up the place seen in the film. The real location behind the fictional camp is Camp No-Be-Bo-Sco, in Hardwick Township, New Jersey.

The "ki ki ki, ma ma ma" sound in Friday the 13th is the work of composer Harry Manfredini. He built it from syllables drawn from the phrase "kill her, mommy."

Manfredini wrote the score for the original 1980 film. This cue is not a melody. It is a short string of clipped syllables.

Each half of the cue comes from one word. The "ki" is taken from "kill." The "ma" is taken from "mommy." Each syllable appears three times as the cue is written.

Not every word of the phrase survives in the sound. The "her" in "kill her, mommy" drops out entirely. What remains is the opening sound of the two words at either end of the phrase.

The phrase behind the sound points to the film's killer, Pamela Voorhees. Its final word, "mommy," fits a story in which a mother is the one committing the murders.

Corey Feldman plays Tommy Jarvis in Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter, released in 1984. Tommy is the character who kills Jason Voorhees in the film.

The Final Chapter reached theaters two years after Friday the 13th Part III. Counting from the original 1980 film, it is the fourth entry in the series.

The title presented the film as the end of the franchise. It was not. Friday the 13th: A New Beginning followed in 1985.

The ending puts Feldman's character at the center of the climax. Tommy, not Jason, is the one who ends the film's run of killings.

A lightning strike brings Jason Voorhees back from the dead in Jason Lives, the 1986 Friday the 13th sequel. Tom McLoughlin directed the film.

Jason had already died on screen before this film. The lightning bolt is the device that returns him, and it puts the series' central villain back at the center of the story.

The title spells out that premise. In Jason Lives, Jason is alive again.

Counting from the original 1980 release, Jason Lives is the sixth Friday the 13th film. It arrived one year after Friday the 13th: A New Beginning.

Jason Goes to Hell, released in 1993, ends with Freddy Krueger's glove pulling Jason's mask underground. Freddy vs. Jason followed in 2003. A reboot that reused the title Friday the 13th arrived in 2009.

The final image of Jason Goes to Hell puts Freddy's glove and Jason's mask in the same frame. It does not show the two characters fighting. The mask is pulled below ground, and the film ends there.

The scene points toward a meeting between the two villains without staging one. It leaves that matchup for a later film.

Freddy vs. Jason reached theaters 10 years after that ending. Ronny Yu directed the film. The crossover put on screen the pairing that the glove scene had only hinted at.

The casting marked a change. Ken Kirzinger played Jason in Freddy vs. Jason. Kane Hodder, who had played Jason in the films just before it, did not take the role for the crossover.

Jason Voorhees is not the killer in the original Friday the 13th. The murderer in the 1980 film is his mother, Pamela Voorhees, played by Betsy Palmer.

Sean S. Cunningham directed the film, and Victor Miller wrote the script. Their story is set at Camp Crystal Lake, the summer camp where the killings take place.

Jason's part in this first installment is small. In the story, he drowned as a boy at Camp Crystal Lake. His death belongs to the film's backstory, not to its run of murders.

He appears on screen only in a shock scene late in the film. That brief moment is the full extent of his role in the original.

The later sequels made Jason the franchise's central figure. In the 1980 film, the character whose name now defines the series is a drowned child, not the attacker.

The answer to "who is the killer in Friday the 13th?" depends on which film the question refers to. For the 1980 original, it is his mother.

Tom Savini created the special effects for the original 1980 Friday the 13th. His work includes the death of Kevin Bacon's character, who is killed by an arrow through the neck.

Bacon is part of the first film's cast. His character does not survive the story.

The arrow scene is one of the killings Savini's effects put on screen in the 1980 film.

Friday the 13th Part III opened in 3D on Aug. 13, 1982. That date fell on a Friday.

The timing put the third film in theaters on the exact day its title names. A series named for an unlucky date had one of its entries premiere on that date.

The 3D format was part of the release itself, not a later reissue. The film arrived in theaters in 3D on its opening date.

Jason Voorhees is not the killer in Friday the 13th: A New Beginning. The 1985 film reveals that a copycat, not Jason, committed its murders.

A New Beginning is the fifth film in the Friday the 13th series. It arrived one year after Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter.

The twist makes it the second film in the series in which Jason does not commit the killings. The first was the 1980 original.

The copycat setup did not carry into the next entry. Jason Lives, the sixth film, returned the real Jason to the center of the series.

Kane Hodder played Jason Voorhees in four Friday the 13th films, released between 1988 and 2001. His run covers The New Blood, Jason Takes Manhattan, Jason Goes to Hell and Jason X $TWTR.

Hodder first took on the role in The New Blood, released in 1988. He returned the following year for Jason Takes Manhattan, released in 1989. Those were his only back-to-back appearances as the character.

The gaps between his films then grew longer. Jason Goes to Hell followed in 1993, four years after Jason Takes Manhattan.

Hodder's final film as the character was Jason X, released in 2001. It arrived eight years after Jason Goes to Hell, the longest break in his run.

From The New Blood to Jason X, Hodder's tenure as Jason spans 13 years.

The 2009 reboot came six years after Freddy vs. Jason. Marcus Nispel directed it. The film carried no subtitle and no number.

It took its name directly from the original 1980 movie, Friday the 13th. The plain title marked it as a reboot rather than another numbered sequel.

The reboot opened on Feb. 13, 2009. That day was a Friday. The film's release date matched its own title.

No one knows for certain why Friday the 13th is considered unlucky. The calendar is more precise: every year has at least one Friday the 13th and no more than three.

The fear of the date has a formal name: paraskevidekatriaphobia. The superstition's origin is unclear. Several historical events are regularly tied to the date. None of them has been shown to be the source of the belief.

The Last Supper is one of the most frequently cited links. It turns up in many retellings of where the superstition began. That connection belongs to folklore, not to established history.

The arrests of the Knights Templar are another. They took place on Friday, Oct. 13, 1307. Popular accounts often point to that day as a starting point. That link is also folklore rather than an established cause.

A later event also shows up in the record. The composer Gioachino Rossini died on Friday, Nov. 13, 1868. His death is often cited in early printed references to the date. A date of death fixes when something happened. It does not explain why a belief began.

The Gregorian calendar repeats its pattern of dates and weekdays every 400 years. Across that cycle, the 13th of a month lands on a Friday 688 times. No other weekday reaches that total.

Friday's lead is slight. A 400-year cycle holds 4,800 months, which means 4,800 13ths. An even split across all seven weekdays would give each day about 686. Friday's 688 sits about two dates above that mark.

Spread over the full cycle, those 688 dates average 1.72 Friday the 13ths per year. No single year can match that average, because each year's count is a whole number. In practice, a given year has one, two or three.

The two halves of this story differ in certainty. The folklore has no confirmed starting point, while the calendar count can be checked to the exact date.

#5361. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one says, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

#5359. 5 recalls and a federal rule that show how ingredient problems spread

Free daily briefing on global business news.

An ingredient recall can spread across many brands when manufacturers share one supplier, as four past recalls and an FDA tracing rule help explain

A single batch of an ingredient can leave one supplier's plant and end up inside products sold under many different brand names. Each of those products carries its own label and its own lot code. When that batch turns out to be contaminated, the recall cannot stop at the supplier's door. It has to follow the ingredient to every company that bought it.

That tracing problem explains why one ingredient recall can reach so far. Manufacturers often buy shared inputs such as flavorings, proteins, pastes and active drug ingredients from a small number of suppliers. A processor may mix one supplier's batch into many finished foods or medicines. Each buyer then has to work out which of its own products used the affected material. It also has to find which batches of those products reached customers.

The basic chain is short. A supplier sells to manufacturers. Manufacturers sell under brand names, and retailers stock those brands side by side. A shopper sees separate products. The supply chain behind them may trace back to one shared source.

Lot codes are the tool meant to make that work possible. A lot code lets a company say exactly which production batches are affected. The company can then pull those batches and leave the rest on sale. The system only holds together if every buyer in the chain keeps records linking incoming ingredient lots to the finished products that used them. A missing record at any step makes it harder to say which finished products are affected.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration sorts recalls into classes based on health risk. Class I is the most serious category. It applies where there is a reasonable probability that using the product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death. Class II and Class III cover lesser risks.

The five examples below show the pattern in different settings. They include a pet food recall, two food ingredient recalls tied to Salmonella, a generic blood pressure drug recall and a federal rule written to speed up tracing. They are a selection, not a complete or ranked list. Each one shows a different part of the tracing problem.

The 2007 Menu Foods recall showed how one tainted input can surface under several pet food brands at once. Wheat gluten contaminated with melamine came from a supplier in China. It went into food that Menu Foods produced for a range of labels.

Menu Foods, based in Ontario, Canada, announced its recall in March 2007. The company worked largely as a contract manufacturer. It made wet foods, such as chunks in gravy, that other companies sold under their own names. Those customers included national brands and store brands.

That business model explains why the problem crossed brand lines. A pet owner reading a can saw a familiar label, not the name of the plant that made it. Nothing on the packaging linked one brand to another. A single contaminated ingredient at one manufacturer still reached shelves under more than one brand name.

Wheat gluten is a concentrated protein extracted from wheat. In wet pet food it helps bind ingredients and form chunks with a meat-like texture. It also contributes to the protein content printed on the label.

Melamine is an industrial chemical used to make plastics and resins. It is rich in nitrogen. Common protein tests estimate protein by measuring nitrogen. Melamine can therefore make a diluted ingredient look more protein-rich than it is.

Investigators also found cyanuric acid, a related compound, in the contaminated material. Melamine and cyanuric acid can combine to form crystals in the kidneys. Affected cats and dogs suffered kidney failure.

The gluten passed through more than one company before it reached pet food. ChemNutra, a Las Vegas importer, brought it into the U.S. from Xuzhou Anying Biologic Technology Development in China. In 2008, a federal grand jury indicted both companies and ChemNutra's owners.

Each handoff added distance between the source of the contamination and the pet owner. Investigators had to work backward from sick animals to finished food, then to the plant and the gluten shipments. They then had to work forward again to every product made with those shipments.

The recall did not stop at Menu Foods. Some other pet food makers that had used wheat gluten from the same importer also recalled their own products. The trail from one importer's shipments led into several separate companies' production lines.

Peanut Corporation of America was not a household brand. It worked as a processor, turning raw peanuts into products that other companies bought in bulk. Investigators focused on its plant in Blakely, Georgia. A second company plant, in Plainview, Texas, also came under scrutiny and was shut down in 2009. The outbreak strain was Salmonella Typhimurium.

That structure shaped the recall. Once investigators identified the Georgia plant as the source, the recall moved outward through the processor's list of buyers. A peanut butter sandwich cracker, a peanut ice cream and a candy bar could all trace back to that one plant.

The case also carried legal consequences. Peanut Corporation of America filed for bankruptcy in February 2009. Its former chief executive, Stewart Parnell, was later convicted on federal charges connected to the outbreak, including conspiracy and fraud. In 2015 he was sentenced to 28 years in prison.

In 2010, a Salmonella problem was tied to hydrolyzed vegetable protein made by Basic Food Flavors of Las Vegas. Food companies that used the ingredient recalled products containing it. The case showed that a minor flavoring, present in small amounts, can still set off many recalls.

Hydrolyzed vegetable protein, often shortened to HVP, is a flavor enhancer. It is made by breaking down protein from plant sources such as soy, corn or wheat into its amino acids. The result has a savory, brothlike taste that deepens the flavor of processed foods.

Manufacturers add it to soups, sauces, dips, snack seasonings and similar products. They use it in small quantities. U.S. ingredient lists run in descending order by weight. HVP therefore tends to sit near the end of a label.

That small dose helps explain how one supplier's output can reach so many products. A modest batch of a flavor enhancer can season a large volume of finished food. The same ingredient can also travel inside a seasoning blend or flavor base that another company mixes before selling it on.

Each of those steps adds a layer to the trace. A food maker that bought a seasoning blend may need records from its blender to learn whether HVP from the affected supplier was inside. Only then can it check its own production records for affected products.

Dry ingredients pose a particular challenge with Salmonella. The bacteria cannot multiply without moisture. They can, however, survive for long periods in low-moisture foods such as powders and seasonings. A dry ingredient does not become safe simply by sitting on a shelf.

How a product is eaten also matters. Thorough cooking can kill Salmonella in a soup simmered at home. Seasoned chips and dips served straight from the container are often eaten with no further cooking.

U.S. rules require a protein hydrolysate's label name to identify its food source, as in "hydrolyzed soy protein." That naming tells consumers what plant the protein came from. It does not tell them which company made it. That is the detail a recall depends on.

The 2018 valsartan recall showed that medicines can follow the same supply pattern as food. Several generic versions of the blood pressure drug were recalled because they contained an impurity called N-nitrosodimethylamine, or NDMA. Their active ingredient came from Zhejiang Huahai Pharmaceutical in China.

Valsartan belongs to a drug class called angiotensin II receptor blockers, often shortened to ARBs. Doctors prescribe it for high blood pressure and heart failure. Many patients take it daily for years. A recall therefore created practical work for pharmacies and prescribers, on top of the safety question.

NDMA is a nitrosamine, a type of chemical that can form during some industrial and food processes. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies NDMA as probably carcinogenic to humans. Its presence in valsartan tablets led to regulatory action in the U.S. and Europe.

The route from one supplier to many labels runs through the active pharmaceutical ingredient, or API. That is the compound that produces a drug's effect. Generic drug companies often buy their API from specialist chemical manufacturers instead of making it themselves.

Those companies then turn the API into finished tablets. They add inactive ingredients, press and package the product, and sell it under their own names. The chemistry happens at one company, while the label belongs to another.

That division of labor meant one API maker could sit behind several finished drugs. Once the impurity was traced to valsartan from Zhejiang Huahai Pharmaceutical, each buyer of that ingredient had to check its own batches. Bottles with different company names on them shared the same upstream source.

The check also had to cover combination pills. Valsartan is sold alone and in single tablets paired with other blood pressure drugs. Any of those products made with the affected ingredient fell into the same review.

Generic substitution made the problem harder for patients to see. A pharmacy can fill a valsartan prescription with any approved generic version. The maker can change from one refill to the next. A patient may not know which company made the tablets in a given bottle.

Pharmacists had to match the manufacturer name and lot number on each container against recall notices. The FDA advised patients on recalled valsartan to keep taking it until a doctor or pharmacist provided a replacement or another treatment. Stopping a blood pressure drug abruptly carries its own risks.

The concern later widened beyond valsartan. Nitrosamine impurities were found in some versions of other ARBs, including losartan and irbesartan, and those products were recalled too. The FDA later issued guidance asking drug makers to assess and control nitrosamine risks in their medicines.

The FDA food traceability rule requires companies that handle foods on the agency's Food Traceability List to keep extra records. Those records are meant to help investigators follow a food and its ingredients through the supply chain faster during an outbreak or recall.

The rule comes from Section 204 of the FDA Food Safety Modernization Act, the food safety law signed in January 2011. The FDA finalized the traceability requirements in November 2022. Compliance was originally due on January 20, 2026. The agency has since extended that date by 30 months, to July 20, 2028.

The rule is built around specific points in a food's journey. The FDA calls these points critical tracking events. They include harvesting, cooling, initial packing, shipping, receiving and transformation. At each event, a company must record key data elements, such as quantities, locations, dates and a traceability lot code.

The traceability lot code ties those records together. A code is assigned when a food is first packed, first received on land after harvest at sea, or transformed into a new product. Transformation covers steps such as cutting, mixing or cooking a food into something else.

When a firm transforms a listed food, it assigns a new lot code to the result. It also records which incoming lots went into it. That link lets an investigator move from a finished product back to a specific ingredient batch.

The rule also sets a deadline for producing records. When the FDA asks, a covered company must hand over the information within 24 hours or within a reasonable time the agency agrees to. In some situations, such as an outbreak investigation, the firm must provide it as an electronic sortable spreadsheet.

The list itself is limited. It names foods including leafy greens, fresh herbs, tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, melons and sprouts. It also covers shell eggs, nut butters, cheeses other than hard cheeses, finfish, crustaceans, molluscan shellfish and ready-to-eat deli salads. Foods that contain a listed item as an ingredient can also be covered. That generally applies only while the listed ingredient stays in the same form, such as fresh.

This scope means the rule does not reach every ingredient. Dry flavorings, flours and many other shared inputs fall outside it. For those, tracing still rests on the one-step-forward, one-step-back records required under the Bioterrorism Act of 2002. Those records show where a company got an ingredient and where it sent its products. They do not carry the Section 204 rule's critical tracking events, key data elements or 24-hour spreadsheet requirement.

#5358. Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Update, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t said what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.
