#5357. Who calls NFL plays? How a play-caller differs from a coordinator

Free daily briefing on global business news.

NFL play-caller vs. coordinator roles explained, from helmet radios and booth versus sideline setups to why head coaches keep or hand over the play sheet

The coach with "offensive coordinator" as a job title is not always the coach deciding what happens on third down. In the NFL, the title and the decision can belong to two different people. One is a job title. The other is a game-day task. The NFL play-caller vs. coordinator split explains much of how a coaching staff divides its work on game day.

A coordinator is an assistant coach who runs one of a team's three units: offense, defense or special teams. The coordinator reports to the head coach and oversees the position coaches in that unit. During the week, the coordinator usually builds the game plan, runs meetings and teaches the scheme to players.

A play-caller does something narrower. That coach picks the specific play, formation or defensive call for each snap while the game is underway. On offense, the call travels by radio to the quarterback. On defense, it goes to one designated player wearing a radio helmet.

In many cases, the coordinator does both jobs. The play sheet can still sit with someone else. Some head coaches keep play-calling for themselves while a coordinator holds the title. Andy Reid, Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan have each been known for calling their own offense. In those setups, the coordinator's role leans toward planning and teaching rather than snap-by-snap decisions.

The difference shapes how credit and blame get handed out. Fans and media often judge an offense or defense by the coordinator's title, even when another coach chose the plays. It also affects how a head coach spends a game. A head coach who calls plays is managing the clock, challenges and personnel at the same time.

The 10 slides that follow break the distinction into its working parts. They cover what each role includes and why the two are separate responsibilities. They explain how the helmet radio and its green dot work, including the cutoff at 15 seconds on the play clock. They compare calling plays from the press box with calling them from the sideline. They also walk through what a defensive call contains and who decides fourth downs. The last slides cover how teams settle who gets the play sheet when they hire a coordinator.

An NFL play-caller is the coach who chooses the specific play, formation or defensive call for each snap of a game. The role is defined by that in-game decision, not by a job title.

On offense, the play-caller picks what the unit runs next. The choice can cover the play itself or the formation the offense lines up in. The call reaches the quarterback through a radio in his helmet.

On defense, the task means selecting the defensive call for the snap. That call does not go to the quarterback. It travels by radio to one designated defensive player instead.

The work repeats throughout the game. A play-caller does not make one choice before kickoff and then step back. Every snap requires a fresh decision, and that decision has to be made before the ball is snapped again.

Who holds the task varies from team to team. The coordinator for that unit usually calls the plays. A head coach can keep the task instead. That is why the play-caller and the coordinator are not always the same person.

Whichever coach holds the play sheet on game day is the one choosing, snap by snap, what the offense or defense runs.

An NFL coordinator is an assistant coach who runs one of a team's three units: the offense, the defense or special teams. The title describes a position in the staff hierarchy, not a single game-day task.

Each unit has its own coordinator. The offensive coordinator oversees the side of the ball trying to score. The defensive coordinator oversees the side trying to stop the opponent. The special teams coordinator oversees the groups that take the field for kicks, punts and returns.

The title sits in the middle of the coaching staff. A coordinator answers to the head coach, who holds authority over the whole team. Below the coordinator are the position coaches assigned to that unit.

That supervisory line is the core of the role. On offense, position coaches typically work with specific groups such as quarterbacks, running backs, wide receivers, tight ends and the offensive line. On defense, they typically handle the defensive line, linebackers and defensive backs. The coordinator directs those coaches so each position group fits the unit's overall approach.

Special teams is built differently from the other two units. Its coordinator does not oversee a fixed group of starters. Kick, punt and return units draw many of their players from the offense and the defense. They play alongside specialists such as the kicker, punter and long snapper. Many of those players also work under position coaches on offense or defense during the week.

The reporting line also limits a coordinator's independence. The head coach sets the direction for the team. The coordinator runs one unit within that direction and answers to the head coach for how it performs.

A coordinator title, on its own, does not settle who selects plays during a game. That task is assigned separately and is not automatically part of the job. An offensive coordinator may or may not be the coach sending in each call on a given Sunday.

Play-calling is one task inside a coordinator's job, not the whole job, and it can belong to someone else. A coordinator usually builds the weekly game plan, leads meetings and teaches the scheme. Choosing plays during the game is a distinct duty.

The two responsibilities sit at different points in the week. Coordinating happens mostly before kickoff. The game plan, the meetings and the teaching all shape what a unit is prepared to run on game day.

Play-calling starts once the game does. It is the choice of a specific play, formation or defensive call for each snap. That choice draws from the plan, but it is made in real time.

The tasks can be separated. One coach does not have to hold both. The coordinator title describes the assistant who runs the offense, the defense or the special teams unit. Nothing in that title requires the same person to pick each play.

A team can have a coordinator who designs and teaches the scheme while another coach makes the in-game calls. In that setup, the coordinator's work shows up in how the unit is prepared. The play-caller's work shows up in which part of that preparation gets used, and when.

The split can happen on either side of the ball. A head coach may keep the offensive calls. A head coach with a defensive background can take over the defensive calls instead. In either case, the coordinator keeps the title and the weekly preparation duties. Whoever holds the play sheet, the coordinator still reports to the head coach and oversees the unit's position coaches.

The overlap also explains why the two roles are easy to confuse. The coordinator usually holds both tasks. That makes the title and the task look like the same thing. They are not. One is a position on the staff chart. The other is a responsibility the staff assigns.

Andy Reid, Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan have each been known for calling their own offense as NFL head coaches. In that arrangement, the head coach picks the offensive plays on game day while an assistant holds the offensive coordinator title.

The setup separates a title from a task. The offensive coordinator keeps the title and still reports to the head coach. The head coach keeps the play sheet and makes the snap-by-snap offensive calls.

All three examples come from the offensive side of the ball. Each coach is associated with choosing the plays himself rather than passing that job to the assistant whose title suggests it.

A play-calling reputation describes what a coach has been known for. It does not show who holds the play sheet for a particular team in a particular season. A head coach can keep the duty or give it to a coordinator, and that choice can change.

The coordinator title alone cannot tell a viewer who chose a given play. In staffs run the way these three coaches have been known to run them, the answer sits with the head coach, not the coordinator.

The NFL lets a play-caller speak directly to the quarterback through a radio receiver inside his helmet. That helmet is marked with a green dot. The link cuts off when 15 seconds remain on the play clock.

Only one quarterback helmet carries the receiver, and the green dot shows which one it is. The coach choosing the play talks into a headset. The call travels from there to that single receiver, and no other offensive player hears it by radio.

The play has to reach the quarterback before the cutoff. After that point, the radio goes silent and he runs the snap without coaching input. Any adjustment from there has to come from the players on the field.

The cutoff makes timing part of the play-caller's job. Choosing the right call is not enough on its own. The call also has to arrive with enough time left for the quarterback to hear it before the link drops. A slow decision on the sideline or in the press box shrinks that window.

The defense uses its own version of the setup. One designated defensive player wears a helmet with a radio. That player is the defense's link to the coaching staff. The defensive call reaches the rest of the unit through him.

The two sides gained this tool at different times. League rules have allowed quarterback radios since 1994. Defensive radios followed in 2008, 14 years later. Through that stretch, only the offense could receive a call by helmet radio.

The 2008 change put both units on matching terms. Each side now works with the same basic arrangement: one connected helmet and one shared cutoff point on the play clock.

Those two limits shape how a coach uses the link. One helmet per unit means a single player carries each call to the rest of his teammates. The fixed cutoff sets how much a coach can say before a snap. It also marks the moment the players take over.

An NFL play-caller works from one of two places on game day: the press box or the sideline. The press box offers a higher view of formations, while the sideline offers direct contact with players.

The choice applies to offense and defense alike. Any coach who holds the play sheet, whether a coordinator or a head coach, works from one of these two spots.

From the press box, the play-caller looks down on the field from above. That elevated angle makes it easier to see how an opponent lines up before the snap. Formations are harder to read from ground level, where players block one another from view.

The sideline trades that overhead view for proximity. A caller standing on the field can talk with players in person between series. Those conversations happen face to face instead of being passed along by another coach.

Neither location cuts the play-caller off from the rest of the staff. Coaches in both spots wear headsets that link them during the game. A caller upstairs can stay in contact with coaches on the field. A caller on the sideline can hear from staff in the box.

The location shapes which kind of information reaches the play-caller most directly. Upstairs, it is the wider picture of the opponent's setup. On the field, it is the players who carry out each call.

A defensive play-call tells 11 players three things before the snap: the front, the coverage and whether to blitz.

The front describes how the defense lines up near the line of scrimmage. It sets where the defensive linemen and linebackers stand before the ball is snapped. A front choice shapes which gaps each player is responsible for against the run.

Fronts are often named by their personnel. A 4-3 front uses four down linemen and three linebackers. A 3-4 front uses three down linemen and four linebackers.

The coverage governs the players farther from the ball. It tells cornerbacks, safeties and linebackers how to handle receivers once the play begins. In man-to-man coverage, a defender follows one assigned player. In zone coverage, defenders guard areas of the field instead of specific opponents. Coverages are also named by structure. Cover 2, for example, splits the deep part of the field between two safeties.

The blitz is the optional part of the call. A blitz sends extra defenders after the quarterback, beyond the players who rush on a standard down. A linebacker or a defensive back can be the added rusher. An extra rusher usually leaves one fewer defender in coverage. That trade-off means the blitz and the coverage have to fit together.

Those three pieces travel as one call, not as separate instructions. The play-caller sends the full call to the one defender wearing a radio helmet. That player then passes it to teammates, either in the huddle or at the line of scrimmage.

The relay makes the radio-helmet player the link between the coaching staff and the rest of the unit. Every teammate depends on him to repeat the call accurately before the snap.

The defensive coordinator is the usual caller. A head coach with a defensive background can take that role instead. When that happens, the coordinator keeps the title. The head coach, not the coordinator, chooses the front, coverage and blitz on each snap.

The head coach generally has final say on fourth down, choosing whether to punt, kick a field goal or go for it. The special teams coordinator advises on that choice, and the head coach makes it.

Fourth down is a decision that sits above any single unit. It does not belong to the offense, the defense or special teams alone. It falls to the coach in charge of the whole team.

Each option sends a different group onto the field. A punt brings out the punting unit. A field goal try brings out the kicking unit. Going for it keeps the offense on the field.

The question on fourth down is not only which play to run. It is which unit takes the next snap.

The special teams coordinator manages the kicking, punting and return units. Two of the three fourth-down options use those units. That places the coordinator's advice inside two of the three choices a head coach weighs.

The return unit covers the other side of the kicking game. It takes the field when the opponent punts or kicks. That group also falls under the special teams coordinator.

The division matches how authority runs on a coaching staff. A coordinator runs a unit and gives input. The head coach decides questions that cross from one unit to another.

A coordinator calls plays only when the head coach hands over that duty. The decision often gets made when a team hires a coordinator. At that point, the head coach chooses whether to delegate the play sheet or keep it.

The authority to decide follows the reporting line. A coordinator answers to the head coach. The head coach therefore sets the terms of the job, including who picks the call for each snap.

The title alone does not settle the question. Two coaches can both be offensive coordinators on different staffs and still do different work on game day. One chooses the call for every snap. The other leaves that choice to the head coach once the game starts.

That split changes how much control one coach has over a unit. A coordinator who calls plays has more direct influence over the unit during games. The order of calls and the response to what the opponent shows run through that coach's headset.

A coordinator who does not call plays fills a different role. That coach works mainly as a planner and a teacher. The coordinator still builds the weekly game plan and teaches the scheme in meetings. That influence shows up in how the unit is prepared, not in the choice of each snap.

Game-day workload is one reason the duty gets delegated. A head coach who calls plays has to handle other game-day decisions at the same time. Many head coaches hand over the play sheet for that reason.

The same choice exists on defense. The defensive coordinator is the usual caller there. A head coach with a defensive background can take that role instead. In that case, the defensive coordinator moves into the planning role.

For a coaching candidate, the assignment shapes the job. Two openings with the same title can carry different authority on game day. One includes control of the play sheet, and the other does not.

Fans and media often give credit or blame for an NFL offense or defense to the coordinator, based on the title. That habit can miss the coach who actually chose each play during the game.

The title is the public label attached to a unit. Who holds the play sheet is harder to see from the stands or on a broadcast. A head coach can keep play-calling while an assistant carries the offensive coordinator title.

The same split can happen on defense. The defensive coordinator usually calls that side of the ball. A head coach with a defensive background can take over that role. The coordinator's name then stays attached to calls made by someone else.

When the roles sit with different coaches, the coordinator's name still tends to absorb the reaction. A stalled drive can be pinned on the coordinator even when the head coach made the call. The reverse also happens. A strong performance can be credited to the coordinator even when the in-game choices came from someone else.

The split is not all-or-nothing. A coordinator who does not call plays usually still builds the weekly game plan and teaches the scheme. That coordinator can shape the plan the calls come from without choosing a single snap.

The head coach's game-day load adds another layer. A head coach who calls plays is also managing the clock. That coach is deciding on challenges and handling personnel at the same time. Each of those duties competes for attention with the next call.

The gap between title and task shapes how a unit's results are judged. The coordinator title names who runs the unit. The play-calling assignment names who chose its plays in a given game. Those can be the same coach or two different ones. Knowing which coach holds the play sheet, not just the title, shows who made those calls.

#5356. Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”

Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

“We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

The end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

#5355. AI Search Is Tipping The Balance In Favor Of Big-Box Stores. Here’s How Small Retailers Can Fight Back

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI search overwhelmingly favors major retailers. Small merchants can take these three steps to get noticed by chatbots.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

This fall, my company took an important message to the heart of New York City.

The call to action: “Prompt Local.” At our pop-up storefront in the East Village, we showed how shoppers can tweak AI search to make it recommend independent retailers. Across the front window, scenes of people searching online were paired with specific prompts designed to steer AI agents toward local businesses.

From working with tens of thousands of merchants, we knew it was time to take a stand. There’s a lot at stake for small retailers, and we’ve got the receipts to prove it. As AI search quickly becomes the norm, those stores are getting lost in the shuffle.

A new study we commissioned shows that nine times out of 10, AI directs shoppers to major retailers. Looking to buy a new road bike in New York? Chances are, ChatGPT will provide a list of national chains, even when there’s a great independent store just around the corner. The buyer didn’t ask for that kind of list. The model decided for them.

For the past two decades, being discoverable online revolved around SEO. The basic question was: Are you showing up in Google results? Search engines learned shoppers’ locations and surfaced nearby businesses.

Those priorities shouldn’t disappear just because answers now come from chatbots. If AI platforms are becoming the new front door to commerce, they share responsibility for which businesses get found.

But small retailers can’t afford to wait for these companies to refine their search results. AI is changing the rules, and stores need to keep up. They have to think not only about whether search engines can find them, but whether AI understands who they are, what they sell, and why they’re worth recommending.

One place to start is by educating customers. Our study found that adding words like “independent” or “locally owned” to AI searches reduced big chains’ share of recommendations to as little as one in 10 on Google’s platforms.

Retailers can spread the word by sharing simple search tips with shoppers in-store, on their websites, and across social media. The more consumers make independent businesses a priority in their searches, the stronger the signal to AI companies that local options deserve greater visibility.

Beyond educating shoppers, here are three more things merchants can do to raise their profile in AI search.

To get AI’s attention, small retailers also need to give them something to find. And the closer a shopper gets to making a purchase, the tougher the competition becomes. Our study showed that when someone names a specific product, a small store’s odds of being the top recommendation fall from roughly one in three to one in 10.

Big retailers also have an advantage when it comes to how much information about them is readily available online. Their catalogs, inventory, product descriptions, reviews, and locations are already highly visible. Small merchants may have deeper expertise and better curation, but AI can’t recommend what it can’t see.

That makes it even more important for retailers to put their inventory online. AI agents increasingly fetch product information directly, which means retail websites may effectively become showrooms for both AI and human shoppers.Here, AI is part of the solution. New tools let retailers showcase their entire product catalog so agents can find what they’re looking for. Besides syncing that inventory with your POS, they write descriptions that make those products easier for AI to discover.

Making a retail website simple for AI to read is critical, too. Behind the scenes, a merchant can clearly label product details like price, brand, and whether an item is in stock, while also giving search and AI crawlers a map of the pages it wants them to find.

When shoppers use an AI chatbot to search, they ask a lot of questions. What jacket styles are hot this fall? Which supportive running shoes are best for beginners? What are the top ergonomic office chairs for working from home?

For independent retailers, that creates another opportunity to get noticed. The key is to establish yourself as an expert by building authority around what you sell.

Useful, substantive content can help. For example, a bike shop could create TikTok or YouTube videos showing how to set up tubeless tires or replace a worn chain. Those clips may look educational, but what they’re really doing is showing the expertise behind the business.

Of all the social platforms, YouTube could be an independent merchant’s best friend. Just ask the small luxury watch dealers who use long-form informational videos to build trust — by exploring topics like how to avoid buying a fake.

YouTube’s connection to Google makes it an even more powerful tool for independent retailers. Gemini regularly surfaces videos from the site, giving merchants another way to get their expertise (and products) in front of shoppers using AI search.

A steady stream of blog posts can do the same thing. By posting weekly about fashion trends, for instance, a women’s clothing boutique gives AI systems more proof that it knows its category inside and out.

If that sounds like a heavy lift, it doesn’t need to be. AI assistants can help write, publish, and manage blog content, while built-in SEO tools help optimize each post for traditional search and make it easier for search engines to crawl and AI systems to understand.

To stand out in AI search, small retailers also need to rethink what social media is for.

Platforms like Reddit, Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube still help stores reach shoppers. But they now do a second job: showing AI what a business sells, what it knows, and what it specializes in.

AI tools are paying attention. Social posts appear in almost 70% of Google’s AI Overview responses. And in Google’s AI mode, they show up in almost half of responses to searches that don’t name a brand — the ones shoppers type before they know your store exists.Meta’s new Muse agent takes this further. Muse works inside Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, which reach 3.6 billion people a day. With a shopper’s permission, it can learn their taste from what they follow, like, save, and share. Every customer who engages with a store’s posts is teaching their agent that the store belongs on their shortlist. Retailers with active, engaged communities are more likely to be recommended.

That’s the real opening for local retailers: AI remembers what shoppers like. Once a customer shows their agent they value a certain kind of store, like a neighborhood bookshop or an independent boutique, it can keep recommending similar places.

For their part, retailers should show up consistently where both shoppers and AI are paying attention. By embracing this new reality, they can turn a potential threat into a reason for customers to make the trip.

This fall, my company took an important message to the heart of New York City.

The call to action: “Prompt Local.” At our pop-up storefront in the East Village, we showed how shoppers can tweak AI search to make it recommend independent retailers. Across the front window, scenes of people searching online were paired with specific prompts designed to steer AI agents toward local businesses.

From working with tens of thousands of merchants, we knew it was time to take a stand. There’s a lot at stake for small retailers, and we’ve got the receipts to prove it. As AI search quickly becomes the norm, those stores are getting lost in the shuffle.

#5354. The speaker of the House holds the gavel, but the job covers much more

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What the speaker of the House does goes well beyond holding the gavel — 10 duties, from shaping floor votes to standing second in line for the presidency

The speaker of the House is best known as the person holding the gavel on the House floor. That image covers only a small share of the job. The speaker helps decide which bills reach a vote, shapes who sits on key committees and leads the majority party. The speaker also stands second in line for the presidency, behind only the vice president.

Any account of what the speaker of the House does starts with a split at the heart of the role. The speaker is an officer of the whole chamber, chosen by a vote of the full House. The speaker is also a party leader, the top-ranking member of whichever party holds the majority. Those two jobs sit side by side. One involves running the institution for every member. The other involves advancing a party's agenda and holding its majority together.

The powers attached to the office are real, but they are not unlimited. The speaker shares control of the floor with the majority leader and the Rules Committee. Rank-and-file members have tools of their own. A discharge petition can push a bill to a vote over leadership objections. A motion to vacate the chair can remove a sitting speaker.

The office's formal outline comes from a single clause in the Constitution. Much of its practical weight comes from House rules, precedent and party custom built up over more than two centuries. Sam Rayburn held the post longer than anyone else, a little over 17 years spread across several stretches between 1940 and 1961.

The 10 slides that follow break the job into its main parts. They cover how the Constitution creates the post, how members elect a speaker and how the speaker runs floor debate. They also explain the influence over scheduling and committees, the party leadership role and the place in presidential succession. The remaining slides cover administrative and ceremonial duties, along with the process for removing a speaker.

The speaker of the House exists because Article I, Section 2 of the Constitution says the House chooses its own speaker and other officers. That short provision is the legal footing for the office.

The power to choose belongs to the House alone. The clause gives the president and the Senate no role in the selection.

That arrangement makes the speaker an officer of the chamber itself. The person in the post owes the job to House members, not to another branch of government.

The same provision reaches beyond the speaker. It also lets the House pick the other officers who help run the institution, not only the person who presides over it.

Nothing in the text says the speaker must be a sitting member of the House. On paper, the chamber could elect someone from outside its ranks. It has never done so. Every speaker so far has been a member.

That unbroken pattern began with Frederick Muhlenberg, who became the first speaker in 1789.

The full House of Representatives elects its speaker at the opening of every new Congress. To win, a candidate needs a majority of the members who vote for a named person. Winning the most votes is not enough on its own.

That threshold depends on who casts a vote for someone. A member who answers "present" or is absent does not count toward the total. With all 435 seats filled and every member naming a candidate, the winning mark is 218 votes. Each "present" vote or absence lowers that mark. The number needed to win can then fall below half of the full chamber.

The first stage takes place before the floor vote. The majority party picks its nominee first, usually in a closed-door vote of its own conference. That private step is meant to line up the party behind one candidate before the whole chamber weighs in. The minority party usually nominates its own candidate as well.

The system relies on party unity. A nominee who loses even a few colleagues on the floor can fall short of a majority. The smaller the majority party's edge, the fewer defections it takes to stall the vote.

Kevin McCarthy's election in January 2023 showed what that looks like in practice. He won the speakership only on the 15th ballot. Every failed round sent the House back to vote again, because no candidate had yet cleared the majority mark.

Because the election takes place at the start of each Congress, the post is never held indefinitely. A sitting speaker who wants to stay in the job has to win the vote again when the next Congress convenes.

The process splits the choice between a party and the full chamber. The majority party chooses the nominee in private. The formal decision still belongs to every member who votes on the House floor.

The speaker of the House is the chamber's presiding officer. The speaker opens each session, recognizes members who want to speak and rules on points of order raised during floor proceedings.

Recognition is the starting point of the floor job. A member who wants to address the House does not simply begin talking. The member first needs recognition from the chair. Granting or withholding it is one of the speaker's presiding powers.

A point of order is an objection that the House is breaking one of its own rules. The presiding officer rules on each one, usually on the advice of the House parliamentarian. Those rulings become precedents that later presiding officers consult.

A ruling from the chair is not always final. Any member can appeal it to the full House, which then decides the question by majority vote. The majority often moves to table such an appeal. If that motion passes, the ruling stands.

The speaker does not have to sit in the chair for every hour of debate. Under House rules, the speaker can name another member to act as speaker pro tempore. That designation can last up to three legislative days without the House's approval. The handoff happens often during routine debate. The member holding the gavel on a given afternoon is frequently someone other than the speaker.

The speaker also steps aside when the House sits as the Committee of the Whole House on the state of the Union. That is the procedural form the House often uses to debate and amend bills. The speaker appoints a different member to chair it.

The speaker keeps the right to vote as a member of the House. In practice, the speaker usually does not cast a vote. House rules do not require the speaker to vote in ordinary proceedings.

There are two main exceptions to that habit. The speaker may vote on major questions. The speaker may also vote when a single ballot would break a tie.

The speaker of the House, working with the majority leader and the Rules Committee, largely decides which bills reach a vote on the House floor. That control over the agenda is one of the job's main sources of power. It is shared, though, not held by the speaker alone.

A bill that clears a House committee has no guaranteed path to the floor. Thousands of bills are introduced in each Congress, and most never receive a floor vote.

The majority leader manages the day-to-day floor schedule and announces the coming week's business. The speaker sets the broader priorities that the schedule follows. Decisions on major legislation are usually made by the two leaders together, in consultation with committee chairs and the majority party's members.

For most significant bills, the route to the floor runs through the Rules Committee. The committee writes a resolution, known as a special rule, that sets the terms of debate. The rule specifies how long members may debate a bill and which amendments, if any, may be offered. The full House must adopt that rule by majority vote before it takes up the bill itself.

A second route covers less contested measures. Under a procedure called suspension of the rules, a bill comes up with 40 minutes of debate and no floor amendments. Passage then requires a two-thirds vote of the members present and voting. Under House rules, the speaker has discretion over whether to recognize members to offer suspension motions.

The majority party also follows informal practices about what it brings forward. The best known is the Hastert rule, named for former Speaker Dennis Hastert. It describes a practice of bringing up only bills backed by a majority of the majority party. It is a custom rather than a written House rule, and speakers have set it aside on some votes.

Members who want to get around the leadership have one main formal tool: the discharge petition. A petition can be filed once a bill has sat in committee for 30 legislative days. If 218 members sign it, the bill can be forced to the floor over the leadership's objections.

That threshold equals a majority of the full 435-member House. When the minority party holds fewer than 218 seats, its members cannot complete a petition on their own. They need signatures from at least some members of the majority party.

The speaker of the House shapes several House committees by choosing who sits on them. In practice, the speaker names the majority-party members of the Rules Committee, along with the House members of conference committees and some select committees.

The Rules Committee writes the resolutions, known as rules, that govern how a bill is handled on the floor. A rule sets how long debate runs and which amendments members may offer. A rule that blocks amendments can keep a bill's text intact all the way to the final vote.

The speaker once ran that panel directly. Until the 1910 revolt against Speaker Joseph Cannon, the speaker chaired the Rules Committee.

Today the speaker does not hold the chairmanship. The speaker still picks the panel's majority-party members, however. Through those picks, the speaker keeps a direct tie to the committee that sets the terms of floor debate.

Conference committees are temporary panels of House and Senate negotiators. They resolve differences between the two chambers' versions of the same bill. The speaker chooses the House side of those teams. Those appointees represent the chamber while a final text is worked out. The compromise they reach then returns to both chambers for a vote.

Select committees are created for a set purpose, often an investigation, instead of serving as permanent standing panels. The speaker names the members of some of these committees. Those choices shape who conducts an investigation and how it proceeds.

Speaker Nancy Pelosi used that authority in 2021. She appointed the members of the House select committee on the Jan. 6 attack. Pelosi had become the first woman to serve as speaker in 2007.

These appointment powers have limits. Choosing committee members does not give the speaker sole control of the House. The majority leader and the wider majority party also influence how the Rules Committee's work reaches the floor.

The speaker of the House is the highest-ranking member of the majority party in the chamber. The speaker is also that party's public face, the person most closely identified with what the House majority wants to do.

That party post sits inside the same office that runs the chamber. The speaker presides over the House on behalf of all its members. The same person also leads one side of it.

The party side of the job centers on holding the majority together. That task grows harder when the margin is narrow. A slim majority leaves little room for members of the speaker's own party to break ranks on a vote.

The arithmetic of a close House shows why. If the minority party votes as a bloc against a measure, a small group of defectors from the majority can be enough to defeat it. That gives a handful of members leverage over the speaker. They can ask for changes to a bill as the price of their support.

The party role also explains why the speaker draws so much public attention. As the majority's most visible figure, the speaker stands in for the party in the House. No rank-and-file member carries that role. When the majority's agenda moves forward or stalls, the speaker is usually the person asked to account for it.

The political weight of the office has deep roots. In the early 1800s, Henry Clay built the speakership into a post that drove policy. Under Clay, the office became a seat of political leadership as well as the chair of the chamber. The modern speakership still carries both parts: chairing the House and pushing the majority's agenda.

The speaker of the House is second in line to the presidency. Under the Presidential Succession Act of 1947, only the vice president stands ahead of the speaker.

The 1947 law also sets the order behind the speaker. The president pro tempore of the Senate comes next. Members of the Cabinet follow after that.

The result places two officers of Congress ahead of every Cabinet member. The speaker and the Senate president pro tempore both outrank the executive branch's department heads in the line of succession.

The arrangement ties the presidency to a post the House fills by its own vote. The officer second in line is the person the House has chosen to run its chamber.

The speaker of the House swears in members at the start of each new Congress and signs enrolled bills before they go to the president. Both duties are formal steps that the chamber's business depends on.

The oath itself comes from the Constitution. Article VI requires members of Congress to be bound by an oath or affirmation to support the Constitution. The oath is the step that turns a member-elect into a sworn member of the House.

On opening day, the newly elected speaker first takes the oath from the dean of the House, the longest continuously serving member. The speaker then administers the oath to the other members together. They raise their right hands and take it as a group, returning members alongside first-term ones.

The House also elects its own officers at the start of each Congress. They include the Clerk, the Sergeant at Arms, the Chief Administrative Officer and the Chaplain. The full chamber chooses them, and the speaker does not appoint them alone. Once in place, they answer to the House leadership. Between them, the Clerk, the Sergeant at Arms and the Chief Administrative Officer keep the chamber's records, security and day-to-day operations running.

Signing enrolled bills happens at the other end of the legislative process. An enrolled bill is the final official copy of a measure that both chambers have passed in identical form. It is printed on parchment by the chamber where the bill began.

The speaker signs that copy. The Senate's presiding officer signs it as well. The signatures attest that the text is the version Congress approved. They do not change any of its contents. House rules also let the speaker designate another member to sign enrolled bills in the speaker's place.

Only after both signatures can the bill be presented to the president. Article I, Section 7 gives the president 10 days, Sundays excepted, to sign or veto it once it arrives. A delay in signing at the Capitol pushes back when that clock starts.

The speaker presides over joint sessions of Congress together with the Senate's presiding officer. The speaker also invites the president to deliver the State of the Union address.

A joint session brings the House and the Senate together for a single proceeding. Neither chamber's officer runs it alone. The speaker shares the rostrum with the Senate's presiding officer, so each chamber has its top officer at the front of the room.

That shared arrangement sets joint sessions apart from ordinary House business. On a normal legislative day, only House members take part, and the Senate conducts its own proceedings separately.

The State of the Union starts with the speaker's invitation. The speaker sends it to the president. The president then appears before both chambers to deliver the address.

The invitation runs from the legislative branch to the executive. The address takes place at the speaker's invitation rather than on the president's own initiative.

During the speech, the speaker sits behind the president. The vice president sits beside the speaker. The arrangement places the officers tied to the House and the Senate side by side for the length of the address.

The speaker comes from the party that holds the House majority. That party is not always the president's party. When the two differ, a leader of the opposing party sits behind the president for the full address.

A motion to vacate the chair is the procedure the House uses to remove a sitting speaker. The House first voted a speaker out on Oct. 3, 2023, when members removed Speaker Kevin McCarthy by a vote of 216 to 210.

If the motion passes, the speaker's chair becomes vacant. The House then has no elected speaker until it chooses a new one.

The McCarthy vote was decided by a margin of six votes. It came in the same Congress that had elected him to the post only months earlier. A switch by a handful of members would have changed the result.

The vacancy lasted 22 days. During that stretch, Patrick McHenry served as speaker pro tempore. He held the chair on a temporary basis and was not elected speaker. McHenry treated the role as limited mainly to overseeing the election of a successor. The House passed no legislation while the chair stayed empty. Floor business effectively waited on the outcome of the speaker race. The vacancy ended on Oct. 25, 2023, when the House elected Mike Johnson.

The rules that govern the motion are set by the House itself. They can change from one Congress to the next. In the 119th Congress, House rules require nine members of the majority party to back a motion to vacate before it is privileged.

A privileged motion takes precedence over ordinary business on the floor. Under the 119th Congress rule, that status depends on support from members of the speaker's own party. Members of the minority party cannot make the motion privileged by themselves. As a result, the most direct threat of removal comes from inside the majority conference rather than from the opposing party.

The motion gives the full House a check on the person it elected to run the chamber. The same body that chooses a speaker can also take the job away.

#5353. What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”

Microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

The company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate issue,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down.

Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

The company’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Microsoft says it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put new limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate issue,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t said what it was.

#5352. Why a House speaker needs a majority of votes cast, not always 218

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How the House elects a speaker, from private party nomination votes to the Clerk-run roll call, the majority threshold, repeated ballots, the oath and the motion to vacate

The top job in the House of Representatives is filled by a vote the Constitution barely describes. The founding document says the House shall choose its Speaker. It says nothing about nominations, ballots, majorities or what happens when no one wins. Those details come from party custom and House precedent.

Understanding how the House elects a speaker starts with a simple point: the process happens in two stages. The first is private. After a November election, each party's House members gather behind closed doors to pick a nominee. The second is public. On the opening day of a new Congress, the full House votes by roll call, with each voting member answering aloud. Only that second vote makes someone Speaker.

The stakes are practical as well as political. Until a Speaker is chosen, the House does not swear in its members or adopt the rules that govern its work. A smooth vote takes one ballot. A divided majority can turn opening day into a days-long standoff.

Recent history shows both ends of that range. In January 2023, Kevin McCarthy needed 15 ballots to win the gavel. That was the most for a Speaker election since before the Civil War. Mike Johnson won on the first ballot on Jan. 3, 2025. The same rules produced both results.

The process does not end with the vote. A sitting Speaker can be removed through a motion to vacate the chair. Once in office, the Speaker presides over the House floor and stands second in the line of presidential succession, behind the vice president.

This guide walks through each step in order. It starts with the constitutional text and the party nomination votes. It then covers the opening-day roll call run by the Clerk of the House, the majority a candidate needs and what happens when ballots fail. It closes with the oath, the rules for removal and the powers that come with the office.

The Constitution gives the House of Representatives the power to choose its own Speaker, and it says very little else about the job. Article I, Section 2, Clause 5 states that the House "shall chuse their Speaker and other Officers."

The spelling "chuse" was a common 18th-century form of "choose." That short clause settles one question: who makes the choice. The House picks its presiding officer. No other branch of government has a role in the selection.

The same clause gives the House one more power. It closes by granting the chamber "the sole Power of Impeachment."

The Senate works under a different arrangement. Article I, Section 3 makes the vice president the President of the Senate. Senators choose their other officers, including a president pro tempore to preside when the vice president is absent. The House has no outside presiding officer of that kind. Its leader comes from its own vote.

The text also leaves gaps. It does not name anyone to lead the chamber before a Speaker takes the chair.

The "other Officers" are left undefined as well. The Constitution does not list who they must be or what duties they carry. Today, House Rule II provides for the election of a Clerk, a Sergeant at Arms, a Chief Administrative Officer and a Chaplain.

The text sets no membership requirement for the Speaker. Nothing in the Constitution says the person chosen must hold a House seat. Under the plain wording, the House could elect someone from outside the chamber.

The House has never done so. Every Speaker has been a member of the House at the time of election. The House elected its first Speaker, Frederick Muhlenberg of Pennsylvania, on April 1, 1789, during the First Congress.

The constitutional basis for the office is a single line. Everything else about the Speaker election, from party nominations to the floor roll call, was built by the House itself.

Each party picks its candidate for Speaker in a private vote of its own House members, held after the November election. That nomination is only a first step. It does not make anyone Speaker. The post is filled by a vote of the full House on the floor.

The two parties run this step through separate organizations. House Republicans meet as the House Republican Conference. House Democrats meet as the House Democratic Caucus. The names differ, but the job at this stage is the same: settle on one person the party will back when the new Congress opens.

These meetings happen behind closed doors. The public learns the outcome, not the internal debate that produced it. The floor vote that follows is different. On opening day, each member's choice becomes part of the public record.

The November 2022 Republican race shows how a party nomination works in practice. Kevin McCarthy, then the House Republican leader, faced a challenge from Andy Biggs of Arizona. Biggs was a former chairman of the House Freedom Caucus. McCarthy won the conference nomination 188 to 31.

That margin gave McCarthy his party's nomination. It did not settle who would hold the gavel. A conference vote measures support inside one party. The floor vote measures support across the entire chamber. The two results do not always match.

The gap matters most when the majority party holds a narrow edge. A nominee in that position has little room to lose votes from within the party. Members who oppose their party's pick in a private meeting are free to carry that opposition into the public roll call.

For the minority party, the private vote serves a different purpose. Its nominee cannot win the speakership while the majority party stays united behind its own candidate. The vote instead settles whose name the party will place in nomination when the House convenes.

A new Congress convenes at noon on Jan. 3, the date set by the 20th Amendment, unless Congress passes a law choosing another day. Until the House elects a Speaker, the Clerk of the House runs the chamber and confirms a quorum before any vote begins.

The Jan. 3 start date goes back to 1933, when the 20th Amendment was ratified. Before then, the Constitution directed Congress to assemble on the first Monday in December. Under that schedule, a newly elected House often did not hold its first regular session until more than a year after its members won their seats.

The amendment's exception clause gets regular use. Congress has used it to set a different opening day by law. The 112th Congress convened on Jan. 5, 2011, and the 114th Congress convened on Jan. 6, 2015.

An officer who is not a member of Congress presides over the opening session. The Clerk is an officer elected by the House to keep its records and manage much of its legislative and administrative work.

Federal law keeps the Clerk from the previous Congress on the job when the new House assembles. That continuity fills the gap before the new House has chosen any officers of its own.

The same law assigns the Clerk a first task. The Clerk prepares the roll of members-elect from the certificates of election that states send after the November vote. That roll is the official list of people who may answer when the House is called to order.

Before the Speaker election starts, the Clerk confirms that a quorum is present. Members-elect record their presence, and the Clerk announces whether enough have responded for the House to proceed. Only then does the chamber move to nominations.

The Clerk's job on opening day is limited to keeping order and conducting the election. If the voting stretches over several days, the Clerk stays in the chair for each session until a Speaker is chosen.

Speaker candidates enter the House contest through formal nominations made on the floor. The chair of each party's conference or caucus rises to place the party's nominee in nomination. The minority party nominates a candidate too, usually its own leader.

Nominations come at the start of the opening-day proceedings, before any member casts a vote. The Clerk of the House recognizes each nominating member in turn. Each name usually comes with a short nominating speech that lays out the party's case for its candidate.

Republicans give the task to the chair of the House Republican Conference. Democrats give it to the chair of the House Democratic Caucus. Each chair is a party officer elected by the party's own House members. A nomination from that officer presents the nominee as the choice of the party as a body, not of a single ally.

The minority party goes through the same formal step. Its nominee is typically the party's top leader in the House. At the opening of the new Congress on Jan. 3, 2023, Hakeem Jeffries was the Democratic nominee.

The minority holds fewer seats than the majority, so its nominee usually lacks the votes to win. The nomination still gives the party's members a named candidate to support when their names are called. It also puts the party's leader on the record as its choice for the chair.

A nomination is not a vote, and it does not close the field. Party chairs make the main nominations, but other members may also rise to place a name before the House. Members can even answer the roll call with the name of someone who was never nominated. Those answers are recorded like any other vote for a named person.

The nominations frame the contest without deciding it. They tell members and the public which candidates the parties are formally backing before balloting begins. Once the names are in, the Clerk moves to the roll call that settles the result.

The House elects its Speaker through a spoken roll call. The Clerk of the House calls each member's name in alphabetical order, and each member answers aloud with the name of the person they want as Speaker.

That spoken format sets the Speaker election apart from most House business. Most recorded votes in the chamber are cast electronically, with members using voting cards at stations on the floor. The Speaker vote does not use that system. Every choice is said out loud, one member at a time.

The call runs through members' surnames from A to Z. Party and seniority do not affect the order. A Republican and a Democrat with neighboring last names answer one after the other.

Members answer with a name rather than "yea" or "nay." The vote is therefore not a simple up-or-down decision on one nominee. A member can name the majority party's candidate or the minority party's candidate. A member can also name someone who was never formally placed in nomination. Whatever name a member gives is recorded as a vote for that person. A member may also answer "present," which records attendance without backing any candidate.

Tellers keep the count as the names are called. These tellers are House members, typically drawn from both parties. A bipartisan count gives each side a direct view of the tally as it builds.

Once the call is complete, the Clerk announces the result. The announcement lists each person who received votes and the number each received. It also states whether any candidate reached the majority needed to win.

The spoken format also leaves a full public record. Every member's choice is heard in the chamber and captured in the official roll call. The Congressional Record prints each member's name alongside the candidate that member supported. Constituents, party leaders and reporters can see exactly how each member voted.

A candidate for Speaker wins by taking a majority of the votes cast for a named person, not a fixed number of seats. The figure of 218 applies only when all 435 members vote and each one names a candidate.

That makes 218 a figure tied to one set of conditions rather than a permanent requirement. The real target can sit below it.

The base of the calculation is the group of members who actually vote for someone by name. When the 435-member House has every member naming a candidate, a majority of that group is 218.

Absences change the math. A member who is not on the floor during the roll call casts no vote. That member drops out of the total that the majority is measured against, and the number required falls with it.

A "present" vote has the same effect on the count. A member who answers "present" takes part in the roll call but backs no named candidate. That answer does not name a person. It is left out of the base used to set the majority. The bar drops again.

This gives a reluctant member a choice beyond backing the nominee or voting for someone else. A lawmaker who will not support the leading candidate can answer "present" or stay away instead of naming a rival. Either step lowers the number the leading candidate needs. It does not add a vote to that candidate's total.

Votes for other named candidates work differently. A member who names someone other than the front-runner stays in the base. That vote keeps the threshold where it is.

The exact number a Speaker needs is set by the votes actually cast. It can be confirmed only once the roll call is complete and every response has been counted. A candidate can therefore win with fewer than 218 votes when absences or "present" answers shrink the base.

If no candidate wins a majority on the first ballot, the House votes again. It keeps holding new roll calls until one candidate wins a majority, and no rule caps the number of ballots.

Each new ballot starts from scratch. The House does not drop the last-place candidate. It does not hold a runoff between the top two finishers or hand the job to whoever leads. The same majority rule applies on every round.

Members are free to change their votes between rounds. A member can stay with an earlier choice, move to another candidate or name a person who drew no support on the previous ballot. Candidates can also be placed in nomination again before a later roll call.

The Clerk of the House stays in the chair through every round. The House can adjourn between ballots and return later. That pause can give party leaders time to negotiate with holdouts away from the floor.

Kevin McCarthy's election at the start of 2023 shows how long the process can run. The California Republican became Speaker on the 15th ballot, on Jan. 7, 2023. Fourteen roll calls had ended without a winner before that one.

A century earlier, the House faced a similar deadlock. Frederick Gillett won the speakership on the ninth ballot in 1923. Eight rounds had failed to produce a majority before members settled on him.

A first-ballot win remains the usual result. Repeated ballots typically arise when the majority party's own members do not unite behind its nominee.

With a narrow majority, a small group of dissenters can withhold enough votes to block their own party's nominee. That can happen even after the nominee has won the private party vote. A dissenter can vote for another person, vote "present" or skip a ballot. Each of those choices changes the count on that round. The number of votes a candidate needs can therefore shift from one ballot to the next.

The Dean of the House, the chamber's longest-serving member, administers the oath of office to a newly elected Speaker. The Speaker then swears in the rest of the members, and the House turns to adopting its rules package.

Before taking the oath, the Speaker-elect is escorted to the chair. By custom, the leader of the other party introduces the winner and hands over the gavel.

The Speaker goes first in this sequence. Until the Speaker vote ends, the people seated in the chamber are members-elect, not sworn members. The new Speaker becomes the first of them to take the oath.

The oath itself traces to Article VI of the Constitution. It requires senators and representatives to be bound by oath or affirmation to support the Constitution. A member-elect becomes a sworn member only after taking it.

The Dean's part in the ceremony rests on seniority, not party. The title goes to whichever member has the longest continuous service in the House. The member who swears in the Speaker can therefore come from the party that lost the gavel.

Once sworn, the Speaker administers the oath to the other members-elect. They take it together as a group on the floor, not one at a time. That single oath turns the members-elect into a sworn House.

With its members sworn, the House also elects its officers, including the Clerk, the Sergeant at Arms and the Chaplain. Those posts are usually filled by adopting a single resolution rather than by separate roll calls.

The rules package comes next. It sets the procedures the chamber will follow for the two-year Congress that has just begun. Adopting it is a separate vote of the full House.

That vote is needed at the start of every Congress. Unlike the Senate, the House is not treated as a continuing body. Its rules do not carry over on their own. Each new House adopts a set, usually building on the previous Congress's rules with changes.

A motion to vacate the chair is the House's way to remove a sitting Speaker. Under the House rules in force in 2023, any member could offer one. On Oct. 3, 2023, the House voted 216 to 210 to remove Kevin McCarthy. He was the first Speaker removed this way.

The motion puts one question to the full chamber: should the office of Speaker be declared vacant? It does not name a replacement. A successful vote ends the sitting Speaker's tenure. Choosing a successor is a separate step.

That split shapes how a removal vote comes together. Members who back a removal do not have to agree on who should hold the gavel next. They only have to agree that the current Speaker should go. A small group of majority-party members can join with the opposing party to reach a majority. Neither side needs a shared plan for what follows.

Six votes separated the 216 members who backed the motion against McCarthy from the 210 who opposed it. The vote came about nine months into his tenure. The motion needs only a simple majority of the members voting. A narrow margin is enough to carry it.

Removing McCarthy left the chair without an elected Speaker. A Speaker pro tempore, drawn from a list McCarthy had filed in advance, presided in the meantime. The House had to run the full election process again, starting with new party nominations. Mike Johnson won the office on Oct. 25, 2023, by a vote of 220 to 209. His election came 22 days after the removal vote.

The two tallies measured different things. The first showed a majority willing to end a speakership. The second showed a majority able to agree on a replacement. Assembling that second majority took more than three weeks.

Under the 2023 rule, a Speaker could face a removal vote at any point in a Congress, not only on the day of the election. The possibility of removal stayed open for the full term.

The Speaker of the House presides over floor proceedings, decides which members are recognized and sets the floor schedule. The office also ranks second in the line of presidential succession, behind only the vice president, under the Presidential Succession Act of 1947.

Each of the three floor powers covers a different part of the chamber's work. Presiding means the Speaker runs House sessions from the chair. Recognition decides which member gets the floor at a given moment.

Control of the floor schedule decides which measures come up for consideration and when. A bill that never reaches the floor cannot get a vote of the full House. The person who sets the calendar shapes what the chamber takes up at all.

These powers put order in the chamber and the flow of its business in the same hands. The member who wins the opening-day roll call gains control over what the House debates, not only a title.

The succession role reaches beyond the House. If both the presidency and the vice presidency were vacant, the Speaker would be next in line. That ranking links a post filled by a vote of House members to the executive branch.

The Speaker's place in the order comes from a statute, the 1947 act, rather than from the Constitution's text. The place in line belongs to the office, not to any individual. Whoever holds the Speaker's chair occupies that position in the succession order. When a new Speaker is elected, including after a removal, the place in line passes to that person.
