#5351. This 54-Year-Old Left Her Full-Time Therapist Job to Focus on a Flavorful Side Hustle Making $10K a Month on Amazon: ‘I Used ChatGPT’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Lana Wimmer wanted to bring a different kind of beverage to market.

This Side Hustle Spotlight Q&A features Lana Wimmer, 54, of St. George, Utah. She started her side hustle Öl Brew (pronounced “cool” without the “c”), a nonalcoholic sparkling fruit malt beverage, while working about 40 hours a week as a mental health therapist. Once she caught herself sitting in a therapy session thinking about Öl Brew, she knew she had to focus on the business full-time. The brand generates about $10,000 a month in revenue on Amazon.  Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

When did you launch the side hustle, and what specific consumer pain point did you want to address? We launched Öl Brew in 2026, about six months ago, but the idea had been with me for eight years. For most of that time, I kept hoping someone else would make these drinks. I had absolutely no ambition to enter the beverage industry.

My husband and I had lived in Europe and the Middle East, where we’d discovered nonalcoholic fruit malt beverages with this wonderful depth, body and flavor. They were nothing like the sodas we had back home. When we returned to the U.S., I couldn’t find anything that compared. The options felt uninspired: soda, sparkling water or a mocktail trying awfully hard to replace alcohol. I didn’t want an imitation of something else. I wanted a genuinely different drinking experience.

How did you validate that people would actually pay for your solution before investing serious money?One evening, I finally shared my idea over dinner with friends. The response was immediate. Everyone wanted better nonalcoholic options; this wasn’t just my personal preference.

I was also watching a shift in consumer behavior, particularly among my own adult children and their friends. They weren’t gathering around alcohol. They were cold plunging, working out and training for HYROX competitions. Their social lives looked different, and so did their beverage choices. Having spent decades as a therapist, I was especially interested in what was driving that shift. People were becoming more intentional about how they spent their time, what they consumed and how they connected.

Those early conversations gave me the conviction to invest although they weren’t proof of purchase. That came later when we got the product onto shelves and watched customers respond. Sometimes you recognize a gap in the market because you’ve been standing in it for years.

Which two or three essential tools, apps or pieces of gear did you buy in your first week, and which ones did you skip to save money?My first tools were a notebook, my computer and ChatGPT. I started writing down everything I wanted to build, followed by a much longer list of everything I didn’t know.

I used ChatGPT to research flavor houses, co-packers, brand management companies, distributors and how the beverage industry actually works. It helped me learn the terminology, understand the process and figure out whom I needed to talk to. But the real education came when I started taking those questions to people with experience. AI gave me a starting point. Industry professionals gave me context, perspective and occasionally some very expensive lessons.

I also listened constantly to business and beverage podcasts, particularly The Game with Alex Hormozi, Tim Bush’s On the Shelf and Joey Pedone’s Sippin’ & Selling. I didn’t spend money on elaborate software systems or expensive subscriptions in the beginning. My priority was understanding the business well enough to make informed decisions. I learned quickly that information is relatively easy to find. Knowing what to do with it is another matter entirely.

What were the first three steps you took in your first 30 days?My first 30 days were focused on three things: Developing a go-to-market plan, identifying our target consumer and first four flavors, and finding the people who could help bring the product to life.

I used AI to help research the industry and build an initial strategy. Then I settled on apple, lemon, peach and pomegranate as our first flavors. I wanted something familiar enough that people would be curious to try it, but different enough that they’d immediately recognize this wasn’t ordinary soda.

Then came the investment. I spent $50,000 hiring a beverage development company to help formulate the drinks and connect us with a co-packer. I also hired a branding company to develop our can designs and brand book. Altogether, the initial upfront cost, including the pilot run and production run, was about $200,000.

Here’s what I learned later: The formulation work could have been arranged without that fee. I didn’t know that at the time. That was an expensive introduction to an industry where relationships, experience and knowing the right questions to ask can save you a tremendous amount of money.

How did you land your first paying customer?Our first paying customer came after our pilot run and initial production, and there was nothing sophisticated about the sales strategy. We walked into a local grocery store, sat down with the manager, introduced ourselves and told him what we were building. He agreed to carry Öl Brew.

Another local farmers market retailer followed, and suddenly our drinks were on shelves, where actual customers could decide if our idea had merit. Those first accounts gave us more than revenue. They gave us feedback, credibility and the opportunity to start building a business in the real world.

After all the planning, design, and money we’d spent, our first sale came from sitting across a table and having a conversation. I rather love that.

Nowadays, which specific tools or platforms help you bring in customers, and what is one feature inside those tools that saves you the most time?We’re using Instagram, TikTok Shop, Amazon, Walmart.com and our Shopify website to introduce consumers to Öl Brew and drive sales. Because we’re bringing an entirely new beverage experience to the American market, our marketing has to do more than create awareness. We have to give people a reason to be curious. Most consumers understand soda. They understand sparkling water. But sparkling fruit malt soda? That’s a conversation starter.

On the operational side, Klaviyo has been particularly useful for automating customer communication through Shopify. We can capture email addresses, create welcome sequences, share promotions and maintain relationships without manually managing every interaction. That kind of automation matters when you’re running lean.

What was the single biggest bottleneck that almost stalled your business, and what exact change or process fixed it?Distribution has been our biggest challenge. The beverage industry has a complicated relationship between retailers and distributors. Retailers want to know who’s distributing your product. Distributors increasingly want retail authorizations before they’ll take on a new brand. Which leaves emerging brands trying to convince both sides to move first.

We would attend trade shows and return with interest from eight distributors across the country. The conversations were promising, the enthusiasm was real, and then everything would stall because we didn’t yet have the retail commitments to support distribution. It was frustrating and forced us to reconsider our approach.

We realized we needed to focus less on how many distributors were interested and more on securing actual retail placements. That meant targeting independent stores and smaller retailers more willing to take a chance on something new. We also brought on an experienced VP of sales to help sharpen our strategy, prioritize accounts and build a more disciplined approach to retail expansion. It’s a significant shift, and we’re beginning to see a clearer path forward.

How many months did it take to reach consistent monthly revenue, and what was your average monthly profit during your first six months?We’re still working toward consistent monthly revenue. We’re only a few months into launch, and building a beverage brand requires significant capital long before the revenue catches up. But we’ve had encouraging early traction.

During Sober October, Öl Brew reached No. 14 in a nonalcoholic beverage ranking on Amazon. We also generated approximately $10,000 in Amazon revenue during October, just months after launching on the platform.

We’re not yet consistently profitable. We’re investing in inventory, marketing, distribution and the team we need to support growth. There’s a part of entrepreneurship that rarely makes it into the success stories: the period when you’re spending money, making adjustments and trying to determine which investments will actually produce results. That’s where we are.

What is your current monthly revenue and profit margin? We’re about six months into launch, with Amazon generating approximately $10,000 in monthly revenue, plus additional sales through retail and other ecommerce channels. We’re still investing heavily in growth, so we haven’t established a consistent net profit margin.

What part of the work do you still handle yourself, and which tasks have you outsourced?As for my time, I spend roughly 10 hours a day on Öl Brew, often more. My work falls into three main areas: brand awareness, retail and distribution, and manufacturing and operations. We’ve outsourced Amazon optimization and SEO, TikTok Shop management and creator partnerships, and much of our branding, marketing and social media execution.

If someone is starting from scratch today, what are common beginner mistakes they should avoid?Don’t rush into hiring. I made the mistake of trusting people who promised far more than they could deliver. Some were convincing, experienced and very good at selling their services. I was excited about building the brand, and that excitement sometimes made me move faster than I should have.

Now, I recommend interviewing at least three to five people or companies before making a significant hire. The interview process itself is an education. You’ll hear different strategies, cost structures and perspectives on what’s possible. Eventually, you’ll begin to recognize who understands the work and who simply knows how to sell it.

And don’t confuse confidence with having all the answers. I started a beverage company at 54 after a career in mental health. I knew a great deal about people and relationships. I knew very little about beverage manufacturing, distribution or retail. That experience has been both humbling and energizing. What I brought into this business wasn’t industry expertise. It was curiosity, conviction and a willingness to learn. I still believe those are some of the most valuable things an entrepreneur can have.

Be ambitious about what you want to build. Just be equally discerning about who you trust to help you build it.

#5350. Amazon picks its Bond: Robert Pattinson to play 007, ending years of speculation over coveted role

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he said in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The New York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

Pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”

Fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others said the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She quickly responded via text.

“No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”

#5349. How a USDA public health alert differs from a recall on meat, poultry and egg products

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A USDA public health alert and a recall both flag potentially unsafe meat, poultry or processed egg products, but they differ in whether the product is still sold

The same package of frozen chicken in a home freezer could end up named in a federal recall or in a public health alert. The label on that notice is not a matter of wording. It tells consumers something specific about where the product is likely to be.

Both kinds of notices come from the Food Safety and Inspection Service, known as FSIS, which is part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. FSIS regulates meat, poultry and processed egg products. The Food and Drug Administration regulates most other foods, including fresh produce and dairy. That split defines what a USDA notice can cover. A USDA notice applies only to the three product categories FSIS oversees. A warning about a bag of spinach comes from the FDA instead.

The core of the USDA public health alert vs. recall question is availability. A recall removes product that is still in commerce, meaning it may still be on store shelves or moving through distribution. A public health alert warns consumers about product that is likely no longer available for purchase but may still be in homes. FSIS also uses alerts when it lacks enough information to request a recall. An alert does not mean the product is safe to eat.

Recalls carry another layer of information. Each one is assigned to Class I, Class II or Class III according to the health risk involved. Public health alerts carry no class at all. USDA recalls are also voluntary actions taken by the company. FSIS does not have mandatory recall authority, though it has other tools to keep unsafe product away from consumers. The FDA, by contrast, holds mandatory recall authority for most foods under the Food Safety Modernization Act.

The 10 slides below cover how each type of notice works and what separates them. They also explain the problems that commonly prompt a notice, from Listeria monocytogenes to undeclared allergens. One slide shows how to match a package to a notice using the establishment number in the USDA mark of inspection. The last two slides cover what to do with an affected product and where to find current notices.

USDA food safety notices come from the Food Safety and Inspection Service, or FSIS. FSIS regulates meat, poultry and processed egg products. The Food and Drug Administration regulates most other foods.

FSIS is an agency of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. A food safety notice that carries the USDA name is an FSIS notice.

The agency's scope is limited to three product categories: meat, poultry and processed egg products. A USDA notice can only involve a product from one of those groups.

That limit makes the issuing agency a useful clue. A notice from FSIS signals that the product involved is meat, poultry or a processed egg product. A USDA notice will not cover a bag of salad or a box of cereal. Those foods fall outside the FSIS categories.

The FDA oversees most of the remaining food supply. A warning about a food outside the three FSIS categories generally comes from the FDA rather than the USDA.

The split also points readers to the right place to check. Someone trying to confirm whether a packaged meat or poultry item is affected should start with FSIS notices. Someone checking on a food outside those categories should look to the FDA instead.

A USDA recall is a company's action to remove meat, poultry or processed egg products from commerce because they may be unsafe or mislabeled. The Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), the USDA agency that oversees those products, publishes the notice that tells the public what is affected.

The key word is commerce. A recall targets product that is still moving through distribution or still available to buyers. The point is to pull that product back before more of it is sold or eaten.

Two kinds of problems can lead to a recall. One is safety, meaning the food itself may pose a hazard to the people who eat it. The other is labeling, meaning the package does not accurately describe what is inside. A labeling problem alone can be enough to prompt a recall.

A USDA recall applies when a meat, poultry or processed egg product is still in commerce, and a public health alert applies when it probably is not. That availability question is the main factor separating the two notices issued by the Food Safety and Inspection Service, or FSIS.

When product is still in commerce, a recall has work to do in the marketplace. Product may be sitting in warehouses, in distribution centers or in store display cases. The company responsible for it has to get it back. The FSIS notice tells the public about a removal that is under way.

A public health alert fits a different situation. The window for taking the product off sale has largely closed. Stores may have sold through their stock, or the item may no longer be offered. A removal from commerce would find little or nothing left to collect. The remaining concern sits in kitchens, refrigerators and home freezers.

Every meat, poultry or processed egg product recall announced through the U.S. Department of Agriculture is a voluntary action by the company responsible for the product. The Food Safety and Inspection Service, the USDA agency that oversees those foods, does not have mandatory recall authority.

That means FSIS cannot order a company to pull its product. What it can do is request a recall. When FSIS makes that request, the decision to remove the product from commerce still formally rests with the company.

The agency has other tools if a company does not act. FSIS can detain product, which keeps it from moving further through commerce. It can also seize product. And it can withdraw inspection services from the establishment involved.

The establishment number is the plant code printed inside the round USDA mark of inspection on meat, poultry and processed egg product packaging. It usually appears as "EST." followed by a number. FSIS notices list this code to identify the plant behind an affected product.

The number points to the facility where the food was produced or processed under federal inspection. It does not identify the brand. A single plant can pack products for several different labels. A single brand can also come from more than one plant. Two packages with the same name on the front can therefore carry different establishment numbers.

The mark itself is a small circle printed on the label. It can sit on the front, the back or the side, depending on the package design.

The FSIS recalls and public health alerts page is the official place to read USDA notices about meat, poultry and processed egg products. Questions can go by phone to the USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline at 1-888-MPHotline (1-888-674-6854).

The Food Safety and Inspection Service, the USDA agency that regulates those three product categories, publishes the page. Recalls and public health alerts are both posted there. A reader can check either kind of action in one place, without looking up a separate source for each.

Each notice spells out how to identify the affected packages. It names the products and gives their package sizes and dates. It also lists the establishment number, which appears inside the USDA mark of inspection as "EST." followed by a number. The full notice, rather than a shortened summary of it, shows every affected item at once.

The package itself offers a second clue. Meat, poultry and processed egg products inspected by FSIS carry the round USDA mark of inspection. That mark ties the product to FSIS oversight. A package bearing it is the kind of item a USDA notice can cover.

Egg items need a closer look. FSIS jurisdiction names processed egg products specifically. The wording of a notice, together with the agency that issued it, shows which category an egg item falls into.

For anyone reading a food safety headline, the issuing agency is the first detail to check. A USDA notice points to meat, poultry or processed egg products. Any other food is most likely an FDA matter.

The scope is narrow. A USDA recall applies only to the three product categories FSIS regulates: meat, poultry and processed egg products.

The FSIS notice serves as the public record of the recall. It names the company involved, describes the affected products and states the reason for the action. It also gives the recall class, which reflects the level of health risk.

Each notice is specific. It lists the product names, package sizes and dates that define which items are covered. It also includes the establishment number from the USDA mark of inspection, which ties the product to the inspected establishment that produced it.

That precision limits the recall's reach. Only the items matching the details in the notice are part of the recall. Other products from the same company, or the same type of food sold under different labels, are not covered unless the notice lists them.

Responsibility for the removal sits with the company. The business that made or distributed the product takes it back from the market, and FSIS makes the action public through its notice.

A public health alert is a consumer warning from the Food Safety and Inspection Service about meat, poultry or processed egg products. It covers products that are likely no longer available for purchase but may still be in people's homes.

FSIS is the agency within the U.S. Department of Agriculture that oversees those three product categories. It turns to an alert in two distinct situations. Each one answers a different question about a potentially unsafe product.

The first question is where the product is. Food bought before a problem came to light can stay in a refrigerator, freezer or pantry after it has disappeared from store shelves. In that case, the people at risk are the households that already took it home, not the stores that once sold it. An alert is written for those households.

The second question is what the agency knows. FSIS issues an alert when it does not have enough information to request a recall. The alert lets the agency tell the public about a concern without having the basis it would need to ask a company to act.

An alert is a different kind of action from a recall. A recall is a company removing product from commerce. An alert is a public warning from FSIS itself, directed at consumers rather than at the supply chain.

FSIS posts its public health alerts on the same web page as its recall notices. Each notice identifies the affected items by product name, package size and dates. Readers can compare those details against what they have at home.

An alert does not declare a product safe. It reflects only that the item is likely no longer for sale. Anyone holding a product named in an alert should follow the instructions in the notice itself. Those instructions may tell consumers to throw the product away or return it as the notice directs.

That is why an alert speaks directly to consumers. Its aim is to reach people who bought the product earlier and may still have it, not to direct a company to clear shelves.

Availability is not the only branch in the decision. FSIS also turns to a public health alert when the information it holds is not sufficient to request a recall. Either way, the alert warns the public without a company removal action attached.

For a shopper reading the headline, the notice type works as a quick signal. A recall points to an item that may still be on sale and could be bought today. An alert points to an item that is likely no longer available for purchase.

An alert is not a sign that the product is safe to eat. It means only that the product is likely gone from stores. Some of it may still be sitting in homes.

FSIS assigns every meat, poultry or processed egg product recall to one of three classes based on the health risk of eating the product. Class I signals the most serious risk, and Class III the least.

Class I covers cases where there is a reasonable probability that eating the product will cause serious health consequences or death. The definition sets two bars at once. One is how likely harm is. The other is how severe that harm would be. A Class I recall involves a product that clears both.

Class II applies when there is a remote probability of adverse health consequences from eating the product. Both measures fall below the Class I standard. The chance of harm is described as remote rather than reasonable. The harm is described as adverse rather than serious or fatal. A remote probability is still a probability of harm.

Class III applies when eating the product will not cause adverse health consequences. It is the only class whose definition rules out adverse health consequences from eating. A recall can cover product that may be mislabeled as well as product that may be unsafe. A Class III recall removes product from commerce for a reason other than a risk from eating it. A labeling error that poses no health risk to the person eating the product fits this class.

The class measures the health risk of eating the product and nothing else. It does not show whether the product is still on store shelves. Other parts of the recall notice describe the affected product itself.

Public health alerts sit outside this three-tier system. FSIS does not assign a class to an alert. The missing class does not mean the product is safe to eat. It reflects that an alert is a different kind of notice from a recall, with no classification step attached.

A request from FSIS therefore comes with those options in reserve. If a company declines, the agency can still act against the product itself or against the plant's inspection.

The FDA works under a different rule. It has mandatory recall authority for most foods under the Food Safety Modernization Act. FDA jurisdiction covers most foods other than meat, poultry and processed egg products. Its mandatory power reaches most of the food supply outside FSIS oversight.

The split means two products in the same grocery cart can fall under different rules. A recalled bag of salad greens or jar of peanut butter falls under the FDA, which can compel a recall. A recalled package of ground beef or chicken sausage falls under FSIS, which can only request one.

For shoppers, the voluntary nature of a USDA recall does not signal a lower level of risk. The word "voluntary" describes how the recall began. The recall class assigned to it describes the health hazard. A Class I recall is still voluntary, even though it covers products with a reasonable probability of serious health consequences or death.

Many USDA recalls and public health alerts trace back to a short list of problems: the bacteria Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7, undeclared allergens, foreign material and misbranding. The cause named in a notice tells a consumer what kind of risk the product carries.

Listeria monocytogenes is a frequent concern in ready-to-eat foods such as deli meats, hot dogs and cooked sausages. People often eat those products without cooking them again. Any contamination that happens after processing can therefore reach the consumer directly. Listeria can also grow at refrigerator temperatures. Many other foodborne bacteria cannot. The illness it causes, listeriosis, poses the greatest danger to pregnant people, newborns, older adults and people with weakened immune systems.

Salmonella is most closely associated with raw poultry. It causes salmonellosis, an illness that typically brings diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps. Thorough cooking kills the bacteria. Cross-contamination from raw meat to cutting boards, hands or other foods can still spread it.

E. coli O157:H7 is a Shiga toxin-producing strain of the bacterium most often linked to ground beef. Grinding can move bacteria from the surface of the meat into the interior. Undercooking may then leave them alive. Some infections lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome, a condition that can cause kidney failure. Young children and older adults face the highest risk of that complication.

Undeclared allergens appear when a product contains an ingredient such as milk, eggs, wheat or soy that its label does not list. This can happen when a package ends up with the wrong label. It can also happen when a recipe changes and the label is not updated. For a person with a food allergy, eating the product can trigger a serious reaction.

Foreign material covers physical objects that should not be in food, such as pieces of plastic, metal, glass or rubber. These can cause choking, cuts to the mouth or dental injuries.

Misbranding is a labeling problem. It can mean the label misstates what is in the package or leaves out required information. An undeclared allergen is one form of misbranding. The category also covers errors that carry no allergy risk, such as an incorrect product name or missing label details.

FSIS notices list the establishment number alongside other identifying details. Those usually include the exact product name as it appears on the label, the package size or weight, and one or more dates. The dates can be a packing or production date, or a use-by or best-by date.

A match on the establishment number alone does not settle the question. The product name, package size and date also need to line up with the notice. A package from the named plant with a date outside the listed range may not be covered. A package with the right product name but a different plant number may not be covered either. A package with a matching name and plant number but a different package size may also fall outside the notice.

Food moved out of its original packaging loses these identifiers. Ground meat repackaged into freezer bags or deli meat moved into storage containers no longer carries the establishment number, the dates or the package size. In that case, the label cannot confirm a match with the notice.

Do not eat a meat, poultry or processed egg product named in a USDA recall or public health alert. Check the refrigerator and the freezer, then throw the product away or return it as the notice directs.

Those steps are identical for both kinds of notice. The difference between a recall and an alert concerns store shelves, not kitchens. Once a product is in a home, the label on the notice does not change what the household should do with it.

Start with the freezer. Frozen meat and poultry can sit at home for a long time after purchase. A product that left stores before any notice appeared may still be in a freezer drawer. That is the situation a public health alert is meant to reach.

Then move to the refrigerator, where fresh and ready-to-eat meat and poultry are usually kept. A notice can name refrigerated products as well as frozen ones.

Hold the package next to the notice before deciding anything. The notice names specific products, package sizes and dates, and only a package that matches those details is affected. A similar item with different details may fall outside the notice.

Check each package separately. Two packages of the same product can carry different sizes or dates, and a notice may cover one without covering the other.

Read the instructions in that particular notice once a package matches. Some notices tell consumers to throw the product away. Others say it may also be returned to the place of purchase. One notice's instructions do not necessarily carry over to the next.

Keep a matched product out of every meal. Do not cook it into a larger dish. Do not give it to someone else. Do not set it aside to decide about later. A matched product has two destinations: the trash or the store, as the notice directs.

A recall notice on the page states its class, from Class I through Class III. A public health alert posted there carries no class. Checking for that label is a quick way to tell which kind of action a listing describes. On a recall, the class also shows how FSIS rated the health risk.

The page lists only USDA-regulated foods. A notice about a product outside meat, poultry and processed egg products will not appear there. Those notices come from the FDA, which regulates most other foods.

The hotline offers a direct phone line to USDA for questions about meat, poultry and processed egg products. Its number is published in two forms. One spells part of it in letters as 1-888-MPHotline. The other gives the digits, 1-888-674-6854. Both versions dial the same line.

Keeping the package nearby during a call makes it possible to read out the product name, package size, dates and establishment number. Those are the same details FSIS uses in a notice to define which products it covers.

#5347. ‘Dillon Brooks? On Kalshi? Hell nah’: LeBron James sues the sports betting app whose AI version of him said it

In an ad, LeBron James sits in an NBA locker room in a No. 23 jersey with “Bron” printed across the back, scrolling through bets on his phone. He stops on a photo of Phoenix Suns forward Dillon Brooks, one of his best-known on-court rivals. “Dillon Brooks? On Kalshi? Hell nah,” he says, in James’ voice.

Except it isn’t James. It’s an AI-generated version of him, made by a two-person startup to sell a sports betting app called Bron. And James, who has an exclusive endorsement deal with Kalshi-rival Polymarket, is now suing.

King James has been at the center of many notable brand deals—spanning massive contracts with Nike, Sprite, and of course, Polymarket. But the NBA’s oldest active player, and his company LBJ Trademarks LLC, is accusing the app’s creator PlayVision Inc. of exploiting his likeness in an AI-generated ad—and using an alleged affiliation with the star to promote itself.

The suit, filed on Nov. 17 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York against the app’s parent company and its cofounders Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby alleges trademark infringement, false endorsement and false advertising. According to the complaint, the founders are PlayVision’s only employees, and it includes  an argument that the company deliberately chose the name Bron and used an AI version of James in its marketing to capitalize on his global recognition.

“The word ‘Bron’ has no dictionary definition and no special meaning in the context of sports analytics, wagering, or artificial intelligence,” the filing read. “Rather, in the context of anything sports-related, it refers to only one man—LeBron James.”

The lawsuit describes the campaign as an effort to create the false impression that James was affiliated with the app, which offers sports betting research tools—including bet tracking and odds comparisons. The complaint is seeking an injunction preventing the defendants from using James’ name and likeness, repayment of profits generated through the alleged infringement, and compensatory and punitive damages.

The complaint accuses the appmakers of violating James’ right of publicity under a 1903 New York law, stemming from a woman whose portrait appeared without her consent on 25,000 posters of Franklin Mills flour—and led to New York State requiring written consent to use a person’s likeness in ads. It also leans on a far newer law: New York’s first-in-the-nation rule signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul in Dec. 2025 that requires ads to disclose when they use an AI-generated “synthetic performer.”

The Bron ad carried no such disclosure, the complaint says.

“The integrity of NBA competition—and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play—is of paramount importance to the league, its players and its fans,” the complaint stated.

Gupta posted the ad to his X account on Nov. 2 with the caption “Where is Bron?”—and the AI figure, shown mostly from behind, copies James’ build and tattoos. It speaks in what the suit says is a synthesized version of his voice. Another scene shows a rider in a Bron cap on a New York City subway car stopped at 14 Street.

The complaint says James’ betting deals, first with DraftKings and now with Polymarket, have focused on football, not basketball, because the NBA bars players from betting on NBA games. By showing him scrolling NBA player props and naming Kalshi, the suit argues, the ad “falsely communicates that Mr. James wagers, or considers wagering, on NBA games and NBA player performance.”

“The Ad catapulted the Bron App from obscurity to controversy, with the Ad gaining a million views within a day—exactly as Defendants intended,” the complaint read. “But Mr. James has no affiliation with Defendants or their product. Defendants’ intentional use of artificial intelligence to steal Mr. James’s name and likeness was instead an unlawful effort to trade on Mr. James’s identity to enrich Defendants.”

The suit alleges the founders built the ad to provoke James. “Defendants calculated that the value of that attention would exceed the cost of any legal consequences, and they treated the violation of Mr. James’s rights as a marketing expense,” it reads.

PlayVision, a California-based company founded in 2025 by Gupta and Zoghby, initially developed AI software designed to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans. Describing itself as “AI moneyball for sports,” the company later launched Bron as an app that marketed itself as a sports analytics and betting research platform—but by spring 2026, it pivoted to consumer betting. The Bron app pulls recommended wagers from more than 150 sportsbooks and prediction markets. It is free to download: Bron Pro costs $29.99 a month or $249.99 a year.

PlayVision and the Bron app did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune.

And according to the complaint, Gupta responded to a cease and desist letter from James’ team on Nov. 5 by suggesting the app would adopt a new name. However, the company had not announced a replacement name when James filed the suit. On Nov. 16, he wrote on X: “We found Bron. Apparently, the lawyers found it too. Find out our new name Wednesday. 10 AM PT.”

At 10:02 AM PT on Wednesday, Gupta posted another video on X showing they had renamed the app to Evie.

The filing, however, still said that’s too little, too late.

“They continue to use the Bron name to this day, prolonging the controversy for as long as it continues to generate attention for the Bron App and violating Mr. James’s rights to serve their marketing goals,” the filing read. “And even a belated name change now would not remedy the exploitation of Mr. James’s brand and goodwill that allowed Defendants to garner these millions of views and attention in the first place.”

The suit also identifies fellow NBA star and former James’ teammate Luka Doncic as another player whose likeness appeared in the app’s campaign. Doncic separately sent the company a cease-and-desist letter, according to the filing.

But that hasn’t intruded on the app’s stride. In response to the suits sent their way, Gupta posted on X—this time, an AI image of the two cofounders sitting in an empty courtroom with the caption: “Taking this to another court. We ain’t done yet.”

#5346. Study: 403 U.S. data centers rival Denmark’s carbon emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

The researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for new clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

#5345. Your Business Is Saving Hours With AI. So Why Are Customers Still Waiting?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Before investing in another automation tool, ask whether the time you’re saving is actually improving your customers’ experience.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recently, while working on a healthcare client’s project, my team encountered a problem that had nothing to do with our ability to do the work.

We needed access to the client’s digital platforms. What should have been a straightforward process became a series of emails, permission issues, authentication problems and confusion over which accounts controlled what.

The actual work wasn’t the obstacle. Getting everything in place so we could do the work was.

I’ve encountered different versions of this problem throughout my consulting career. Teams have the expertise. The technology exists. Everyone wants to move forward. Yet progress stalls because the underlying process is more complicated than anyone realized.

It made me think about how businesses are approaching artificial intelligence. We’re investing in tools that promise to make work faster, but how often do we stop to examine what’s slowing the business down in the first place?

When entrepreneurs think about productivity, they naturally focus on the time employees spend completing tasks. How quickly can we produce a report? How much time can we save creating content? Can AI respond to routine inquiries? Those are reasonable questions.

But consider what happened in the healthcare project. Automating another task wouldn’t have resolved who owned the account, who could authorize access or how the team should handle authentication. Those were process and accountability problems.

This is why I believe every business should examine its workflows before investing heavily in automation.

I’ve previously written about why entrepreneurs should examine workflows before hiring more employees. The same principle applies to technology.

If responsibilities are unclear and information is scattered, automation may simply help a flawed process move faster.

A business owner might celebrate saving 20 hours a week. The customer is asking a different question: Why am I still waiting?

That gap is easy to overlook because internal performance metrics don’t always reflect the customer experience.

Imagine improving the speed of customer service responses while leaving the underlying resolution process unchanged. Customers might receive answers sooner but still wait days for their problems to be addressed.

The business reports an efficiency improvement. Customers experience little difference. I see a similar disconnect in marketing. Companies sometimes invest in generating more leads without examining what happens after those leads arrive.

As I explored in my article about why businesses can spend more on marketing while attracting fewer customers, more activity doesn’t automatically translate into better commercial results. The lesson applies to AI as well.

Measure the outcome, not just the activity that produced it.

One thing I’ve learned from managing complex projects is that technology cannot replace clear ownership. Someone still needs to make decisions, resolve exceptions and take responsibility when something goes wrong.

Before automating a process, I ask three questions:

If those answers aren’t clear, technology isn’t the first thing I would fix.

For example, automated appointment reminders can reduce administrative effort. But if patients cannot easily reschedule or reach someone when they need help, the experience remains frustrating.

The same is true for sales, onboarding and service delivery. Customers appreciate convenience, but they also want confidence that someone is paying attention.

This may be the most important question entrepreneurs should ask about AI.

Saving time is only valuable when businesses put that time to better use. This is the AI productivity trap: Faster work doesn’t necessarily mean faster growth. The real opportunity lies in using that efficiency to improve customer relationships, solve problems and create measurable business value.

Suppose a new system saves your team 10 hours every week. What do you do with that time? Do you reinvest it in customer relationships? Improve service quality? Reduce expenses? Give employees more opportunities to solve problems that technology cannot handle?

Or does that time simply disappear into additional meetings and administrative work? The answer matters.

In my earlier Entrepreneur article about why business growth doesn’t always improve profitability, I discussed the importance of looking beyond top-line results. Productivity deserves the same scrutiny.

An efficient business isn’t necessarily a profitable one, and a productive team isn’t automatically delivering a better customer experience.

Entrepreneurs need to decide how efficiency gains will create value before assuming they will.

My advice is simple: Choose one process that repeatedly creates problems. It might be customer onboarding, appointment scheduling, account access, proposal approvals or resolving support requests. Follow that process from beginning to end.

Talk to the people involved. Identify where information gets lost, approvals stall or responsibilities become unclear. Then ask whether the problem requires automation at all.

Sometimes the answer is a better system. Sometimes it’s eliminating an unnecessary approval. Sometimes it’s giving one person clear responsibility for following through.

Make one change, measure what happens, and expand what works. You may discover that the most valuable improvement costs considerably less than another software subscription.

I’m enthusiastic about what AI can do for entrepreneurs, especially smaller businesses competing with organizations that have significantly greater resources. But I don’t believe adopting more technology automatically makes a company more competitive.

The healthcare project reinforced something I’ve seen repeatedly: Even capable teams with good technology can struggle when the underlying process isn’t working.

Your customers don’t see how many hours you save internally. They notice whether you deliver what you promised, respond when they need you and make their lives easier.

Before celebrating how much faster your business has become, make sure your customers can feel the difference.

We needed access to the client’s digital platforms. What should have been a straightforward process became a series of emails, permission issues, authentication problems and confusion over which accounts controlled what.

The actual work wasn’t the obstacle. Getting everything in place so we could do the work was.

#5344. Washington convinces 4 AI chatbots to plan terror attacks as flawed patches across the internet breaks banks and airlines

Government investigators posing as would-be attackers got ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok to produce workable plans for a bombing and an attack on the power grid, each in less than 12 hours, according to a Government Accountability Office report released Wednesday.

The report landed at the end of a week in which AI has already been tied to real damage, though nobody has blamed a terrorist. On Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton linked an outage on the NSA’s classified network to patching, saying institutions are patching “because these vulnerabilities have been identified,” on Fox Business. “That is what has happened at the NSA today,” he said. Fox Business reported the flaws in question were in PHP, which AI-assisted researchers found over the summer. Testifying before the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday, Clayton called the week’s breakdowns at Microsoft, the FAA, banks and the NSA “separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes,” according to The Washington Post.

“If Congress does not act, it is a question of when—not if—a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat who requested the report, said, per Nextgov. She plans to hold at least one hearing on AI safety early next year.

Every chatbot’s safeguards were triggered, and testers got around them “by using common safeguard-bypassing techniques,” GAO wrote. Two of the chatbots produced plans for an improvised explosive device meant to cause mass casualties, aimed at a hotel parking garage and a convention center. The other two gave instructions for attacking electrical substations, naming specific drone and firearm models and how to buy them.

“We got the nefarious information that we were after. So, in this case, those safeguards didn’t work,” said Kevin Walsh, GAO’s director of IT and cybersecurity. The report cites a June statement in which Anthropic said every safeguard used in the industry is vulnerable to jailbreaks.

The caveats matter. Each platform was tested on a single scenario, and Walsh said the testing doesn’t represent “a statistically significant sample.” GAO won’t say which chatbot produced which plan. It defines “viable” as meaning a person “would likely be able to carry out the actions,” and it didn’t test every step. GAO found some details were wrong: in one case, a chatbot’s map put roads in the wrong places. OpenAI told ABC the testing “took place months ago on an older version of ChatGPT,” and Google said it used “earlier models.” Anthropic wrote that it doesn’t dispute “a determined tester can get harmful content” from its system.

GAO made no recommendations. The report doesn’t address AI’s role in finding software flaws, or patching.

Bug hunters have logged 100,222 software vulnerabilities so far this year, more than double 2025’s total, according to a VulnCheck count that crossed 100,000 on Nov. 13, The Register reported. “There’s no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we’re seeing,” VulnCheck’s Josh Bressers said. Microsoft fixed 1,094 flaws on its Nov. 10 Patch Tuesday, after 1,474 in October.

Each one is a patch someone has to install. “Emergency patches go into core infrastructure within hours, often without the full testing cycle,” Yuval Itzchakov, CTO and co-founder of the offensive security company A Security, told Reuters. “That speed and scale of change is itself a source of failure.”

The PHP flaws show the squeeze. AI-assisted teams at OpenAI, Wiz and Calif found bugs affecting every PHP version released in the last decade, Fortune reported when they were disclosed Oct. 21. PHP runs 70% of websites, according to Wiz. The PHP Foundation told sites to patch immediately or go offline until they could.

Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, extended the patching explanation to the rest of the week. “If you’re trying to patch 10 or 12 in a single week, you have these kind of outages,” he said on CNN, per a transcript.

The companies, the NSA and the FAA blamed AI on the record. The NSA said its outage came during “scheduled routine maintenance,” per Politico. The FAA blamed legacy equipment, and asked whether its upgrades caused the ground stop, it said “No.” Microsoft blamed its outage in part on a bug introduced in a July update, and Chase blamed a software bug.

Most of the flaws AI is finding will never be used in an attack. Only about 1.4% of this year’s vulnerabilities are in VulnCheck’s catalog of known exploited flaws. They still have to be patched.

Chris Krebs, former director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, said on NBC’s TODAY that the outages weren’t attacks but companies finding vulnerabilities with AI and patching them. “The patching is not done. The vulnerability discovery is not done,” he said. “The next 12 to 18 months are going to be a bumpy ride.”

#5343. Former UW AI researchers Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin raise $110M for AI startup Noeri

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 10:38 am

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company said.

It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company said.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.
